subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF MINISTER'S STATEMENT CONCERNING IMMIGRANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration regarding that most unfortunate, foolish and unacceptable statement of his which he made to a Liberal meeting. I understand he indicated in a statement attributed to him that immigrants who may antagonize native born Canadians should not be brought into the country. On what basis could the minister make such a statement, and to which countries was he referring, keeping in mind that with that statement alone he has destroyed any credibility of this government respecting immigration, and in fact has almost destroyed the work of the joint Senate and House of Commons committee which travelled the country seeking the views of all citizens regarding immigration?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF MINISTER'S STATEMENT CONCERNING IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. I would have thanked him a lot more if he had taken the trouble, as most members of the press did, knowing my attitude to immigrants, to check what I said before spreading across the country a false and malicious statement. I most assuredly did not make that statement and, as has been my experience in talking to any group, I make certain that everything I say is put down on tape.
[Mr. Speaker.)
I indicated that we had benefited in Canada greatly as a result of the immigrant population. In many cases these immigrants came here not only to receive the many benefits of Canada but they have in fact been beneficial to Canadians. I said that my predecessor, for example, had indicated we were now in the process of screening out some people who would take jobs that ordinarily Canadians could handle. The point I was endeavouring to make was that we would have them feeling antagonistic toward immigrants if we brought in large numbers of immigrants to take jobs away from Canadians, jobs that Canadians could fill. That would have the effect of making Canadians feel antagonistic toward them, and that is the last thing that I want to see happen.
Then, I went on to reiterate that in many, many instances these people came in as entrepreneurs, not to take jobs away from Canadians but in fact to create jobs for Canadians. If the reporter present on that occasion had seen fit to report all of my statement, I think this unfortunate report would not have received the publicity it did. I want to say that I am particularly appreciative of CJOH in Ottawa, which took the time and made the effort to bring a cameraman and crew to my house because that station did not believe this minister of immigration would make that kind of a statement. The reporters at that station at least saw fit to seek an explanation.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance may I direct a question to the acting Prime Minister or the acting Minister of Finance. But we are now talking politics and it is a good start for his electoral campaign to make such a fuss. As a Quebec member, I wish him the best of luck because I know he is taking on a very difficult job. According to the comments I received this week, he will have a lot to account for to the Quebec people as he will certainly have to face over there the same ultimatums he was presented with, here, in this Chamber. He has accepted a most difficult task, this is why he has my sympathy and I wish him good luck.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to my hon. friend and colleague with mixed emotions which I am sure are shared by all members, some of which have already been expressed. I certainly regret his departure from the House of Commons. If not the most colourful and dynamic member of the House, he has certainly been among the most colourful and dynamic. His rising to speak in this chamber always assured that the seats were rapidly filled in order to listen to his fiery and effective presentation.
On the other hand, it is heartening to realize that the hon. member still has a sense of purpose and the enthusiasm to enter the lists in the Province of Quebec, and that when other politicians may be thinking of retiring he is taking on a new challenge in his native province. In the more than ten years he has spent in the House he was worked effectively not only for his own constituency but for the people of Canada. He has held a number of very important portfolios through which he has had considerable impact upon the people and the institutions of the country. He can be assured that he is leaving the House with the knowledge that his contribution has been substantial. All I can say is, we wish him well and good luck in his new endeavour. It may be that, when he has completed his assignment in the National Assembly, we can look forward to seeing him back again in the House of Commons.

It is my obligation to accept officially the resignation of the hon. member for Langelier, but before doing so I should like to add a few words and extend to him my personal thanks. The hon. member for Langelier is a very distinguished member of parliament who, in spite of his spirit,

The hon. member has distinguished himself by being a passionate and devoted fighter for the French fact in Canada, an endeavour which has stood him in good stead among his countrymen as well as among all members of the House, regardless of how heated the battle may have been. His clear understanding of that fact, and his passionate devotion to it, have served all Canadians during his time in this House. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to raise a point of order at this time. I am sorry that the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) is not here. I was looking for him on Friday, but he was not here then either. This matter occurred on Thursday evening and relates to his activities in the House as chief government whip.
I want to bring this point of order to your attention because I think the actions of the hon. member for St. Boniface clearly reflect upon the responsibilities and duties of each and every one of the members of parliament, regardless of the side of the House on which we sit. I refer to the fact that the chief government whip-and this has been my observation-has been keeping an attendance record, I think particularly of members of the opposition.
I rise at this point because in his remarks last Thursday evening, as reported at page 347 of Hansard, during the course of a speech being made at the time by my colleague from Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie), he mentioned the fact that he had been keeping a record of attendance and could establish when members of our party were here or were not here. The implication in his remark, Mr. Speaker, is that if by chance a member on this side did not happen to be in the House of Commons at any particular time he was not performing the tasks for which he was elected. Personally I, and I think certainly Your Honour as Speaker of the House presiding over our deliberations, would be most anxious to make sure that there is no reflection cast on the carrying out of the duties and responsibilities of members of parliament. I say to the hon. member for St. Boniface, if he reads this record, that all of us
October 25, 1976

are obliged to make our declaration, as is provided for, respecting our attendance and the carrying out of our responsibilities in order to receive our emolument as members of parliament. We all have responsibilities to our constituents.
The hon. member for St. Boniface's own colleagues have been saying publicly that part of our duties as members involves getting out to our constituencies. We have committee responsibilities. We have responsibilities as members of parliamentary delegations. The mere fact that we are not sitting in this House on a particular day or for a particular period of time should not, with respect, be interpreted as being some sort of abdication of our responsibilities as members of parliament.
The reason I raise this point, Mr. Speaker, is that it seems to me that as Speaker of the House, as the chief magistrate of the House, there should be some direction from yourself with respect to the keeping of attendance by any member for a purpose which is inconsistent with the rights and responsibilities of a member of parliament. If 1 may quote what the hon. member for St. Boniface said:
I will prove that you are never here five days a week and I have got the records right here. Anybody who wants to see them 1 have them right here.
I say that those words are in fact a very serious reflection on the attendance of members of this House and on the carrying out of their responsibilities. I ask Your Honour whether you would please give consideration to making the direction that the chief government whip cease and desist from carrying out this schooltime attendance proposition of his. If he wants to keep attendance let him keep it of his own members. They have a lot to answer for themselves.

Mr. Speaker, 1 think the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) would prefer to reply to that himself. 1 might say that the reason he was unavailable on Friday was that he was having a serious operation on his jaw. I hear some hon. members opposite laughing. It is not a humorous matter. We are not children here. We should be able to recognize a serious problem which occurs to backs, jaws, arms. That sort of thing does happen.
How was that recorded in the book? How are his actions recorded in the book?

1 might point out that the same kind of remark from the hon. member was the reason the whip made the reply he did. Possibly the interchange between the two hon. members should be discussed. 1 think the whip could set the matter straight, and certainly we should hear the total story.

This point is raised by way of a point of order and it has been replied to. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) may have something to add to it. I say "scarcely ever" only because it might be possible to convince the Chair that they could in some way be in order, but they are almost always totally irrelevant to the matter being debated, to start with, and possibly out of order on a number of other grounds.
Private Members' Public Bills While the Chair could never do anything to interfere with note-keeping by any member of the House-because after all that is a personal exercise for any member of the chamber to undertake-the use of it in debate would, in my view, be extremely questionable so far as any reflection on the personal performance of any member is concerned. I fail to see how that could be in order, in the first place, in terms of relevancy; and in the second place it likely would be very close to this kind of personal reflection upon the conduct of a member that has traditionally been ruled out of order. Therefore, while the practice cannot be prevented, I fail to see how it could ever be used at all in the course of debates in this chamber.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before beginning my remarks, I would like to tell the House how much I regret Mr. Marchand's (Langelier) departure. However, I am convinced that every one recognizes in him a dedicated man with an honest mind and very clear ideas. I am also convinced that with all those qualities, he will offer the National Assembly of Quebec what it might be lacking, that is a political judgment which goes beyond the boundaries of Quebec, but which considers and analyses its problem in the light of the international situation.
Mr. Speaker, I want want to congratulate both my colleagues the member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance) and the member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) for their answer to the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. The quality of their interventions has demonstrated how serious and efficient can be the participation of young members in this House.
Mr. Speaker, a year ago, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced to the Canadians the decision of the government to establish controls on prices and incomes. In his comments on the Speech from the Throne, the Prime Minister reiterated his faith in the anti-inflation program and his will to

maintain it until 1978 if the economic situation of the country so requires.
I do not want to mention statistics here. It has been done several times and they indicate that in 12 months the dangerous inflationary pressure has diminished. Despite statements from opposition parties despite protests from unions and from certain businessmen who showed precious little enlightenment in spite of the importance of their role, I believe that price and income controls are accepted by most Canadians and that this three year program will succeed in breaking up inflation psychosis. I reiterate my support for the program, so much so that inflation still remains the most serious among the threats to the economic stability in this country.
I would now like to talk about one of those problems closely related to that of inflation: the employer-employee relations issue. Demoralizing effects of inflation do not affect only the economy; they also are a threat to the very nature of our institutions. Our collective bargaining system was seriously shaken by the inflationary wave of the last few years. Collective bargaining now takes place in a tense climate, and labour relations are suffering from it. Before price and wage controls, wage demands had become increasingly more contrary to the reality of economic growth, of productivity, unemployment and international competition.
In Canada, while the production increase was only 2 per cent and that of wages reached 18 per cent, the wage increase in the United States at the same time did not go over 9 per cent while productivity rose to 5 per cent. In West Germany, productivity went up by 7 per cent and wages by 8 per cent.
After having appealed without avail to the good faith of all Canadians, the government decided in 1975 to set price and income controls. While inflation has been reduced to a still unacceptable but more tolerable rate and the economic recovery is well under way, the fight is far from being won. The reduced rate of the productivity increase occurring at the same time as higher wage settlements jeopardizes the competiveness of our industries, reducing the attraction of this country for the establishment of new undertakings. At the present time, the needs of new investments is heavily felt but the climate of our labour relations is not propitious.
Thus Quebec Industry and Commerce Minister Guy St-Pierre stated at the beginning of October 1976, and I quote:
Quebec has lost several industrial projects as a result of an unprecedented number of conflicts. It is impossible for me to ask for new capital with such results; the present uneasiness destroys our efforts.
At the level of industrial policy Canada is now leading for men-days lost as a result of strikes or lockouts. Thus loss of time due to work stoppages as a result of strikes and lockouts reached 1,183,080 men-days June last; there were 248 work stoppages which affected 190,197 workers. The increasing number of lost working days is prejudicial to all those concerned and impede a satisfactory development of the economy.
It is absolutely necessary to improve the atmosphere of our labour-management relations if we want to avoid increased
October 25, 1976

social tensions and if we want to improve the productivity of Canadian industry and keep our competitive position on the international markets, thus attracting new investments to our country.
We must now consider the very important problem of labour-management relations and steer them along a new course. Labour-management relations should develop in a more cooperative less antagonistic context, especially when the anti-inflation program will no longer be applied. Consequently, it is incumbent on the government to create the atmosphere which can help us look constantly for new means to boost productivity and create better working relations.
The government was aware of that problem in the Speech from the Throne when it declared that the improvement of labour-management relations is an essential pre-condition to economic stability. The government still considers the collective bargaining system to be one of the best ways of ensuring fair wages and of determining the working conditions in a democratic society; it does not think that the solution is to be found in excessive restriction of collective bargaining rights. However, as the rules of the game of the present Canadian society are quite different from what they were a few years ago, the government thinks that it is important to develop better mechanisms for settling disputes.
Consequently, the government proposes to work with the provinces and with labour and business communities to develop a number of initiatives aimed at improving labour-management relations. It intends, among other things, to establish a collective bargaining information centre which will offer objective data on the economy and compensation to all parties. Consequently, as union members will have all pertinent data concerning the operations of such or such economic sector, they will be able to avoid making extravagant wage claims which do not take into account the economic situation of the enterprise, which threaten its evolution and even, in certain cases, its survival.
Employees should become increasingly aware that the possibility of permanent employment depends on the viability and profitability of the company and that, on the long term, constant increases in real salary can only come from better productivity. Moreover, the government aims at encouraging workers in each plant to participate more in decisions concerning their working conditions. We must realize that the situation of workers has changed; today's average worker is more educated and more socially aware than ever before and he is less and less willing to accept unconditionally his role as a worker.
In the last few years, the concept of industrial democracy has reached beyond collective bargaining of working conditions. The modern worker wants a more satisfying work experience, which means that he wants to free himself from monotonous and repetitive work, from the pressures of the assembly line, and wants to have some sort of motivation and a sense of personal achievement. On the other hand, management must be aware of this social evolution and be more open-minded in the future.
The Address-Mr. B. Loiselle
In view of the present economic situation, the techno-structure must take into account the new strength relationship between the various production factors. While in the past the capital factor was the main element in all decision making processes, in view of the increasingly stable capacity of our economy to produce the savings that it needs, this factor has been replaced by the manpower factor; to have the most positive effect possible, this manpower must be increasingly recognized. This is what the techno-structure must do; this is the challenge that it must face. Should we not think of making companies more aware of their responsibilities for employee training, employment security and quality of the work environment? Should we not also think of including, as part of new mechanisms to encourage motivation, an increasing participation of employees in company management and profit sharing?
The Conservatives will certainly rebel against this suggestion, but there have been interesting cooperative management experiences in certain European countries. In many areas, labour participation in the decision making process and the greater satisfaction provided by participation have caused important increases in production as well as qualitative and other product improvements. Many foreign labour leaders think of the labour participation tactic as a means of giving something to union members in addition to their usual economic gains. The governments have encouraged the adoption of participation plans to reduce labour problems and promote industrial peace and economic stability. Employee participation in Europe operates under two main systems: participation of representatives or dicrect participation. Participation through representatives provides for the election or appointment of a certain number of employees to boards of directors or other organizations in charge of making the decisions within the corporation so as to represent the interests of workers.
Direct participation gives the employee control over organization and execution in his immediate work environment. Nearly all employees participate in the activities of the corporation and the first areas to be affected are generally at the lowest level in the working environment-those that are usually the most important ones for the employees themselves.
In the mid 1940s Scandinavia set up employee participation plans in the form of boards of workers within the plant. Since then, such boards have been a standard in most European countries. That is how since 1952 all plants in West Germany employing more than 20 workers are compelled under the law to put a board of workers elected by the employees in charge of monitoring the implementation of all regulations, laws and collective agreements applying to the workers. Boards also participate in drafting corporate by-laws on working hours, job allowances, the conduct and welfare of employees. Since 1971, all hirings, layoffs and promotions require prior agreement from the board of workers, and management must give the board full details on finance, production, sales, investment, working methods, proposed changes to the plants and other matters important to the employees.
Of course, all participation plans did not have the same success and in certain cases the workers in fact acquired only a

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. B. Loiselle
minimum power of decision-making. But one of the remarkable things about labour in Europe-except France and Italy-was the very small number of industrial conflicts reported in nearly a quarter of a century.
Although participation schemes have not been applied without involving some difficulties such, experiences suggest that it is possible to replace disputes by collaboration.
In our society, the main part of the dispute during negotiations derives from the perception held by parties of the negotiation process itself. Too much enphasis has been placed on what is called "distributive negotiations" in which each party is attempting to maximize its share. In such a situation, the gains made on one side are necessarily the losses of the other side. Such direct confrontation is toned down when parties are committed to an integral negotiation where both parties recognize they have common objectives and each one can help the other in reaching an end to their mutual advantage. Such a process assumes the sharing of information to allow for the exploration of common interest areas and the solution of common problems.
Although I have already mentioned it, I think it is important for me to repeat that confrontation should make way for cooperation. Both parties should realize that capital and labour are factors combining towards production. Each contributes to the productive process, each is entitled to a share of the product and each has an interest in business operation. One requirement for collaboration is consultation which should become the usual process and "emergency negotiations" ought to be avoided.
Basic issues such as the increasing anxiety brought about by the impact of automation and technological advances, cannot be resolved by a small negotiating team working under pressure for a few months every two or three years. We must wonder how collective bargaining, which is essentially a system used by opponents, could be adapted to make room for cooperation and increased consultation. The impact on collective bargaining of two related factors-namely constant and high job opportunities in the post war period and serious inflationary pressures-fanned the conflict between parties' interests and national interests. Under those conditions the competition between and within unions and employers caused negotiations to take place under a pressure which has, in its turn, resulted in higher wages and prices to an extent which cannot be totally explained by the present labour and market conditions. Consequently, public interest in collective bargaining is not restricted to reducing labour differences and its regrettable effect upon the community, as the public has become increasingly aware of the dangers inherent in the results of the collective bargaining process.
The challenge collective bargaining has now to meet is to preserve the advantages of a system which makes possible bilateral participation in the determination of working conditions, without imposing excessive social costs on the tax payers who would eventually refuse to assume them. The role of collective bargaining will become increasingly more complex as time goes by. It is not possible to return to the system where
[Mr. Loiselle (Chambly).J
unions and management were left alone and free to settle their conflicts, without consideration for wider economic, social and political consequences.
Collective bargaining will inevitably take place in a general context of economic and political realities which will impose constraints. As a matter of fact, the Canadian economy will be confronted very soon with a serious demographic problem: from the '80s and thereafter, we shall have to see to the maintenance of our economic development, to choose between massive influx of immigrants and the implementation or promotion of a more advanced technology. Increased productivity will depend on the realization of either of these conditions. However, both organized labour and management will have to make great efforts to ensure that this transition is carried out as smoothly as possible. A massive influx of immigrants would certainly result in social pressures, while the implementation of a new technology would certainly entail problems for unqualified workers. If these two powers do not cooperate to cope with this forthcoming problem, both our economy and the Canadian perspectives will suffer.
Mr. Speaker, another problem that should be given priority by our government and the Canadian people is the establis-ment of a new constitution or its patriation. Both levels of government, federal and provincial, should agree as soon as possible on an amendment formula. We must not forget that the constitution of Canada was adopted in 1867, over one hundred years ago. When it was passed, some sectors were within the exclusive jurisdiction of one or other levels of government. Since then Canadian government and society have been constantly changing and this is why the provinces tried, through various means, to extend their jurisdiction without raising questions about the sectors which were put under their jurisdiction. But the federal government itself, through what may be called indirect means or through the courts, never did stop encroaching on provincial jurisdictions, much more according to the problems to be solved than according to the legislation.
Such evolution, which sometimes created tension between the federal and provincial governments, flows from the very nature of our confederative system. Thus we should now be more innovative in establishing a new constitution as regards the amendments that should be introduced so that it can meet the present needs and be in line with the future evolution of Canada. In the light of recent experience in areas such as energy, communications, transport, where we could see that the rules of the game had changed, we should all try to do our best to find a common ground, a simple and acceptable formula which would among other things make it possible for the federal government to take action in some areas of provincial responsibility when the well being of the Canadian society as a whole is at stake-and I hope the partisans of provincial power will not become infuriated by this. This is what the federal government did recently when establishing a single price for oil, and a similar intervention will perhaps be needed in the future for electric power if the provinces disagree. Such
October 25, 1976

interventions should be possible under definite circumstances, which would ensure the respect and the integrity of provincial responsibility.
The amending formula must also provide for linguistic and cultural guarantees for French-speaking Canadians who-and this bears repeating-formed and still form the majority as the people who created this country. However, we must accept without discrimination that the former English-speaking minority grew in importance, particularly with the arrival of immigrants who, given the North American context, freely chose to join them. I think that the French-Canadian society which accepted this fact while giving in the most liberal manner possible the full rights of Canadian citizens, has the right to require from these same persons an absolute respect of their rights both in the area of language and culture. Therefore the amending formula must provide for such guarantees. Our former governments, without exception, were all defenders of individual and collective rights, of the equality of all citizens before the law no matter what their native language, religion or race.
Following recent and deplorable events, theories which are getting support seem to ignore the bases of the past policy, which I mentioned before, although it has succeeded in preserving our national unity. In a democracy like ours, there is place for any kind of theories and, incidentally, a member of the cabinet resigned recently to support a thesis which surely rallies a minority of Canadians but which is in total contradiction with the past and present policy of our government.
If I praise the courage of a man who takes such a decision in order to conform with his own integrity, I think at the same time that all members in the House, and I hope I am being heard from the other side, whatever party they belong to, who no longer agree with a policy on official languages granting equal rights to Canadians should rise and resign. Such a decision should not be taken for electoral considerations but rather for the consideration that each member has for himself.
As a Quebecer member, I reiterate my faith in Canadian society and the federal system; but it must be clear to everyone that this faith is not unconditional and that our people will only agree to participate in this great Canadian nation to the extent that they feel wanted and accepted with their own peculiarities, their own character as we, French Quebecers, respect and love our English Quebec brothers.

speechtext:
Before saying a few words on the subject of the Canadian penitentiary system I want to deal with a very urgent situation which exists in the Yukon, and I am glad to see the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) in his seat because it concerns an area of the Yukon with which he is familiar and which he has visited. I am speaking of the town of Faro and the tragic situation which now exists there with the miners having been on strike since June 30. One would think that the work force at that mine would be on strike because of a dispute with management, but that is not the case at all. Management and the union negotiated a collective bargaining agreement in April of this year and agreed on the amount of increase in wages that all classifications of workers would be receiving.
Then, as required by law, the matter was submitted to the Anti-Inflation Board, which rolled back the agreed upon wage rate to 12 per cent in the first year. Management and the union together put a joint request to the A IB, because of the seriousness of the rollback, to have the AIB review their decision. The AIB did just that. Their decision to roll back the increase to 12 per cent was reviewed and the decision was to allow an increase of 14 per cent. But that was still less than half of what the workers and management had agreed upon, and the matter, at the request of both management and labour, was referred to the administrator of the AIB, Mr. Tansley. This gentleman rolled back the wage rate from 14 per cent to 8 per cent.
The steelworkers's union at Anvil have taken the position throughout that the rollback was much too severe and that it was inexplicable. Both management and labour were aghast when the administrator brought in the decision of 8 per cent. The union has been on strike since June 30. There were approximately 500 workers at that mine and well over 100 have now submitted formal, written resignations and they and their families have moved out of the Yukon. The union has been on strike against the Anti-Inflation Board for almost three months. Let me emphasize that they have been on strike against the Anti-Inflation Board, not against management. Management wants to go back to work. It is prepared to stand by the negotiated collective bargaining agreement. The union also wants to go back to work, but it certainly does not want to go back at 8 per cent, which has no bearing on historical relationships, even in the area, where Cassiar asbestos miners in northern British Columbia are receiving a greater increase than the 8 per cent set by the administrator.
As I understand it, there are three stated objectives of the AIB, and certainly we hear them often enough from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and from members of the AIB. One is to contain the rate of inflation and reduce it, if possible, in the country. The second is to maintain production, and the third is to lower the rate of unemployment. All three objectives in this instance have been thwarted by the action of a board set up by the government. Production at that mine has

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Nielsen
ceased absolutely since June 30. Unemployment at that mine has gone up by the total work force of 500. It has had a ripple effect throughout the Yukon. It has put some 170 White Pass drivers out of work. It has cut their shipping schedule in half, and that has affected the work force in Vancouver, where the shipping originates and where it has its destination on the back haul. Other ripple effects in the Yukon have caused unemployment to climb alarmingly.
As far as containing the rate of inflation is concerned- because the biggest user of power in the Yukon is that mine and because section 10 of the Northern Canada Power Commission Act requires the system to be self-sustaining-the consumer will be expected to bear, unless the government introduces some relief legislation, the added costs of increased rates in order to pay for the revenue which is being lost because of this strike of the miners.
The other day when I questioned him in the House, the Minister of Finance said that the best thing the workers at Anvil could do would be to go back to work. To add confusion to the tragic situation created by the AIB, apparently with the full support of the government, we have a decision by the Canada Labour Relations Board, which falls under the jurisdiction of the minister, that the strike is a legal one, and the reasons given by the CLRB for declaring the strike a legal one is that the AIB interfered in the collective bargaining process. To my mind this surely is not what the government intends to happen with respect to the actions and activities of the AIB and the administrator. It is having the most serious and harmful effects on the economy of the Yukon. The economy of the Yukon is never going to recover from the three months of this strike. Revenues and wages are lost forever. The value to Canada of the production of that mine-which is not insignificant, I might add, as the minister well knows-is lost forever. It can never be made up.
All the Anti-Inflation Board has to do-and I am sure the government could urge upon the board a reconsideration of the matter-is to apply sensible standards in the north. I raised the matter when the legislation was before the House a year ago. You cannot apply southern standards to northern high-cost areas. You cannot apply the standards which exist in Toronto, Edmonton, Halifax or Vancouver to high-cost areas in the north. In the town of Faro a gallon of regular gasoline costs $1.25. Contrast that with the cost of gasoline in other localities in Canada. A gallon of home heating fuel in Whitehorse costs 64 cents. Compare that with fuel costs for home heating fuels in the rest of Canada. In Ottawa a two quart container of milk costs $1.09. Compare that with the $1.62 in Whitehorse. That was the price three weeks ago; it has probably gone up since then. In all fairness there is no way the guidelines set by the government under which the AIB operates should be applicable to an extremely high cost area such as the north.
Who is to blame the steelworkers for going out on strike against that AIB decision when we have to face these increased costs? People in the north cannot possibly bring up families and sustain themselves at a standard equivalent to

similar job holders in the south on a wage rate approaching the same amount, and yet the administrator's decision to roll it back to 8 per cent actually sets the wage rate of those miners lower than a comparable worker in southern Canada receives.
Another stated objective of the AIB is to contain prices. I have already given some examples of food prices in the Yukon. There was a famous preliminary report published by the chairman of the Food Prices Review Board many months ago with respect to food prices in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, and one of the chief recommendations in that report was that a further study be made into the cost of food in those areas. We have not seen hide nor hair of any indication that that second report will be forthcoming.
When we referred to the AIB the question of Northern Canada Power Commission rates going up in the case of the Yukon in one year by 78 per cent, we were told that the AIB has no jurisdiction. When we complained about CNT telephone rates going up-they escape me at the moment, but they are far in excess of the guidelines set down-we were told that the AIB would not take jurisdiction to inquire into those rates. The NCPC intends to increase the rate for electricity in Fort Smith in Northwest Territories by 56 per cent, and yet the AIB does nothing about containing those prices.
It seems to me that the other function of the AIB is failing miserably in so far as the two jurisdictions in the north are concerned. I would be urging-if it were not for the fact that I think it offends my approach to responsible government in the Yukon-the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) to instruct his commissioner in the Yukon to intervene with some back to work legislation similar to that passed in this House last Friday. However, I do not want to do that because if any constitutional initiative does exist, it should be taken up by our own Yukon legislative assembly.
That is one solution, and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development might take that under consideration. I am not suggesting that he direct his commissioner. I am suggesting he make the suggestion to his commissioner that that kind of approach might be considered by the Yukon legislative assembly.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

I question the merits of the Anti-Inflation Act if these types of increases are allowed to happen while the wages of workers are being tightly controlled.

Who can blame the miners of Anvil for going out on strike, not against management but against the AIB? That is having a savage effect on the economy, in my constituency at any rate.
While I have the time, I want to say a word or two about the Canadian penitentiaries system. I am glad to see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in his seat, because I am sure this concerns him. We set up a committee on October 6 because of the urgent situation that our leader thought existed in the country with respect to the administration of the Canadian penitentiaries system. He set up a special task force from among our own caucus to inquire into the Canadian penal system. The government, belatedly, saw that there was, in fact, need for such an inquiry. They decided to establish a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
I had talks with the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) as to the establishment of this committee and our participation in it. We want to participate in an impartial inquiry that will produce meaningful results. We want to participate in the parliamentary process that will produce an in-depth inquiry, not just into the maximum security penitentiaries in the country, where most of the trouble is receiving the headlines, but into the whole of the system. For that reason we decided to place the objective of our special caucus committee on the shelf and go along with the establishment of a parliamentary subcommittee to inquire into the very serious problems which now confront the system.
When I first had those discussions with the Solicitor General, the members of the subcommittee were discussed as being four Liberal members, four Conservative members, and one each from the NDP and Social Credit. In further discussions with the Solicitor General the following day, he informed me
The Address-Mr. Nielsen
that he was sorry if there was anything misleading, but he assumed in discussing those four, four, one and one figures that the Liberal party would have the chair. I went along with that after discussing it with my colleagues. It was done on the assumption that the subcommittee would be set up on the basis of five members from the Liberal party, four from the Conservative party, and one each from the NDP and Social Credit parties.
When the Solicitor General introduced his motion for the establishment of this subcommittee, I raised the matter of number of members. He reneged on the five, four, one and one figures. He would not give me a positive answer with regard to those numbers. He said, in effect, that the approval he got was for the normal representation in parliament. I hoped that what he meant was that it would be a simple majority for the Liberal party of five members, four from the Progressive Conservative party and one each from the NDP and Social Credit.

Our prison system is in a mess. There have been uprisings, hostage-takings, murders and suicides. Deplorable conditions exist in our Canadian penal system. It cries out for some kind of solution. The best summation that I have seen recently with regard to the situation that exists is in an article by Allan Fotheringham in the October 18 issue of Maclean's. It is carried under the headline "Canada does not have to execute people any more. It just sentences them to neglect." He goes into the background of the establishment and growth or malformation of the penal system in Canada since it was set up almost 140 years ago with the building of Kingston. The sadness is that the hypocrites do not realize they are hypocrites. The hypocrites are the Liberal members of parliament who give the impression they have abolished death from the land. It prefers to ignore the cruel reality. As the custodian responsible for the Canadian prison system, the Liberals have to answer for the fact that more than 11 inmates die every year in our prisons. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in this debate. At the outset I should like to add my good wishes to those already extended to the hon. member for Langelier (Mr. Marchand) and wish him well in his future endeavours in Quebec. I should also like, at this point, to congratulate the new Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) on his appointment. I wish him all the luck in the world. He faces a big challenge and many people across the country are counting on him. So far, relatively few requests have been made upon him but there was one made by my hon. friend from Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), the leader of our party, asking him to look into a situation at Cross Lake where the water supply was very bad. The people there had been seeking rectification of this situation for six years, through various former ministers, and I am very happy to note that the new minister saw fit to act promptly and rectify the situation. The people from Cross Lake send their thanks to him. I hope this is an example of the way in which the hon. gentleman intends to act in the future.
So, Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the minister on his new post and wish him all the luck in the world. Certainly, I shall offer him whatever help I can. Since he is not in the chamber today, I hope his colleagues will pass on my good wishes.
I should like to make a few suggestions regarding what I think the minister should do in the Indian Affairs department. First of all, there is the question of land claims in the Northwest Territories and Yukon in particular, and in general other claims by our native people all across the country. I think the minister should move a little faster in this area, especially in
The Address-Mr. Firth
those constituencies in which the native people would like to sit down around a table and discuss native claims. I consider the settling of these claims, particularly in the Northwest Territories, northern development. I suggest that once these claims have been settled we can move forward a little faster and deal with those problems that are of everyday concern to our native people and which are not receiving sufficient attention at this time.
Indian affairs and northern development are both under the jurisdiction of one department or ministry, and many times these two departments come into conflict. Therefore, I suggest that the minister should give serious consideration to dividing the department so that Indian affairs stand alone. It is an extremely important department and, as I mentioned previously, the minister has a great challenge in changing the attitudes of departmental officials and improving the image Canada has in the eyes of the rest of the world in regard to our treatment of our native peoples. I suggest northern development come within the Department of the Environment, or with fisheries or some other department, where there will not be so much conflict.
I would also suggest that the minister immediately hire capable native people from all across the country for very important decision-making positions within that department. At this time I do not think he would be able to name more than five or six native people who are in decision-making positions in the Indian Affairs Department. I do not have the figures with me, but I would be very surprised if there are more than five or six.
Another suggestion that I think would be useful is that the minister offer early retirement to some members of the department who have been there a long time and may not be doing quite such a good job as would some younger person who might be more effective. This would make the department more responsible to the native people of this country. As it is now, a lot of times it seems as though the department is more the enemy of the native people than their ally.
I would also suggest that another healthy move for the department to make is for it to be more co-operative with native organizations from all across this wonderful country of ours. These organizations have a better understanding of what the immediate problems are on the reserves, in different parts of the territories, and so on. Thus, the department will be more effective. The millions of dollars allocated to the department are really not reaching those areas where they can be spent effectively, and the suggestion I have made would, I think, help see that this money does get to the grass roots level where it would do most good. The minister faces a very big challenge, and many people are counting on him. With a majority government, and working with native organizations, I think the minister is in a good position to do a lot more for our native people than has been done in the past.
Talking of the past, Mr. Speaker, and of the effectiveness of previous ministers of the department, I should like to refer to what I think is a very scarey situation having to do with the sterilization of native women in the Northwest Territories.

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Firth
This example goes back to October 9, 1970, when the former leader of this party, Mr. David Lewis, the then hon. member for York South, asked a question of the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development as reported at page 16 of Hansard. It is now October, 1976, six years down the pipe, and still no answer has been received on this very important matter. Let me put the question on the record. The then hon. member for York South asked:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on a rather serious matter. Is the minister aware that a program of sterilization of native Eskimo women was apparently introduced in the Holman Island community on Victoria Island, that five women have been so sterilized and that some others are being considered? If he is aware, will he inform the House who authorized this unnecessary and inhuman program, in view of the availability of birth control methods?
The minister at that time was the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), and he answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I have no information on this problem. The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of his question, so I have had an investigation made but I have not yet received any report.
I am not aware that any authorization was given by my department. Health services in the Northwest Territories are under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I therefore asked one of my department's officers this morning to get in touch immediately with the representatives of the department of national health in order to determine whether any authorization had actually been given or whether the facts alleged by my hon. friend were correct.
As soon as I obtain further information, I shall be happy to inform the House, but, at this time, I do not believe that such an authorization was given. If such action took place it must have been because of some local or individual initiative, rather than under a government policy.
So at that date the Liberal government said it did not have a policy of sterilization of native women in the Northwest Territories. Although the question was asked six years ago, there has still been no answer. I have good reason to believe that a sterilization program has been continuing in the Northwest Territories and that a lot of people have been sterilized. People in the north, as well as myself, are asking for answers to a lot of questions.
I do have a few figures before me, Mr. Speaker, but they cover only a small part of the Northwest Territories. As an example of what appears to be happening in the north, in Repulse Bay, out of 22 women between 30 and 50 years of age, 10 have been sterilized-a percentage of 45 per cent. In Chesterfield Inlet, out of 23 women between 30 and 50, 6 have been sterilized, for a percentage of 26 per cent. In Pelly Bay, out of 18 women between the ages of 30 and 50, five have been sterilized, or 27 per cent. In Gjoa Haven, out of 41 women between 30 and 50, 13 have been sterilized, or 31 per cent.
The numbers have been quoted in the Sunday Express and other newspapers. The question of the sterilization of native women in the Northwest Territories has been raised by the Inuit Tapirisat, the representative of the northern peoples of those parts. The question was also mentioned in the Sunday Express and in the Globe and Mail and was brought to my attention by Father Lechat, a well respected and well known

man of the north. He is concerned about this problem and raises many questions about it.
I ask the government, which has not answered questions concerning this area as well as other areas, does this represent government policy? Is this, indeed, policy? If so, how many people have been affected by it? How long has this program been going on, and why is it being carried out? Are white people involved in it as well? Is the program being explained to people taking part in it? Do the women who have been sterilized know exactly what the consequences are? Do they understand fully what it is all about? Has it been explained to them in terms they can understand? I know these are difficult questions to answer.
I know of a white lady who discussed this question with doctors, friends and others experienced in the area. She decided, after consultation, to go through with the operation, but said sometime afterwards that if she had known exactly what its consequences would be, how it would change her, she would never have agreed to go through with it.
The government has not been able to say whether this is policy. I wonder if the government has the guts to undertake an inquiry, find out exactly what is going on and explain to the Canadian people what this is all about. When you couple what is happening with ideas put forward in a training manual for the correctional institute in Yellowknife, a manual which describes the native people as shiftless, lazy and goodness knows what else in unkind terms, you wonder how many sick people, including civil servants, in those parts are making major decisions affecting the people's lives. Therefore, I ask the government to look seriously at that program and let us know exactly what is happening.
I now touch upon another area of concern-housing. In March 1974-and the year was fairly exciting in this House, as I recall-the minister responsible for housing announced that 50,000 units in a five-year period would be built under the government's rural and native housing program. The program itself was under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Unfortunately, the program has not worked. It seems that the program is in a shambles. It has operated almost for two years. I do not know how many houses were built under it, but I have not seen any in the north, the one place in which they ought to be built.
Housing everywhere is a basic human right. This being a cold country, housing programs should be given greater priority. We need good housing programs in all parts of the country. We need a super-good housing program in the north, where the climate is extreme. Housing is in short supply in many areas, including mine. Adequate housing can help us solve many of the social ills afflicting people in various parts of the country. Good housing helps to keep the basic family unit together. Good housing would keep our native peoples together and improve their health conditions. Good housing, and improvements in health, enable people to do better work and keep their jobs. I know of many in my constituency who could do good work, but cannot because they lack adequate housing. These people cannot hold on to better jobs because they have
October 25, 1976

no place in which to rest and eat a good meal before going back to work. They have nowhere to enjoy life.
Good housing would help to curb alcoholism, which afflicts not only people of the NWT but people generally in northern countries. Good housing, again, is the answer. As well, adequate housing would allow people to work in home industries. They could support themselves by doing soapstone carving, needlework, and so on. Such activities can be carried on in the spare room of the home, if the person has one, the bonus being that the traditional way of life could be maintained. That is another point in favour of a good housing program.
A countrywide good housing program would help to create jobs in this country. It would support small industries, especially small construction firms. As I say, there are many arguments in favour of a good housing program. Therefore, I wonder why, since the program was announced almost two years ago, it has not worked as well as it should. I think the minister is obligated to find out why the program is not working and he should make the necessary corrections. As I said earlier, housing is a basic human right. The government should do everything possible to make sure that as many houses as possible are built.
I am led to believe that bungling civil servants are responsible for the rural and native housing program not working. I do not know if it is all the government's fault; perhaps people at the local level who may not be involved with the government are also responsible. No matter where the blame lies, the question should be looked into. The minister should find out what is wrong and get the show on the road.
I want to speak briefly on something called northern development, which is a pretty big topic. Elaving perused the Speech from the Throne, I find that again the north has been neglected. Important areas of concern for the north are not even mentioned. These questions concern not only northerners but people in the rest of the country. Major decisions affecting the north will affect the rest of the country. I am thinking of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. The Speech from the Throne did not mention it. There was no mention of the Arctic Islands gas pipeline, and no mention of transportation systems, whether involving ships in the High Arctic, aircraft, better roads, better airports, better navigational facilities and more and improved weather stations.
No mention was made of environmental priorities for the NWT, and there was no mention of possible provincial status for the Yukon or the NWT. There was no mention of the government's thinking with respect to changing the status of the NWT, that is, for dividing it into two territories, one to be a province and the other a territory. No mention was made of native claims. No mention has been made of these things in recent Speeches from the Throne. I have listened to two or three, and we seem to be left out all the time. We do not particularly like that. Even though there are only 40,000 of us up there, we feel the north is very important to all of Canada. We believe some very important decisions will have to be made about that area in the next few years. There probably will be some pretty important issues arising in that area within two or
The Address-Mr. Firth
three years, or even within a year and a half. It looks as if there is a move toward a minority situation in which we hear that the NDP will have a little more fun squeezing some things from the government.
There is no mention in the throne speech of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. In looking at this situation, one wonders whether the large oil companies are very serious about building a pipeline there. I recall that when it was first mentioned, the Atlantic Richfield Company announced it intended to go ahead. However, from the figures I have been able to dig up today, it does not seem to me that there is enough gas or oil in the Mackenzie Valley to warrant a pipeline. I do not think they intended to build one in the first place. Even if they did, possibly it was more in the form of bluff than anything else to enhance their bargaining position with the companies in the east.
It has not been proven that there is enough gas in the Mackenzie delta to warrant the building of a pipeline. Even if it were built, the purpose would not be to move several trillion cubic feet of gas, but to tap the cold, clear ice water from the Slave Lake, Bear Lake and the Mackenzie because of the skunky water in the south and the fact that the people must have good clean water. So that would be one of the main reasons. The United States government would like to have a pipeline up there for that purpose. This is worth thinking about. I still think the oil companies are not very serious about building this pipeline and that probably it will never be built in any event.
There was no mention in the throne speech about the structure of what is called the NWT government, which is not actually a government but, rather, an administration. It is my opinion that there are far too many civil servants in the north now. It is a very large area-1,350,000 square miles. There are only 40,000 people, and every fifth one is a civil servant.

speechtext: Very shortly. In addition, the provisions of the human rights bill have been strengthened with regard to the question of equal pay. The throne speech, in remarks related to the human rights legislation, also touched upon a second major aspect of the human rights legislation we will be bringing forward: the protection of rights to privacy with respect to information collected by the government. There are two main aspects to this. One is protection from harassment for information by government departments and agencies.
October 25, 1976

I share the concern of many people that we are a nation becoming addicted to information-gathering about individuals and small businesses without much thought about the need for it or about the cost and inconvenience imposed upon those individuals or small businesses in collecting it. That is a matter the Minister of State (Small Businesses) (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) have touched upon. Data collecting or information collecting should not mean open season on taxpayers' time or money. The new legislation would ensure that government demands for information are rationalized, co-ordinated and restrained to an absolute minimum.
The second aspect of this question relates to personal information solicited by the government and stored in government information files or data banks. I have already said that this legislation will narrow and restrain government access to information from the citizen. It will also broaden citizens' access to personal information about them in government files. It will give individuals the right to find out what federal government records contain personal information about themselves used to make decisions affecting them. They will have the right to examine and correct such information. They will have the right to know the uses to which the information is put and to prevent its use for purposes other than those for which it was intended. It will provide a major increase in the accountability of government to the citizen for the administrative acts affecting that citizen.
Having listened to the debate, I note it is agreed by all that there are some personal information records to which there should not be access. In the earlier legislation of which I speak, those exemptions would have been decided by government regulation. In the new bill, because of the delay in passage, we have been able to develop a legislative or statutory scheme setting out explicit criteria that any information records withheld would have to meet. These restrictions on access should be reduced to the minimum possible, consistent with our parliamentary system. We want to ensure the maximum access to personal information that the public interest will allow. Our aim is to secure to the greatest extent possible the right of the individual to know and to see the personal information on which decisions affecting him or her are made.

In the unified family courts, procedures would be aimed at reconciliation and rehabilitation. I discussed this matter with my provincial counterparts at the conference of attorneys general in Vancouver in June which I hosted. Perhaps I might quote from the communique issued by that conference:
Ministers agreed that priority should be given to the development of unified family courts with broad jurisdiction over all legal matters respecting the family unit.
There was some disagreement over the level at which such courts should be sited, but I am confident that this issue can be satisfactorily resolved and that we can get on with the business of reform in these particular courts which touch so many Canadians. I will be meeting, in the coming months, with ministers of the provinces in an effort to establish, where appropriate, unified family courts. Indeed, negotiations in this direction are already well under way in several provinces and I am confident that progress can be made such as was indicated by the attorney general for Ontario the other day in forecasting possible legislation in that province.
The Law Reform Commission also stressed that there are three economic functions to marriage, wage earning, home care and child rearing, and that the present law on matrimonial property really recognizes only the first, which is usually the contribution of the husband or the wage earning provision and does not recognize the two economic functions which are usually the woman's contribution of home care and child rearing. The commission recommended that the law should provide for the equal sharing of property acquired through the earnings of either or both spouses during the marriage. There would be some exceptions relating to gifts, inheritances, bequests or trusts. The recommendation affecting matrimonial property are of immeasurable importance to married women in Canada. It takes direct aim at the anachronism which exists in the law of most provinces and which was highlighted by the

Supreme Court of Canada in its decision in the now famous case of Murdoch v. Murdoch.
Our ministerial discussions in Vancouver, in June, touched upon this particular subject, and at that time provincial attorneys general expressed the view that matrimonial property is exclusively a provincial matter. This is not a unanimous view. Obviously, the Law Reform Commission had different experts and different views on the federal role involved relating to matrimonial property. The conference did indicate the ministers agreed that provincial governments would be urged to press forward with reform of matrimonial property laws reflecting the concept of marriage as a partnership of equals. I understand, again from press reports, that the attorney general of Ontario plans to table some proposals in this regard very shortly.
I welcome such initiatives to be taken by the provinces and will continue to consult with them to that end. I would point out, however, that if it is their exclusive jurisdiction, they have a responsibility to act, and to act expeditiously. If the provinces do not move expeditiously to put in place meaningful changes in the law relating to matrimonial property to take account of the economic needs and the rights of both spouses, there will obviously be increasing pressure on this parliament to endeavour to try to implement the recommendations, in one form or another, of the Law Reform Commission's report relating to the disposal of matrimonial property. Canadian women should not have to wait much longer for provincial action in this regard. I hope that provincial attorneys general will take note of my remarks, that if it is their jurisdiction, as claimed by them, they should act expeditiously in this area.
We will go forward in the immediate future on three aspects relating to family law. The first is negotiations with the provinces toward the establishment in the provinces of unified family courts. The second is changes in the law relating to matrimonial property to better take account of the economic needs and rights of both parties. The third is formal consultation with those in the community across Canada regarding the other recommendations of the Law Reform Commission's report on family law.
I appreciate the courtesy of the House in allowing me to complete my speech. This is the last day of the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. speechtext:
Let us have a little bit of total truth, not truth by degree. I have no doubt about the future of our country. Yet the lack of will of this directionless government is cause for profound disquiet. As Oliver Wendell Holmes aptly put it:
I find the great thing in this world is not so much where we stand, as in what direction we are moving.
To reach the port of heaven, we must sail sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it, but we must sail, and not drift, nor lie at anchor.
This government will not reach the port of heaven, or even get within sight of the fairway buoys, if this Speech from the Throne is any indication of the legislation that is coming forward. It is a latter day tragedy. This government has allowed itself to drift. It is in the doldrums of indifference. The captain is unsure of what course to take, and the navigator, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), will not even share the charts with the public of Canada. We are entitled to know the direction the government is going to take and the purpose of its journey, but it is sealed because it is confidential and "eyes only".
As the Minister of Justice said, we are in the last few hours of this debate. I have found four or five topics which concern me and my constituents. I hope they will commend themselves to hon. members. These topics are the constitution, the faltering effort of the government to face the issue of freedom of information, problems relating to overlapping jurisdictions, an idea for improving the consultative process between government and management and labour, and, lastly, a personal proposal for solving an international irritant, namely, the ownership of Machias Seal Island at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy. I wish to use this as an example of something the United States and Canada might do together. Because I believe in short speeches, I can only highlight some of the implications of the policy areas about which I have spoken.
With regard to the Official Languages Act, which has been talked about by other people, I wish to restate clearly the commitment I made to it, for its splendid purpose, by my votes in this House in the past. I know I say this at some personal risk, but I think it is time some people in this country spoke out in favour of the reasonable sharing of what we have here. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) put the matter in historical perspective and we should be grateful to him for doing so. There is no need for Canada, which is a carefully constructed experiment involving recognition of fundamental rights in language and culture, to fly apart. It is time
422

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Fairweather
for conciliation, not for confrontation. It is time for the celebration of what we Canadians share together, rather than for the intoning of funeral dirges mourning our lack of will to go on.
I am fed up with Cassandras who are abroad in this land prophesying the end of our country. Canada will live long after those apostles of gloom have passed away. May I ask those who may listen to this statement, including our colleagues from Quebec, to remember that some people express such views at a certain risk, and when voices are raised or importun-ings are heard I ask them to remember that those who share the aspirations of this country are glad to do so, glad to stand up and say so. But can we not have the same language, that is, the truth, from one end of the country to the other, whether it is English or French?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What irony, when the evidence is all around us that Canadians appreciate and treasure our heritage and want to guard it, that there should be those in various parts of the country who would tear down what we have built together and hazard the future of our nation with their narrow stridency. Mere lip service to the commitment of this country is unacceptable.
On the subject of the constitution I would say this: I may sound "preachy" today, but I believe that insolence and petulance are accurate descriptions of the tone of the exchange of letters between some premiers and the Prime Minister of Canada. For Canada's sake, let us cool down this issue. I admit that the government has a mandate provided by stark numbers-if that is all we care about-but I submit it has no mandate at the moment of will in favour of the constitutional debate. The whole debate seems to me to be arcane, characterized by intemporate bulletins lobbing from capital to capital and almost entirely misunderstood by the public which parliament is elected to serve.
A constitution cannot be the private property of some government or some constitutional lawyer advising the government. A constitution which cannot be understood by the people is nothing more than a lawyer's document fit to be hidden away in some file. I believe a constitution should be as clear as the beatitudes and, in its starkness, as eloquent as the Gettysburg Address. The rest of this debate is almost unbelievably out of touch with the mood and aspirations of the people of this country.
I am sad to say this, but I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who for one reason or another has lost the essential elements of good will and trust of the Canadian people, should put the constitutional debate into cold storage until the public of Canada has had the opportunity to say who will lead the country in the years ahead.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!
