speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we live in a time of increasing complexity and confusion, a time when the citizen who

wishes to play a responsible role in our democratic system is confronted by an almost overwhelming tangle of bureaucratic red tape. My hon. friend from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) will long be remembered for his efforts on behalf of a freedom of information act. This is the last part of the twentieth century, and we are still fiddling in this parliament. What worries me is that there may be another government diversion, that we may be faced with another white, grey or red paper postponing a decision the need for which is obvious. This question has been studied by parliament, by the Privy Council, by those who understand our system of government. It is time, now, for a freedom of information act and I very much hope there will be no postponement or diversion by way of green papers and the like. We already know all we need to know about the subject. The appointment of one more committee would be exceedingly disillusioning to those who are interested in this aspect of policy.
Another point I wish to raise has to do with the overlapping of jurisdictions. It seems to me that this is an impediment which hinders the wise governing of the country at every turn and prevents us from going ahead as we ought. Decision making is constantly hampered by the existence of overlapping jurisdictions, meaning that one must wade through a bureaucratic maze, searching from one level of government to the other, with the result that everyone's problem becomes no one's problem. I have a couple of examples which I could use to illustrate this contention. Many people will be unfamiliar with the part of the country about which I speak, but I will take that risk anyway.
The dilemma produced by these overlapping jurisdictions becomes apparent as it affects the coast of the bay of Fundy in a community known as Red Head which is literally eroding or sliding into the sea. Much the same thing is happening along the shores of the Kennebecasis River at Sussex. Citizens groups who are anxious, not for government hand outs but for policies which will help them help themselves, have been continually frustrated, and if I may say so modestly, I too, have been frustrated by the hours I have spent trying to find out which of the many agencies of government are responsible for ending this imminent threat.
The citizens' groups in these communities have organized themselves in an effort to prevent further disaster in their communities, but they need help and, as I say, I have spent hours trying to find out the particular department of the federal or provincial government with which responsibility lies. But the buck gets passed from one level of government to the next, from one the department to the next, and I hope that the new Minister of the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), a New Brunswicker for whom we have the greatest respect, will be able to tackle this maze of shared jurisdiction and find a way through it for us. I must say, however, that I am discouraged at the prospects for action if the present system of buck-passing goes on. The government has simply not overcome difficulties of governing a complex system, so inertia, it seems to me, is too often the end result.
October 25, 1976

I wish to say a word or two about the consultative process. Just as serious is the government's failure to provide consensus policies brought about by co-operative consultation between the private and public sectors, between government, management and labour. Instead, what we have seen is an adversary system that has submerged the common interest. Governments used to be thought to speak for the common interest. Unhappily, in recent years, this has not been the case. Professor Paul Malles, a former senior member of the staff of the Economic Council of Canada, has some interesting things to say about ways in which we can facilitate consensus policies, in a pamphlet from the Conference Board of Canada which I am sure my colleagues will want to read. I think if we were to expunge the word "problem" from our vocabulary for a year or so, Canadians would be very much better off. In any event, the good professor suggests that our federal system, our diversified geography, climate and resources, and the limited organizational base for business and labour to speak with a collective voice, are realities of our country that make the road to consensus policies very long and difficult. But he suggests a road that we have to travel.
The challenges are clear. This government, I am sorry to say, has not met them. The alternative is more divisiveness and more unilateral intervention by government. The public has increasingly rejected this alternative. If I may quote Professor Malles, he has this to say:
Canada's economic problems would be greatly eased if Canadians could somehow develop consultative arrangements that would encourage them to work together in unison, toward commonly agreed upon goals, harnessing the energies of all three of the social partners in a co-operative effort toward mutually advantageous objectives.
This consultation cannot go on if the elements of consultation continue to be hidden, where everything is marked "Secret" or "Confidential". The attitude is, "Don't let anybody see it. Be careful, the public might want to know". The trouble with this government is that they are afraid to share the decisions that have to be made for this country. Professor Malles cites consultative arrangements through institutions of consultation and negotiation between interested partners and government in Europe that are linked in one form or another to planning bodies set up by government. I believe that we must look toward similar arrangements in this country. I do not think that it is a matter of very much pride to Canada that almost every one of the western European countries have in place, and in some cases have long had in place, a much better system of management-labour consultation.
Lastly-you will be glad to know I mean "lastly," Mr. Speaker-through eons of time the oceans and remote breeding islands have sheltered and protected animals and birds which today are finding it increasingly difficult to cope with the encroachments of civilization. Machias Seal Island is a challenge to part of what still remains. Such is the excitement, beauty and uniqueness of the island that it has been studied and visited by world famous naturalists, photographers and writers. The United States National Audubon Society takes
The Address-Mr. Herbert
great interest in the safety of the birds. I am delighted to tell the House that Jack and Rita Russell, the light-keepers on this island, are committed conservationists. Mary Majka, of Caledonia Mountain, New Brunswick, is a naturalist who has embellished the life of our province with her dedication. These people are anxious about the future of this and other great breeding grounds of our natural heritage. Constitutional lawyers, cartographers and other experts in the foreign service of Canada and the United States are at this very minute engaged in a long and frustrating argument about title to this 15-acre island which is 12 miles south of Grand Manan and 9 miles off the coast of Maine. Machias Seal is the outermost of the islands forming the Grand Manan archipelago.
My own modest and personal idea, as a member of parliament, gleaned from others who have thought about this question is that we forget about the national sovereignty of Machias Seal Island and use the wonderful example of the Roosevelt Campobello International Park which provided for the first time an international sharing of title to land. The United States is joint owner of the Roosevelt Campobello Park, and I suggest that this island also be declared an international bird sanctuary. I suggest-and members might have to go to their dictionaries and look this word up, as I had to do-a co-imperium for birds; in other words, that sovereignty over these 15 acres be shared by the United States and Canada. The constitutional lawyers would all have heart attacks, the cartographers would have to fold away their maps, and the birds would continue to do what they have done through eons of time-breed and lay their eggs.
The United States and the Canadian wildlife services could contract out guardianship, protection and management of the islands to the private sector, to Nature Canada, the United States audubon society, and so on. I might also mention, for the British Columbians present, that this co-imperium might be an excellent solution to the irritant on our west coast, namely, Point Roberts where Canadians occupy the territory but it is part of the United States. In any event, surely our two countries should be able to work this out together.
A nation, St. Augustine said, is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish. I believe very profoundly that it is time we spoke about the things we cherish in this country. By doing this we determine the quality of our nation. We must take great care that we know what these things are that we share, and many members who have taken part in this debate have added to the knowledge of our shared inheritance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend in these remarks to discuss three subjects of particular importance in the province of Quebec. The three subjects are immigration policy, the language question, including Bill 22, and the constitution. Firstly, though, it is highly relevant to refer to the population change in the constituency of Vaudreuil between the centennial census taken in 1971 and the census taken this year, just five years later. The population is exploding, having shot up from 119,000 in 1971 to almost 136,000 in 1976. This is recognizable both in the extensive new house
424

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Herbert
building that one can see and in the new citizen statistics that are supplied to members. Areas such as Pierrefonds, Kirkland, lie Perrot, Vaudreuil, St. Lazare and Rigaud have all seen impressive residential construction. This new home building is to be augmented by- extensive development plans such as those on beautiful lie Bizard.
Talking to house builders leaves the distinct impression that the majority of the families buying these new homes are English-speaking. This impression is supported by the new citizen statistics which indicate that in the last four years 85 per cent of the new citizens in this region list English as their language. On the island of Montreal, the population increase in the Vaudreuil constituency has exceeded 17 per cent in the five-year period of 1971 to 1976. Off the island, in the land area enclosed by the Ottawa and St. Lawrence Rivers and the Ontario border, the population increase has been even greater, almost 19 per cent in five years.
There are two key points to be made from these statistics. Firstly, it appears to give the lie to the oft repeated statement that the English are moving out of the province of Quebec. Secondly, it supports the contention of the government of the province of Quebec that federal immigration policy could negate the cultural and educational programs and planning in areas which are acknowledged to be 100 per cent provincial jurisdictions. Thus, it is absolutely essential, if only for reasons of orderly planning, that the provincial government participate actively in the formation and application of immigration policy. Let me try to make a more forceful illustration of this point. The federal government has, of course, already acted to avoid such an extreme case. It would be catastrophic in its consequences to establish an immigration quota for this year of, say, 200,000 persons and then to permit them all to establish in one of the big cities with its attractive labour market and high salaries.
Whilst the importance of participation in the establishment of immigration policy is more obvious in Quebec, for language and cultural reasons, it is equally important for good economic planning. The industrial growth of the province is a key consideration if the standard of living and the general prosperity is to advance at a rate adequate to satisfy our expectations. The manufacturing sector particularly must be developed to take greater advantage of the natural resources with which this province has been blessed.
From immigration it is natural to turn to the language question. This is undoubtedly the hottest issue in the country today, for two reasons, both of which are extreme: the government is shoving French down English throats and only the separation of Quebec can guarantee the preservation of the French language and culture. First let us look at what the federal government has done, or at least has tried to do. In 1974, at the executive level of certain key departments, the French-speaking representation was still under 10 per cent. In general, very little progress has been accomplished in the use of French as a working language. The total cost of bilingualism in the public service is about $135 million. A further $30 million is allocated to national defence. It is interesting, how-

ever, to stop at this point, to compare the implementation of language policies in the Department of National Defence with the public service generally. The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson), the recently resigned minister of national defence, said:
For promotion to the rank of major and above linguistic ability in a second official language is a factor.
He then goes on to describe how the scoring system determines relative merit based on "performance and potential". Thus, linguistic ability in a second official language, whether English of French, enhances an officer's position with respect to promotion to the rank of major or above in relation to a unilingual contemporary when all other factors are equal. As the hon. member for Winnipeg South said:
The department is endeavouring to establish an Anglophone/Francophone balance of personnel in the forces corresponding to the national ratio of the two groups.
It is this approach that I have personally promoted for the public service. It is not easy for a person who has passed his or her youth to learn a second language. It becomes substantially impossible when there is a force, when French is being shoved down the unilingual English throat. The English appear not to want it, so why force them. Keep the language courses available on a volunteer basis only and recognize the ability to speak a second language as the asset that it is when candidates are being considered for promotion.
That brings me to Bill 22, and since one of the major contentious issues in this bill has concerned education I should like to make reference first to federal involvement in this field. The federal government grants between $135 million and $140 million to the provinces for their second language programs. It is assumed that for a province to organize and maintain two parallel systems of education, where the language of education in each is different, is more expensive than if it had only one system of education for all its students. We are reimbursing Quebec for the extra costs it incurs in providing for the English minority and equally sophisticated system of education as that which it provides for the majority. Although great progress has been made in this respect in other provinces such as Ontario and Manitoba, Quebec more than any other province, achieves this objective. Quebec is the only province where second official language instruction is compulsory at the secondary level for both the Francophones and the Anglophones.
The government of Quebec does its best to assure good quality education for its students. An OECD committee of experts on education reported recently that Quebec is the only province of Canada where the objectives in education seem to be clearly defined. The province of Quebec is second after Ontario for its per capita spending in education, even though Quebec is not the second richest province in Canada.
Now I will comment on Bill 22 and repeat what I said two years ago, "People in the province of Quebec can well take care of themselves without Bill 22." However, the bill was promised and has been passed. Even after the adoption of Bill 22 Quebec is still, among all Canadian provinces, the one which treats the language of the minority, on her territory, with the most equity, the most liberalism and the greatest
October 25, 1976

generosity. If the other nine provinces suddenly decided to show the same respect toward their own official language minorities we would witness a miraculous blooming across the whole country. The Montreal Gazette said:
Whatever the failings of Quebec's Bill 22, it still preserves a substantial place for English education in the province. Manitoba and Ontario should be prepared to do no less for their French minorities.
Let us examine the bill for a moment. The only real teeth in the law are in the section-empowering the government to withhold subsidies, contracts and certain other advantages from companies not favouring French. Significantly, the law provides for fines in only one section, that is, for those failing to provide French on product labels, warranties, menus and wine lists.
The law states that all official texts and documents emanating from public bodies, the provincial government, its departments and agencies, municipalities, urban communities and their various agencies such as transit commissions, school boards, colleges and universities, must be in French, but adds that these may be accompanied by an English version. In the other provinces across the country the English version prevails over the French. Every individual has the right to address all these bodies in French or English. In cases where at least 10 per cent of the persons served by a municipal or school body are English-speaking, and this is the case for at least two-thirds of those bodies in the province, both French and English must be used in official texts, if this is already the practice.
The law states that no one will be employed or promoted in the public administration unless he has an appropriate knowledge of French. There could be unilingual English public servants in Quebec, provided they were not in direct contact with the public. Remarks addressed to the chair in any area of the public administration may be in French or in English, at the option of the persons addressing the remarks. This gives English-speaking Quebeckers a right spelled out at present in no law.
In education, the law states that pupils must have a sufficient knowledge of the language of instruction, French or English, to receive their instruction in the language. The law also says that the education minister may, in accordance with the regulations, set tests to ascertain that the pupils have sufficient knowledge of the language of instruction to receive their instruction in that language. Personally, I do no believe that there should be an entrenched right to choose the language of schooling when the child is not able to speak that language. However, on a non-legislated entitlement basis I am particularly happy to see the successful immersion schooling in our constituency today. However, there has been one contentious issue that looks as if it may be nearing resolution, that is, the division that can be created in an immigrant family. A family coming to this country has not expected the right to demand French schooling in the English provinces. Nevertheless, it has been possible for a family settling in Quebec to choose to send their children to an English school, even though English was not their language. It does not make sense to divide the children and the family by legislation which was not
The Address-Mr. Baldwin
in existence when they made their decision to choose Quebec. The numbers are relatively few. Future immigrants will know the rules. A small change in the application of Bill 22 will remove this very emotionally charged and understandable issue.
Hand in hand with the discussion of immigration policy and language rights must go the discussion of jurisdictional responsibilities and our constitution. One cannot deny that the constitution was formulated and signed at a time when it would have been difficult to envisage the changes that have actually taken place since confederation. To name one aspect alone, the religious attitude, would suggest that our forefathers did not even think it necessary to contemplate and make provision for such a change.
There are extremely few in this country who are not firmly convinced that a revised constitution should be formulated and amendable in Canada. It is my personal conviction that changes in the constitution affecting immigration policy, communications responsibility and cultural sovereignty, are far from insurmountable obstacles. These are primarily emotional issues and good common sense is likely to prevail. For example, in the field of communications the federal government can hardly fail to recognize the impact of this highly-developed sector on education and culture. However, there is one acknowledged provincial area of responsibility that is looming as a major stumbling block to an agreement; that is, the effective level of control of resources. This question, probably more than all others, must be studied in its totally national context because of its major economic impact. Whether we discuss British Columbia lumber, Alberta oil, Saskatchewan minerals or Quebec hydro-electric power, it is questionable whether we can live in harmony as a nation if we are not able to recognize the national interest first. Surely no one province should be able to hold a gun to the heads of the other provinces. We are, obviously, going through a preliminary bargaining session. Advancing technology, the development of the third world, with its impact on our economy, and the good common sense of the Canadian people will surely lead our federal and ten provincial governments toward an accord. When we reach that long-awaited agreement, it is my hope that at that point in time we make the national declaration of our new and 100 per cent Canadian constitution. I am, personally, opposed to wasting any plane fare to pick up a piece of paper in England.
I will conclude by repeating an extract from last month's Observer:
One of our greatest possessions in Canada is our heritage of two peoples with two cultures and two languages. Our future and the future of our children will be immeasurably enriched if we can keep this country together; it will be deeply impoverished if we divide. We like to believe that we are a tolerant people, but we should never tolerate racial or cultural intolerance. And we would hope that Canadians might so act as to contribute to their pride in themselves and appreciation of our language and traditions.

Mr. Speaker, may I first express the traditional and very heartfelt congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, to those eminent persons who have

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Baldwin
occupied or reoccupied positions in the chair, and to the new cabinet ministers who might have a reasonably limited time to become accustomed to the glory that is temporarily theirs.
1 sometimes think that perhaps a speech from the throne is an anachronism, but when 1 heard that strong, honest and extraordinarily eloquent speech by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) this afternoon I thought that makes us realize that this is a good occasion for speeches of this kind.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: However, the writers of the present speech seem to have really covered the waterfront. They appear to have left out very little except a cure for the common cold and the Ten Commandments. I am informed that since October 18 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been looking at the Ten Commandments and is going to have the Privy Council make a study of them and have them made available publicly. They will probably show up, in my humble opinion, as an annex to the anti-inflation program regulations.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: All ten of them?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Almost. If the items which show up in the Speech from the Throne sound vaguely familiar, they are, because they have shown up in so many other throne speeches. Inflation, unemployment, small business, competition, bilingualism, agriculture, national unity, labour relations, social assistance, transportation, federal-provincial relations and constitutional problems have, under the same or different names, been referred in such speeches for the last 100 years.
In fact, some of these problems were around on the occasion of the bringing together of the individual provinces to cause confederation. In most cases these are tough problems, conundrums which are related to the permanent characteristics of human beings as individuals and collectively as society. They will not easily yield to final solutions and are likely to be around for the next 100 years. I hope future governments will be more honest and open than the present one and will admit there are no miraculous cures but just present remedies for existing symptoms. The people seem to know this. They are pragmatic and instinctively more intelligent than their rulers. They recognize that the limitations, the accelerating distrust and the loss of faith in the manner of our governing stems from this.
It is a deep, angry and abiding aversion to the way we are ruled, rather than to acts of default, error and omission that turns the public off. It is the rigidity and over-discipline of political parties, particularly the party in power, a lack of effective rules in the House, which places the government, the cabinet and the civil service far outside the scope of meaningful public or parliamentary challenge. It is the enormous increase of delegated authority.

I have here Canada Gazette 110, number 19, with 200 pages of nothing but regulations and orders in council. This is the kind of thing which the people of this country are faced with. Above all, it is the impenetrable veil of secrecy behind which bureaucrats and ministers are able to carry on their arbitrary powers free from adequate challenge. This has progressed to the stage where there is no longer a responsible government.
This is not only my view. 1 have here the editorial of July, 1976, from "Round Table" dealing with the situation in the United Kingdom. I quote from that article at page 216. It talks about the United Kingdom, but the only difference between the U.K. and Canada is about five years. It reads:
The convention of ministerial responsibility has almost reached a point where it is but a memory with antique charm.
It is a ludicrous fiction to suggest at this point that the House of Commons can exercise any real control over the government on the principle that the members who sit in the executive council, the Privy Council, are members of the House of Commons whom their peers in the House can at any given moment eject from office. This is nonsense. It has happened twice in 50 years, and on both those occasions it was because we had a minority government and the minor party, which, for reasons best known to itself, saw fit at the time to act in this way because they said, "That is enough; we will put the government out." It was not a question of responsible government at all. Most individual members are now limited to the role of an ombudsman in respect of their own constituents or, as supporters of the party in power, waiting and scheming to come into the cabinet.
It is not an insignificant role, 1 do not downgrade it, it is a very important role; but far less than the proper concept and function that this House should have. In short, with very little real opposition from the public press or parliaments, power has slipped into the hands of the bureaucrats and whoever happens to be prime minister. They not only administer, but in most cases make policy, and I doubt if any government-certainly no government so far-has shown the capacity, the strength, the know-how or even the will to do anything about it.
There is only one place where the scales can be more nearly brought into balance, and that is on the floor of the House. If it can be done-and I am not sure that it can now-it will be only by reason of tremendous effort by members on both sides of the House. This side cannot do it alone. It will require the co-operation and the support of some hon. members on the backbenches on the other side of the House. Indeed, it may be asking too much at this time to overcome the inertia, the easy ride with the status quo and the unhappiness about having to challenge City Hall.
The major item in any package to bring this about is the right of the public to know the real truth about the actions of government and the concomitant duty of officials to disclose the facts. If anyone wants to take the time and trouble to go back over many years and review the inception of major programs in this country, either capital construction or social benefit plans, it will be found that in almost all cases they were
October 25, 1976

launched with false statements as to their initial and continuing cost and their effect.
From the refitting of the Bonaventure to the quasi-welfare proposals of the UIC of several years ago, from federal contributions to Expo to the ill-fated hydrofoil project, there has been deception or lies or appalling ignorance or gross negligence and, sometimes, a mixture of all. I can say this without doubting the intrinsic value of many of these proposals. It is incredible that supposedly intelligent and conscientious people with access to the facts and statistics should have been allowed to peddle the propaganda which they did.
In my judgment, if there had been the opportunity for public access to the factual material, the various programs would have been tailored to reality and the enormous deficits and Fiscal irresponsibility which constituted such a large element of inflation would not have occurred. If the officials and the ministers who put together these schemes had known at that time that they would be compelled by an adequate and working freedom of information law to publish the true facts, and had realized that the data would be subjected to contemporary scrutiny both in and out of parliament, it could well had been a different story.
It is an interesting sidelight that when we did find out something of the real horror stories behind many of these programs, it was as a result of the reports of the Auditor General. By the time the report came out into the open, the horses were gone, the door was locked and many years had elapsed. But bear in mind that it was only because the Auditor General had the right by law, under the pertinent provisions of the Financial Administration Act, to go to the public service and secure all the documents he desired and have access to the books of account. Without that right, the Auditor General would be in no better condition than we are, or than the public or the press. The Auditor General has his own freedom of information law and because of that, although often it is too late, we find out the facts.
I note with interest the words in the Speech from the Throne about freedom of information. They could mean anything, or nothing. If the government has in fact accepted the proposals made from this side of the House by myself and by my colleagues, and developed in the committee, and is prepared to produce a meaningful, workable, valuable freedom of information law with teeth, then I say, "More power to you. Go ahead with it." But I challenge them to do that. The members of all the opposition parties and, I believe, many members on the other side, want that kind of thing. I am authorized to say that when the Conservative party forms the government after the next election, if there is no valid freedom of information act produced by this government it will be enacted in the first session of such a Conservative administration.

speechtext:
We have been hearing that we have no policy. I reject that. Here is a policy on a major issue which, in my opinion, is of equal importance with the other issues which
The Address-Mr. Baldwin
have been brought up. What policy does the government have?
I say that there is an opportunity for the government to let us know where they stand. I say to hon. members opposite that we are dealing with a major issue. People all over the country are aroused, and not only in this country but in other democratic countries, because of the events of the past few years. There are people all over the country, such as people from the organization called "Access" in this city.
I have travelled throughout Canada and have spoken in about 15 cities on this issue. There are large numbers of people who strongly support and demand that this measure be enacted. I say to hon. members, not as a threat but as a statement, that if it is not passed, this government is in even more serious trouble than I would otherwise expect it to be. If, as I suspect is the case, the top mandarins and one or two cabinet ministers who really run this country and flourish in the dark places of the secret society refuse to allow the parliament and the government to pass a law of this kind, then I have to say that the hon. gentlemen who form the government, this group of political dinosaurs, are really ready for the bone-yard.
Whom the Gods would destroy, they First make mad. To talk as they do in the Speech from the Throne about Finding the middle way, to suggest that there will be consultation with different groups in the country, to try to Find that way and then to deny to us, to the public and to the media, the facts and material on which we can evaluate the position of the government is like the prologue to a tragedy. People do not trust the government. They are cynical about its motives. They are fed up with being kept in the dark. That just will not wash any more. The public will live with honest disagreements. They expect that mistakes will be made. But they will no longer sit idly by and be hoodwinked by trickery and deception.
The Prime Minister and the government ought to realize that this is one of the main causes of the voters' disaffection with them, and the Prime Minister is kidding himself if he puts the blame on bilingualism and wage and price controls. The manner of governing and the way these matters were handled have touched the raw nerve of public indignation, and the details we now know make this plain beyond any reasonable doubt. The October, 1975, anti-inflation program was conceived in trickery, born in confusion and deceit and nourished on evasion, secrecy and blunders. There is no wonder that the public is unhappy.
At the time of its passage, the official languages bill was not ill-received in Canada. The anger and frustation of today has come about because it is now plain that the terms of the bill constituted a facade behind which the government had planned and had available from the beginning regulations to use abrasive and ill-judged methods of implementation, but hid the fact at the time of debate. I reject the contention of the Prime Minister and his friends that Canadians dislike the present government so intensely because they do not understand these programs. That is a gratuitous insult to the public.

The Address-Mr. Baldwin
The public understands only too well. If this government had been forthright and honest about all the details of the proposals, and if there had been public and parliamentary debate based on the truth, the situation would not have deteriorated to the present dismal state. But the trouble is that the government is congenitally incapable of being frank and open and the entire country is suffering because of it. With their track record in sensitive and potentially divisive and exceedingly difficult matters, how can the Prime Minister demand sympathetic understanding from people affected by the language policy, or expect wholehearted co-operation from trade unions, businesses and others who are whacked about by the antiinflation program?
To be viable, effective and in the public interest, a freedom of information act has certain minimum requirements, and all the countless instances of government secrecy bear me out in this. There has to be a declaration of the right of the public to access to all government documents which, with certain exceptions, include computer tapes. These exceptions must be clearly and precisely described. All applications for disclosure must be dealt with simply and expeditiously.
Finally, any refusal by the government to give the information must be appealable to an independent court or tribunal whose decision is binding on both sides, and the onus ought to be on the government to establish that the document should not be released. With that in mind, I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), after he had completed his contribution to this debate, a question with regard to a collateral issue; that is, with regard to the right of people to demand access to their own personal and private files and, if the information in those files is incorrect, to demand rectification. That may be all very well, but let us suppose that rectification is refused. Many of us know-because we have seen illustrations from our own constituents-of people who have on record about them false, improper and incorrect information. The right which the Minister of Justice spoke of in his speech today is useless. It is of no value unless there is a final resort to an independent tribunal to compel the government-or a private corporation, when we come down to that stage-to make rectification.
The minister waffled on that. He talked about a review. A review by whom? By Messrs. Michael Pitfield, Gordon Robertson and Gordon Osbaldeston? They are inestimably fine gentleman, but not the kind of people I want to have to resort to in order to challenge the actions of the government. I am reminded of one of my early days in court, as a young lawyer, when I defended a man charged with bootlegging.

speechtext:
There are other aspects of the requisition of the required elements of a freedom of information bill, but we cannot settle for less than the above. The sheer size of the civil service, both provincial and federal, makes it repugnant to our sense of fairness, justice and sound government to place in their collective hands the right, at their whim and without challenge or appeal, to remove document of public interest from the scrutiny of parliament, the public and the press.
What has been the reaction of the government so far through its spokesmen in the committees, in the House and in different parts of Canada? There are various objections, but the main bureaucratic resistance-and the government's spokesmen, acting on behalf of the bureaucracy, are making these apologies-is based on three things. The first is an unwillingness to submit to the jurisdiction of an independent tribunal. On that I have said as much as I need to say. The government feels it should have the right to have the last word and to have the final veto. I think it is unthinkable and unacceptable to leave to bureaucrats the opportunity to decide what documents in their possession should be made public. There is a refusal to produce working papers or so-called internal documents. Any exemption of this kind provides a bottomless pit into which all government data can sink out of sight. These are the kinds of objections which precipitate the leakage of documents, a demeaning and humiliating method of acquiring information.
There are some leaks that we know of. Governments leak documents purposely to try to manipulate public opinion. Sometimes people leak documents for revenge or for gain, but I am thinking of the genuine case of the civil servant, torn between conscience and the oath of secrecy, who knows that the government, in breach of factual information put before it, is ignoring facts and statistics and is going off in a direction which it thinks is more politically advisable but wrong. What is the position of the civil servant of that kind? Too often this leads to leaks. I suggest that the introduction of a proper freedom of information bill would eliminate at least 75 per cent to 80 per cent of leaks of this kind.
Finally, the third reason the government advances for refusing is that the government says our system is different. I have heard that argument advanced all over the world. I have heard it in Austria, France, Britain and Australia, and not too many years ago there was a case in the United States where some very eminent lawyers were arguing in the supreme court of the United States. They said, "We have a unique and distinctive system of government in the United States: We have the separation of powers: It is absolutely unthinkable that this material should be opened up to public survey." That was the argument made to the supreme court of the United States by the lawyers for Richard Nixon.
October 25, 1976

I have heard almost the same words repeated in this country time after time by government spokesmen. They maintain that we cannot have a freedom of information bill here, that we cannot allow an independent tribunal to make a decision on it because our system is different. This is a specious argument made by people who see themselves as Horatious standing at the bridge, defending the grounds of privilege and absolutism and the opportunities for vast patronage. This is the true reason why people on the government side are afraid to have a bill that will work.
The rights which we seek to obtain by legislation of this kind are not extravagant or improper. It was said hundreds of years ago that a people which means to govern itself must have the power that knowledge brings. It is their money that is taxed from them and spent by others; it is their property, their privileges, their well-being that is affected. Nobody, not even the Prime Minister, and probably not even the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey), acquires extraordinary gifts by being sworn into cabinet. No civil servant, no matter how high his rank or his experience, automatically obtains the mystique and the gift of divine wisdom.
There is the little story about James I speaking to the judges-a practice you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that has come down to the present day with the executive speaking to judges-that which concerns the mystery of power is not lawful to be disclosed, because to do so is to wade into the mystical reverence that belongs to who sit on the throne of God. I know there are a few of the bureaucracy who do not think they sit on the throne of God; but there are still about 10 per cent for whom the jury is still out.
Mr. Speaker, civil servants and others are subject to the frailties and faults of the rest of us. Because they are dealing with our affairs, they must be accountable to parliament on behalf of the people we represent. I recognize that the business of governing is complex and difficult and requires quick and effective action. I am not suggesting that parliament should govern. We cannot govern. That is for government. But government must exercise that authority on all occasions subject to the knowledge that they will have to account for it. The power to govern is a trust and, like any trust, there has to be an accounting. It is not enough to rely on the clumsy and blunt weapon of periodic elections, essential as they may be. This accountability has to be on a day to day, week to week and a monthly basis.
That is one side of the coin, Mr. Speaker. The other side is the right of people to have easy, simple and expeditious access to facts and information they are particularly interested in: their own files, as is suggested by the terms of the new human rights bill; data about the quality of the food they eat; the products they buy-are they safe or hazardous; information about immigration; environmental and pollution data; information about decisions of boards or tribunals that affect them; claims for social benefits; and the 1,001 things that intimately affect their lives. This will not come easily. People who wield power and great authority which others do not possess will not
The Address-Hon. D. J. MacDonald readily yield it. They will obstruct, argue and rationalize and offer specious and irrelevant excuses. This is a struggle which I suspect will be hard, tough and long, but it can provide a chance for members on both sides of the House, if they want, to bring about a renaissance of responsible government. It may be our last chance.
Mr. Speaker, we have no God-given assurance that our method of governing ourselves will be eternal. Surely no system can, or should, survive when it rests on a shifting foundation of political dishonesty and organized government lying. This applies to most democratic countries at the present time. This is the stage to which they have developed. If people understand that their representatives are unable or unwilling to look after their interests against the actions of big government, they are going to find some other way.

speechtext:
My responsibilities to the people of Canada, in my portfolio as Minister of Veterans Affairs, have been varied and challenging during the past months. Today I am happy to say Canadian veterans are enjoying one of the most comprehensive programs for veterans to be found in the world. There are many things that we as Canadians should be thankful for today. One of them is peace and freedom, for which we paid no small price. Another is the natural bounty of this great land of ours. Another is the quality of life we enjoy thanks to our own endeavours and accomplishments. We are fortunate, as a nation, compared to most nations of the world today. But we have largely created our own good fortune by bending our backs to the task of building something valuable and distinctive.
According to the last census, there are still nearly a million veterans living in Canada. A major portion of these are married, and many of them still have dependent children. Accordingly, we estimate there are probably nearly two million Canadian citizens who are potentially entitled to one or more benefits under the various pieces of veterans' legislation. This year, its golden anniversary year, the Royal Canadian Legion has decided to organize a very special campaign known as Operation Service. It is aimed at making contact with every

October 25, 1976
The Address-Hon. D. J. MacDonald war veteran and ex-service person and their survivors, to make sure that they are fully aware of their rights and privileges.
The veterans' charter, one of the best in the world, represents tangible recognition of Canada's debt to those who gave their services and, in some cases, their lives for their homeland. Yet, astonishingly, large numbers of ex-servicemen, and probably an even higher percentage of widows, have failed to seek the benefits to which they are entitled. This has happened despite the ongoing efforts of the Legion, other veterans' organizations and the Department of Veterans Affairs to publicize the provisions of the veterans' charter.
1 would like to tell the hon. members that today it is because of action such as Operation Service that I will continue to respect the voice of the national council of veterans' associations, and especially the Royal Canadian Legion who are always so essentially helpful to both me and my senior officials whenever we sit down to discuss matters such as benefits and hospital care for the veteran. These organizations talk sense and they talk both from the mind and the heart. My department will continue to press for changes in legislation which are in keeping with our times and with the spirit and intent of the veterans' charter. Also, Mr. Speaker, I should like to reiterate what I announced in the House of Commons on September 29-that casual earnings exemptions for more than 90,000 war veterans' allowance and civilian war allowance recipients have been increased by 50 per cent. Veterans and widows will now be able to accept additional casual employment to supplement their allowances and increase their well-being. In other words, it will give those who want to work the chance to do so.
Another important aspect to the operation of my portfolio, Mr. Speaker, is remembrance. This is the responsibility of all Canadians to those who fell in defence of our country, and it is our duty to remember and revere their sacrifice-soldiers, sailors and airmen who secured for Canada the freedom we now enjoy. I trust I have demonstrated to hon. members that my department is well aware of the obligations it has to those who so gallantly offered their services to our country in time of war. We will continue to honour those obligations. I would be remiss, Mr. Speaker, if I did not thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for the kind remarks which he expressed last Thursday.
As we start this new session of parliament I would like to take a look back at the summer months and a look ahead to what has been forecast by the Speech from the Throne. The past summer has been an extremely busy one for me and the other members of cabinet. As well as my travels to Prince Edward Island and my own constituency, it was my pleasure to travel during the summer months to Winnipeg and other parts of Manitoba, to Saskatchewan, to various parts of Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. On each of those occasions I had the opportunity to meet large groups of Canadians and discuss the situations and problems facing our country today, and wherever I travelled I found people very aware of the

effort being undertaken by the government, and very concerned that solutions should be found.
The situations which seem constantly to come to the fore are bilingualism and the economy, and I feel both are well in hand. There are criticisms of the bilingualism program and the way it is being implemented. This criticism is useful and constructive to the government, provided it is founded on reason and not on prejudice. We must never forget Canada was founded by two races of people who vowed to work together in a unique type of country where all enjoyed linguistic and cultural equality. We must not deviate from that, for if and when we succeed in having a country composed of two races enjoying truly equal rights, we shall be unique among countries of the world and will a shining example to other lands and peoples. I have a belief that this particular program is widely, almost universally, supported by Canadians on principle, and while there may be small disagreements regarding implementation, it certainly will lead to a truly bilingual society.
Another area on which discussion has centred for the past year or two is the economy. It is now just over one year since the controls programs was implemented, and to my mind it is a success. On October 14, labour held its day of protest, and to all intents and purposes it could only be described as a failure. Large numbers of union members and labour in general stayed at work because they realized their relative position had improved a great deal in one year.
The rational and thoughtful people of Canada realize we cannot go on taking more out of the economy than we are prepared, through our productivity, to put back in. All segments of society must work together to defeat inflation, and it is unfortunate that one group, big labour, feels it must confront the rest of the country and demand more than its share from business, government and, indeed, from those on limited and fixed incomes who suffer most from the ravages of inflation. It sometimes seems that these disputes centre entirely on the basis of the person's own personal needs, while no thoughts are given to the well-being of the country or to other segments of society. At times like these it would seem more sensible to me if all the participants would take a long, sober look at what is happening and governed themselves and their organizations accordingly.
The anti-inflation program is working, and working well. The economy is proceeding along the path of a moderate recovery, registering about 5 per cent growth in real terms. The recovery is being led by increases in consumer expenditure, residential housing activities and export of goods and services. Business commitment has been weak, as can be expected at this stage of the cycle in view of the fact that not all companies are yet operating at full capacity.
We know where we stand at the present time with the economy. However, we must also look to the future. Bearing that in mind, I would like to mention briefly the general philosophy of the government as expressed in the Speech from the Throne, and the plans which have been formulated for the months and years ahead. Of particular interest to those of us
October 25, 1976

in areas of high unemployment are plans to create a year-round, comprehensive, direct job-creation program directed toward areas of chronic high unemployment. Other programs will provide more job opportunities and improved employment counselling for young people. The government does not intend to compete with the private sector for the services of unemployed workers, but will create jobs in areas where its efforts will be a necessary supplement to private sector activity. As hon. members know, we have already enjoyed, in Prince Edward Island, the benefits of the community employment strategy. This new program should expand on the good work already undertaken by Manpower and Immigration.
Transportation is always an important issue on Prince Edward Island. In the Speech from the Throne the government said "changes will be introduced to the national transportation act to protect against unfair freight rates". This is a step which will fit into two areas of government policy, regional development and the competition policy. We on Prince Edward Island are very aware of the energy crisis and the problems related to our dependence on foreign energy. When he visited us last month, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) officially opened the Ark which is dedicated to the search for alternative forms of energy. In the Speech from the Throne, the government committed itself to-
-place further emphasis on research and development of renewable energy sources and on means of improving the efficiency with which energy is used in Canada, particularly the thermal efficiency of residential and commercial buildings.
Housing is another priority area of the present government. The goal of one million new house owners in the next four years remains a key element of the government's housing policy. In concert with other levels of government and the private sector, the government will work to increase the efficiency and input of Canada's total housing effort.
A while ago I mentioned regional development, a principle to which the government remains committed. This has, of course, been a dominant factor in Prince Edward Island life since the policy of regional development was undertaken. The government has, once again, outlined its commitments to small business, recognizing that these are the mainstay of Canada's economy. They continue to be our economic backbone. The government will provide measures to assist small businesses by improving access to financial assistance and other services provided by government departments.
The Speech from the Throne was an interesting and valuable document giving much reason for optimism across Canada in general and Prince Edward Island in particular. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the privilege of speaking today.

It is customary to extend one's good wishes to newly appointed or newly reshuffled cabinet ministers. This is a bit more difficult these days because one must check the morning paper every day to see who is still around. But I do wish the survivors well. In the lame-duck category in which they find themselves, they will need a plentitude of good will. I will be plenteously generous with them.
[DOT] (noo)
I am glad my old friend and fellow-islander, the Minister of Veterans Affairs is still in his post. I also hope that the move of a segment of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Charlottetown will take place while he is still minister so that we may both have an opportunity to attend the ceremonial opening.
It is hard to sort out the winners and losers in the kind of shuffle the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) engaged in a few weeks ago. But surely one victim was the man who least deserved it, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mac-Eachen). This distinguished maritimer, skilled debater, and splendid scholar was doing a good job as Secretary of State for External Affairs and was gaining confidence and international respect as day followed day. So he is withdrawn from the international scene, from the world of diplomacy, to what? To be the adjutant in the Prime Minister's last stand. If he were Demosthenes and Plato combined, the President of the Privy Council could not so function in this House as to make this government look good. While it might have been a noble gesture for him to know his true Grit loyalty it will, I fear, prove something less than a brilliant exercise in judgment. How cruel to expect him to avert the inevitable, to arrest the irresistible.
This government's caravan, with its cargo of disillusionment, dissension, decrepitude, and debility is on a downward course and while, from time to time, a square wheel is removed, another one is added and it is always hard to make useful salutary changes when plunging downhill. There are some who say the government is going nowhere. I disagree. I think it is headed for that well known destination described by Mackenzie King in a rare moment of candour as the "Valley of Humiliation".

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie
The present government is passing through a phase well known to tottering administrations. I have witnessed it in my own lifetime and I have read about it in the history of Canada. The reaction is traditional: first, blame the press-and that process is certainly under way. The next is to make the same look different by indulging in some sort of cabinet shuffle, making the new look old and the old look original. The third step is to present to the people a Speech from the Throne which will offend none and attract all. Last-and this technique is, I must admit, a new one because of the development of the electronic media-spend millions of dollars on the principle that if you tell the people often enough they will eventually catch on and realize that the government is right and that they are wrong.
How futile is all of this! How many Canadians can recall today even 50 per cent of the glittering generalities contained in the Speech from the Throne-and most of them were more general than glittering? Mr. Speaker, these exercises, these tinkerings will not work, nor should they work. For as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) so rightly noted, the government is seeking not to change itself but to cajole the public into changing its perception of the government.
There is an old saying that Hell knows no fury like a woman scorned. I have not scorned a woman, but I have read this adage. And I would say that a government faces no fury like an electorate misled. What happened in St. John's West and Ottawa-Carleton is but a forerunner of what is to come. If it is too late to say repent, at least I can say "beware". And when the change does come it will not be because of any great difference in ideology or because the country is moving to the left, or to the right-I do not think those terms are very meaningful in Canada. It will be because the people are sick and tired of being poorly governed.

speechtext:
How long has it been since this great, prosperous and wonderful nation has had an efficient government in charge of its affairs? That is what the people are wanting. They are crying out for good administration. But, Mr. Speaker, you know my temperament. You know I do not want to indulge long in criticism, even of the gentlest variety. Being a man of great solace and solicitude, I know there is pain and anxiety across the way. I remember when I sat across the way and the omens were pretty clear; it was not kind to predict what we all knew, in our hearts, was going to happen.
On a much more positive note I would like to say how moved I was to hear the many tributes from all parties in the House and from Mr. Speaker which were tendered to the Hon. John Angus MacLean, then member for Malpeque and, prior to that, member for Queens-one of the last two dual ridings in Canada. For 11 years Mr. MacLean and I jointly represented the people of Queens which contains the City of Charlottetown, the cradle of confederation. A man of honour, wisdom, and ability he was a great colleague and I treasure the opportunity given me to serve as his running mate. I salute him as a friend and political comrade of nearly 20 years standing.

The relatively long recess allowed me the happy opportunity of spending a good many consecutive weeks in my home province-than which there is none more beautiful. Prince Edward Island, like the Atlantic region generally, is particularly sensitive to the dominion government's actions and non-actions.
During the last session I cautioned the then Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development against the imposition of fees in the Prince Edward Island National Park. This past summer has shown a striking decrease in visitors to the park. It has also placed heavy pressure on areas adjoining the park. I need hardly say that this makes for a serious environmental problem and increases the strain on the resources of the province and of its government. I am interested in the full story of last summer. How will the cost of establishing toll gates compare with the revenue intake from a reduced number of visitors?
Other members have discussed the gravity of the transportation situation, especially, but not exclusively, as it affects Atlantic Canada. The user-pay policy is as iniquitous as it is against the spirit of Canadian federalism. As my colleague, Mr. MacLean, once said in Charlottetown, the people of P.E.I. have learned that "Otto Lang" is two four letter words!
The whole great nation-building exercise which began in Charlottetown in 1864 was designed to do many things. One of the first was to share the inequalities and to make an effort to redress the imbalances of the extremities of the new dominion, with special provisions written into the original document to compensate for the special needs of certain areas. Almost immediately after the dominion was formed, further special arrangements, subsidies and the like, were provided for. I do not accept the suggestion of certain ministers that you must have policies that are universally applied all across the country. We have had it otherwise since 1867.
Since I am talking about our country's early days and its founding fathers, I should like to make one more plea for a little historical accuracy in today's constitutional discussions and posturings. It has now become popular to use the word "patriation". I suspect that this was the inspiration of some of the brains trust in the Prime Minister's office; I cannot imagine it coming from anywhere else.
Purists might shrink from either word, but if we must use this expression it should be "repatriation". Despite its name, one quite appropriate for the time, the British North America Act is the product not of British but of Canadian statescraft. It was made in Canada by Canadian leaders for the governance of a new Canadian state. As John A. Macdonald said, most of the decisions were made in Charlottetown, a city which I have the honour to represent.
I see the Minister of Veterans Affairs is not here now, but I must say I agreed completely with what he said about the principles of bilingualism. However, I know he will be pleased to recall, as I was, the historic note that among the fathers of confederation French was not the tongue of the majority. Nor
October 25, 1976

was English. The mother tongue of the majority of these illustrious men was Gaelic, as it was of the ancestors of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and myself.
It is demeaning of the work of our founding fathers not to suggest that we are bringing home the constitution, where it was worked out by political men in political discussion in the finest exercise of political statecraft. So let it be "repatriation", if, Sir, you will pardon the reiteration.
Historically, governments have seen the need to make special arrangements for special needs and circumstances. The iron clad, rigid, universalist approach of ministers which has been revealed in recent years does not deal with a nation's basic need. It does not help hold the country together.
Apart from transportation, reference has been made by colleagues of mine to a very grave problem, the high electricity costs in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. On the "late show" last week, to a tremendous audience, I gave specific details of this problem and I know that the appropriate minister- because he was present-will be working on the matter. However, I must renew my plea to deal urgently with an urgent problem.
The answer, of course, in the long run is development of the Fundy tides, but a measure of assistance should be extended by way of a temporary subsidy to deal with a temporary but grave situation. In Prince Edward Island I am proud that steps have been taken by enterprising people in the field of technology to produce wind powered energy, but because of the imposition of stiff taxes on component parts it is difficult for islanders or other Canadians to convert to this form of energy. At a time when one minister is suggesting to Canadian to watch the use of depleting but popular forms of energy and to move to something else, you will find that minister's colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin), making it difficult, through their interpretation of legislation and the legislation they present, for people to convert to this very obvious, useful and I think timely form of energy production. I ask for consistency in this regard as in others.
Since I know there are many great orators waiting to follow me and, since I usually do not take all the time that is allotted, may I finally make the plea, as I and my colleagues have done so many times, that on the matter of dealing with regional economic disparity let all members of the government be on the same course. There is no use in one minister who heads the Department of Regional Economic Expansion trying-and I believe most ministers have tried-to conquer this great problem in confederation, this grave disparity, inequity and inequality, if all his other colleagues in the government pay absolutely no attention to such a concept.
Recently my colleague, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), and the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) dealt with this problem powerfully and well and I support every argument that they made. It is a sham, a mockery, to talk about fighting regional disparity, as the Minister of Veterans Affairs has done, unless the whole gov-
The Address-Mr. Francis
ernment is geared in that direction. It ill suffices to have one minister dealing with the matter within a limited range of initiative if his colleagues do not grasp this central truth, that this country is not prosperous if any of its segments or regions are not partaking of the general prosperity and development.
It is shocking in the Atlantic region and in certain other regions to see that the gulf, instead of narrowing, is widening. There are lots of reasons for conflict within confederation. They are not all over culture, language, and political labels. They are over the lack of fairness, the lack of the use of governmental machinery to distribute the wealth of the nation to all its people. That surely is what a dominion government is for. That surely is the challenge to those in power in a dominion government. That is what I ask, that is what I urge, and that is what I put forward as one of the great priorities, not for my region alone but for the whole country. There will then be in this land a degree of equity and regional equality, and our citizens will not suffer if they do not live in a province that has great mineral wealth or other attributes of great economic success. If this message and it alone can get through, something will have been accomplished in all these long years of pleading, arguing, and trying to give a helpful direction to a sometimes helpless government.

speechtext:
On October 10, 1974, a little over two years ago, I participated in the previous debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I have taken the trouble to look back at what I had to say then and it seems to me that these subjects were of interest. There was the problem of amending the law concerning the Public Service Staff Relations Act. The Finkelman report had been laid before us a few months previously, and subsequently a committee of this place and the other place laboured at some length and produced a report. I understand there was reference in the Speech from the Throne to having legislation placed before this House before very long. I welcome it, Mr. Speaker, but it is long overdue.
At that time I also mentioned problems of the National Capital Commission, as did other hon. members. A joint committee of the other place and this House is reviewing these matters. I note that the position of chairman of that particular

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Francis
commission has been vacant for some four months. I hope the government will move promptly to name a replacement.
There was also in my speech an earnest plea for the creation of a ministry of the public service. In no respect have I changed my views. I hope that the government will see fit to reconsider and give some recognition to my suggestion.
I also spoke about bilingualism. At that time I was concerned about complaints I was receiving about public servants who had been moved from Ottawa to Hull and the application of Bill 22 to them. I no longer hear that kind of complaint; I hope this is a good sign. However, the policy of bilingualism in the public service of Canada is in need of drastic review. I welcome references on the subject in the Speech from the Throne and look forward to the presentation of measures in the period ahead.
The Commissioner of Official Languages has told us what a good thing it is to have our youth educated in schools in the two official languages, instead of spending much greater sums of money on an adult education program. Again, I welcome references to this topic in the Speech from the Throne. At the risk of being tedious I suggest that some of us brought forward such suggestions sometime previously. Our suggestions were not as welcome, at least not welcome in the way similar suggestions emanating from the language commissioner and others are welcome today.
I hope there will be a major expansion of grants for second language training in Canada. This of course will involve consultation with the provinces, because education is a provincial matter. The federal government will want to make sure that its funds are actually spent for the purpose.
This past summer a report was brought down concerning language teaching in the public service. The Bibeau Report on language training had some refreshing things to say, and I pay tribute to Professor Bibeau for an honest job. He said that too many positions have been designated as bilingual without regard to the actual need to use a second language. Many such positions should not have been designated as bilingual. This has been especially true in the national capital region. In particular, the requirement that every supervisor of two or more persons in the national capital should be bilingual was extreme and unnecessary and should be removed.
I am sure that hon. members on the other side of the House will contend that the application of bilingual policies in the public service was a factor in the recent by-election in the Ottawa-Carleton constituency.

Well, there is no doubt that the voters intended to convey a message, and there is no concealment of that fact. A victory of 11,000 votes two years ago was turned into a defeat by 16,000 votes in October, 1976. What were the voters saying? That is the question.
Let us put aside the campaign for a moment. I believe that a large number of faithful supporters of the party were turned off from the day of the nominating convention. I believe that

the successful candidate at that convention was not adequately briefed about the implications of the language policy in the public service. He was not made aware of the deep distrust which many voters in this area feel, not only with regard to the application of the policy but with regard to the government's intentions concerning the policy.
In many ways the National Capital Commission region, 40 per cent of its population being Francophone, is a microcosm of Canada. National issues are often sensed here before they are sensed in other parts of Canada.
The credibility of the Liberal party is at stake. Just what does our party stand for in the application of bilingual policies? For that matter, what do the opposition parties stand for, because they have given us no indication in this debate or any other debate of what they would do if they were in power- and this applies to the NDP as well as to the official opposition.
