speechtext:
Speaking to the Liberal party in Toronto recently, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) faced squarely the implications of what the Gallup poll has been saying about my party. We all know what the implications will be for our country if my party is reduced to one representing French Canada, with a handfull of seats outside French Canada, and if the Conservative party is to represent English-speaking Canada, with a small number of seats in French Canada. We know what the implications will be for our country, and we should all let that knowledge weigh on our consciences. The Prime Minister threw out a challenge to our rank and file. He said that if, recognizing the grave threat to national unity, we were to sit back and allow this to happen, Canada would be destroyed and we would feel guilty for the rest of our lives.
Speaking in this debate the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) said that there was a heavy responsibility on English-speaking ministers to explain the government's policies. Many have said that the solution is to hire better communicators. Mr. Speaker, it is not just a problem of communication; it is not just a problem of the rank and file, the "grassroots", to use an expression I do not like, doing its job. It is not just a question of English-speaking or French-speaking ministers doing their jobs. There is, I submit, an even deeper malaise in our party.
The President of the Treasury Board also said something about throne speech debates: they come from the heart, without restriction on subject matter.

I intend to speak about three speeches delivered by government backbenchers; I am referring to the members for Matane (Mr. De Bane), Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) and Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier). First I would like to point out that within the Liberal party, there are two different standards. When a French-speaking government member criticizes the policy of the government-he is free to do so-nobody objects. But when an English-speaking member dares criticize
October 25, 1976

the bilingual policy, some people say: He is against bilingualism, he is against Quebecers and French-speaking people, he is even supposed to be narrow-minded. With this attitude, he will remain a backbencher for a long time. That is true, Mr. Speaker.

I now return to the speeches to which I referred. In many ways they are different; but in many ways they are appallingly alike. They all speak of ancient wrongs. Some of them go back centuries. They demand immediate measures to rectify ancient wrongs. Not one of the three referred to Bill 22, or to the efforts of people such as the former hon. member for Lange-lier, (Mr. Marchand), or to the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) to tell Mr. Bourassa that our efforts to sell bilingualism outside Quebec are seriously impaired by his repression of minority language rights within Quebec. 1 am told that at least two of these there have spoken on other occasions against Bill 22. Careful reading of their speeches leaves me under the impression that all three really accept the bill. They feel that Quebecers have somehow failed to communicate Bill 22's true meaning to English-speaking Canada. Perhaps they too should hire better communicators.
What truly frightens me is the use of statistics by both the hon. member for Matane and the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont. By picking and choosing this department and that department they draw highly inflammatory conclusions. They both refer to the percentages of Francophones in senior management posts in the public service, and infer that no progress has been made in advancing the careers of Francophones. They nowhere refer to the fact that while the percentage of Francophones across Canada is 27 per cent, the percentage of Francophones in the entire public service is over 27 per cent. They nowhere refer to the fact that of 1,122 university graduates hired in 1975-out of whose ranks future managers are likely to be recruited-no fewer than 333 were Francophones, or nearly 30 per cent. There is no mention of the distinct progress made in the over-all levels of management within the last three years-something like 18.5 per cent, according to Public Service Commission statistics, for Francophones in management categories. That figure has gone up to 20.6 per cent.
Distinct progress is being made. But, if one were to read their speeches one would gather there has been an absolutely dismal denial of opportunity to Francophones in the public service. When they pick out this department and that department they do not mention the Secretary of State's Department, for example, the House of Commons staff, or the mint, all of which have high percentages of Francophones at all levels. Indeed, when some activities of the Mint were moved to Winnipeg, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) insisted on a quota of at least one third Francophones for all posts.
When, however, 400 positions in the same Department of Supply and Services were moved to Matane we could well ask
The Address-Mr. Francis
what guarantees if any were provided for Anglophones? The hon. member for Matane cited statistics presumably from the Bibeau Report to the effect that Francophones are not permitted to work in French. A very important part of the answer to that problem is the creation of units working in French. [Translation]
The government clearly intends to set up units to encourage French-speaking civil servants to work in their mother tongue. However, if the government intends to pay bonuses for bilingualism, we must consider the results. For example, will those working in French-speaking units receive bonuses for bilingualism? Evidently not.

Let us just think of what the effect of a policy of bilingual bonuses is. Are we going to pay the people who take their training at government expense for that very modest achievement in bilingualism to which Mr. Bibeau referred? Are we going to say that everybody in a designated position will get a bonus for speaking two languages when it has been very clear that a large number of the designated positions do not use two languages? How can the hon. member for Matane and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont suggest that the government immediately take measures for bilingual bonuses and then complain that the government does not undertake policies to encourage the greater use of French? French language units are the means by which there is a direct encouragement of French language work in the public service, and one policy works against the other.
In fairness to the hon. member for Matane he implies that he does not really believe in the policy of national bilingualism. He refers to a two-nation solution. On page 351 of Hansard of October 21 he is quoted as follows:
That is one of the reasons why I think the concept of a bilingual Canada is a faulty political solution to the cultural problems that must be posed in different terms. An analysis of the destiny of French Canada and English Canada in North America and their quest for identity Finally always boils down to two national communities with close historical links pursuing their future in an independent way.
I would like to know how many members on this side of the House agree with these views. I, for one, do not.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont was responding to statements made by the former minister of national defence giving his views on entrenching language rights in the constitution. The member's emotional response in the light of the dreadful historical background of Manitoba is understandable. He and others, however, come dangerously close to a doctrine that the rest of us are guilty of heinous crimes by reason of our ancestry. There is no conceivable way by which I, or any other living Canadian, can atone for the sins of the Peace of Paris, General Murray, Lord Durham, or the government of Manitoba in 1890.
What I am prepared to do, and what others are, I am sure, prepared to do, is look at today's situation in a fresh light and to try to do what is fair and just, with full respect for human rights and cultural values. The argument of "cent ans d'injus-tice" simply proves too much. It can be, and has been conjured

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Francis
up to say, that because of the terrible wrongs of the past, other wrongs are justified today. Can't we rise above this level and just once try to forget the past?
I want to say that I am not impressed by the argument of the former minister of national defence, and I have read his statement very carefully. I for one am quite prepared to discuss and consider entrenchment of language rights in the constitution, but on a basis of full equality for the English language minority in Quebec as well as for the French language minority outside Quebec.
My colleague from Ottawa-Vanier refers to the million French-speaking Canadians living outside Quebec. He argues that they are in constant danger of assimilation, that their pre-eminent status in relation to other minorities has not been sufficiently recognized, and demands special programs on their behalf. Indeed, he goes much further. At page 286 of Hansard of October 20 he is quoted as saying:
And so it is that the French-speaking minority in Canada, whether implicitly or explicitly, demands a special kind of protection, greater than that of official equality, in order to defend itself against the risk of anglicization ...
What are the limits of "a special kind of protection, greater than that of official equality"? It seems to me that demands on this basis are capable of being escalated indefinitely. It is this aspect of vague, escalating and never-ending demands that has irritated many Canadians, particularly those whose origins are neither English nor French.
In the city of Ottawa and in this region we have made very substantial gains in protecting the rights of the French minority. I welcome in my own constituency the Ecole Champlain. I welcome a French language secondary school and regret that it was not established many years before. We have made progress; we have done things. A speech which does not give due recognition to the fact that there is some good will and good faith on behalf of a majority in the community is a disservice to those on whose behalf the hon. member presumes to speak.
I am coming to the end of my speech, but I wish to make one further point. The Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, the so-called Laurendeau-Dunton Commission, grappled at length with these problems. At the time I did not appreciate the contribution which they made, but I hereby wish to pay my tribute to them. The solution was that Canada should be a bilingual and multicultural nation. To me, Mr. Speaker, it makes a lot of sense.
Each of the three speakers to whom I referred made numerous references to Canada's "bicultural" character. I really wonder if any one of them has accepted multiculturalism, despite some references to it. Their references on careful reading are not sympathetic to multiculturalism. This is a great pity. The new Canadian communities are not likely to be attracted to the French language if they are not made welcome, and the record of Bill 22 in denying them the basic human right to choose one official language of Canada for their children is deplorable.
I for one would have liked the Prime Minister to have named a special minister of the cabinet with an exclusive

responsibility for multiculturalism. In saying this I mean no disrespect for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) who is a very much overworked man with a large range of duties.
I am concerned that there is an obligation on our party to define just what we mean by our bilingualism policy. There is an equal obligation on parties on the other side of the House.
I think certain questions must be answered. Do the speeches coming from a number of Liberal backbenchers actually represent policy of the government of the day? I do not think they do. But the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), speaking in this House, cited two of the speeches with approval. He did not in any way criticize them although he certainly gave a pretty sharp blast to the former minister of national defence.
In the present atmosphere the tone of the speeches has contributed to a serious deterioration in relationships between English language and French language communities. The doctrine of guilt by ancestry is a terribly dangerous one to espouse.
The suggestion that the Francophone minorities want something more than official equality is, I submit, something which will take a lot of explaining and a lot of professional communicators to have accepted in this country.
The doctrine of bilingual bonuses in the public service will create a great deal of difficulty in the light of the excessive designation of bilingual positions. There is the need to encourage units working in French and the fact that so many people learn their second language at government expense. It will be difficult to persuade others who did not learn a second language at government expense that those who went to expensive language training schools should also be paid extra bonuses for having succeeded in their modest degree of bilingualism in the courses.
I think the hon. members of this House are entitled to ask the Secretary of State, the Prime Minister and those who speak for the government, when the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont said as recorded at page 132 of Hansard on October 20 this year that the resolutions on official bilingualism should be amended so that only persons who are bilingual at the time of appointment can succeed to designated positions in the public service, whether or not this is government policy.
I think there is an obligation on the Secretary of State to make this clear. The Secretary of State presumably read this speech to see whether or not this is government policy. If hon. members want to know why there is concern, confusion, and discontent in the public service, they only have to look at this kind of speech.
There are many reasons why the voters in the by-elections on October 18 expressed their displeasure. In part it was a general frustration after 13 years of government by one party, in part the concern about decentralization, about the immense complications of collective bargaining. But I think fundamental to the issue in the Ottawa area is a grave concern about where we are going and what we are doing in the field of language policy. We are entitled to more than platitudes. I
October 25, 1976

hope that in the period ahead government spokesmen will issue clarifications of the government's position which will assist all of us in defending a policy which I believe is essential.
I believe in bilingualism in the public service across Canada.
1 believe in the rights of Francophone minorities across Canada and of Anglophone minorities in Quebec. I believe in the measures that have to be taken under the constitution for the protection and achievement of these goals, but I believe we have heard in this debate in the House a number of extreme positions that have done nothing to set the record straight.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking this opportunity to reply to the Speech from the Throne I should like to commend the mover and the seconder of the Address in Reply, the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) and the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance). I would also like to say how pleased I was to hear the Governor General read part of the Speech from the Throne. I commend him on his recovery and I wish to pay a special tribute to Her Excellency, Madam Leger, for the excellent job that she did and for the clear and articulate way in which she read the major portion of the Speech from the Throne.
I should like to point out as an aside, Mr. Speaker, that for us commoners who, of course, are only allowed to stand at the bar in the other place and hear the Speech from the Throne- and some of us are reasonably interested in the contents-it was very difficult to hear it, apart from Mr. Speaker himself and some of the staff, because of the constant noise that was going on. I hope that in the future when the Speech from the Throne is read those hon. members who wish to visit back and forth will refrain from doing so and will stay in their own rooms, or in the Chamber here, so that all this noise can be avoided. To my mind this is a discourtesy to the Governor General and, in this case, to Madam Leger.
It becomes more difficult with every throne speech that this government delivers for those of us in the opposition to respond. It is virtually impossible to respond in specific terms to a throne speech that is simply a mishmash of generalities and theories. I suppose that there is some purpose in this kind of approach to legislation, however. If and when any bills flow directly from the throne speech, no one will be able to tell whether or not they represent the views expressed in the speech. I do not imagine it makes any difference though, because the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has been trying for a very long time to walk down both sides of the street at the same time.
That would be a difficult thing to do, even in the best of times, but it must be especially trying at a time when the Prime Minister is looking over his shoulder to see which of his cabinet ministers is packing his bags. It seems to me that someone could set up a lucrative business ghost-writing letters of resignation for Liberal cabinet ministers. And, since it would not require any more training, that same person could even draw up some new Liberal economic policies. Just as in the case of the resignation letters, the dates could be typed in later.
The Address-Mr. Darling
I could learn to live with these zero content throne speeches and budgets-and in fact we have had to learn to live with them because that is all we have been getting over the past eight years-but I become pretty concerned when I hear the Prime Minister propose two conflicting solutions to a serious problem, usually within the space of a day, or an hour in some cases.
His answers to questions about the future of the anti-inflation program are a good case in point. On the one hand the Prime Minister butters up labour, management, and all the rest of us by saying that economic controls could very well be lifted well in advance of the target date of December of next year. Then, almost in the same breath, he says that we might have to get used to the idea of controls well beyond the cut-off date. The Prime Minister says that controls could become a fact of life into the distant future, and in fact he has stated that some form of control over our economy could become a permanent aspect of our society.
While the Prime Minister might think that that is the easy way out of a tight corner, to try to confuse us by showing both sides of the coin at the same time is simply ludicrous, Mr. Speaker. All you have to do to get the Prime Minister talking out of both sides of his mouth is to ask what we can expect in the way of post-control economic policy. What comes out is a real side-show, with the Prime Minister in the role of Edgar Bergen, and the Finance Minister (Mr. Macdonald) in the role of Charlie McCarthy. When I buy tickets to a side-show, I do so in the full knowledge that I am going to be entertained. But when I ask a serious question about a very serious matter affecting our country, I do not want to be entertained; I want to be informed. I want a straight answer. Anybody can answer a question by saying that it will either be this or it will be that.
When I think of the Prime Minister's dexterity in answering questions I am reminded of a story circulating at the present time about U.S. presidential candidate Jimmy Carter. Apparently Carter has acquired some of the Prime Minister's expertise in fielding questions. Carter likes to compare himself to past figures in U.S. history who have acquired fame. It seems that when Carter was a little boy his father came into the House one day and said, "Somebody has been snipping off the tops of the peanut plants, and I have to ask you-did you do it?" Carter replied, "I cannot tell a lie, father; maybe I did, and maybe I didn't".
Another example of the Prime Minister's tightrope act concerns the controversial bilingualism program, a program that was supposedly designed to unify the country but has instead become the most divisive policy ever inflicted on our country by any government in our history. The Prime Minister has been saying lately that the government is planning measures to modify or soften the impact of the bilingualism program. And yet, only two days after the throne speech, one of the most respected members of the cabinet resigned because the Prime Minister is committed to an entirely different approach to bilingualism.
The Prime Minister is committed to the formula whereby French is to be enshrined in the constitution on an equal if not

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Darling
superior footing with English, with Quebec having a veto over any future proposed amendments to the constitution affecting language or cultural rights. This would give Quebec effective control over the constitution in perpetuity, tying the hands of all elected governments into the future. We now know beyond a shadow of a doubt why the Prime Minister is so anxious to patriate our constitution that he would consider acting unilaterally to get it over here and under his control. I am deeply concerned about what he could do with the constitution, considering that he has a passive and acquiescent majority in this House.
I fear for the future of our country, Mr. Speaker. I have to say that the government's misrepresentation of the true purpose of the bilingualism program has been underscored by the resignation of the minister of national defence and by the statement that the minister gave to the press outlining his reasons for leaving the cabinet. The minister pointed out, among other things, that the government's bilingualism program has been a failure, and that it would be a serious mistake to entrench French language rights in the constitution and give Quebec a one province veto over future amendments to our constitution. My own view is that, as much as I would like to see the British North America Act here in Canada, I would rather leave it in Britain for a while longer than risk the dangers inherent in having it brought to Canada only to serve as the personal political instrument of the present Prime Minister and the premier of Quebec.
There is another example of double-talk in the throne speech, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to comment on. This is not the only example of double-talk in the speech; in fact this document is filled with them. I refer to the statement on immigration policy, to wit:
You will be asked to consider amendments to the Immigration Act, designed to promote Canada's regional and urban development goals, promote family unity, achieve a balance between immigration levels and employment opportunities, and preserve Canada's reputation as an open, tolerant society which welcomes the energy and diversity of people from all parts of the world.
That is a very high sounding and impressive phrase, but I would call it mere puffery. There is no explanation in the speech as to what this particular phrase means, any more than there are explanations elsewhere in the speech for other such phrases. All we can assume from this is that a silly statement uttered some time ago by the former minister of manpower and immigration did indeed represent government policy.
The minister suggested that we might have to consider ways to compel immigrants to settle in rural and even remote areas of the country as a condition of being allowed to come to Canada. We are told that this would greatly reduce the flow of immigrants to our cities, help populate rural areas and even the less desirable areas of the northern regions. How the government could possibly connect this policy with the high-flown phrase "open and tolerant society" we will probably never know. Telling people where they can or cannot live is certainly not my idea of tolerance or openness. It brings to my mind the countries of eastern Europe, and it would be a very

serious mistake to allow this government or any other Canadian government to have the power to decide where our people can or cannot live.
If that is to be a part of the future immigration policy of Canada, perhaps it is time for us to ask ourselves some serious questions about where we are going. If we give our government the power to force immigrants to live in certain specified towns, areas or regions, that same power can be brought to bear on Canadians already living in the country. If anybody doubts this, I ask him to consider the stupid and tragic situation in Montreal and other parts of Quebec with regard to the issue of education. The new law regarding what language the children of immigrant families in Quebec can be educated in reflects the thinking of the Communist countries of Europe, and I doubt very seriously that any of the thousands of Italian immigrants in Montreal write to their friends and relatives about the open and tolerant situation in Quebec.
That reference to family unity in the statement on immigration policy has me puzzled, but I suppose it was just thrown in to give the statement a nice homey touch.
Speaking of homey touches, let us consider the way the government tried to squirm out of the commitment it made to the provinces back in 1969 to share the cost of provincial medicare programs. I do not have to remind hon. members about what a shock it was when the Prime Minister caused a bill to be introduced in this House earlier this year which would allow the federal government to dishonour that commitment. In the federal-provincial first ministers' conference held in Ottawa in the first week of June of this year the Prime Minister said that this was the dawn of a new era in federal-provincial fiscal co-operation. What a farce! It was the dawn of a new era of federal government cop-outs.
In the throne speech we are told that extensive discussions between the federal government and the provinces have resulted in a new framework for the sharing of costs and for making social service programs more responsive. The plain fact is that the provinces have been left holding the bag, and the federal government is concentrating in areas in which it can extend federal control over programs which rightfully belong under provincial jurisdiction.
The public treasury is thus being used to extend federal control without at the same time resulting in an improvement in the level of services. I believe that the government plans to bludgeon the provinces into accepting a universal, federally controlled and financed medicare scheme, and possibly a universal hospitalization plan, and I have no doubt that that is the real significance of the small paragraph in the throne speech dealing with this matter.
There is a veiled reference to the intention of the government to seek extension of the Canada Pension Plan to involve housewives, but no clear commitment. I hope we will soon hear of some concrete steps being taken in this direction. I am a firm believer in the need for and the justice of extending old age security benefits to widows and spinsters from age 60, with a means test, and for including housewives in the Canada Pension Plan. In too many cases these people are forced to

turn to welfare programs to see them through those difficult years until they qualify for the old age pension. This is downgrading, and it is poor economics.
By simply extending the universality of the old age pension plan, we would remove a load from the shoulders of municipal agencies whose primary function is to serve the short term needs of the disadvantaged. That function does not at the present time fall within the sphere of operations of other agencies.
Hon. members will note that I specifically mentioned spinsters and widows and not male persons. I did so because I feel that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) might be willing to go one step further, and I am quite sure that if legislation to this effect were brought in, it would certainly be welcomed by the great majority of Canadians.
As a small businessman of some years standing I have a particular interest in this type of economic activity. I do not require the services or the assistance of a government agency at this point as far as my own business is concerned because, when I last checked, it was being operated reasonably well. Some people tell me that it is being operated even better than when I operated it. It is operated by my two sons, and it is quite a prosperous business. However, there are thousands of small businesses in Canada today which could do with some assistance by way of low or fixed interest loans, preferably from a government agency or a government sponsored private lending institution.
As other hon. members have said about this particular subject, small businesses in Canada are our largest single employer, and if we are going to be really serious about tackling the unemployment problem in a meaningful way then we have to tie our efforts in with Manpower. I am one of those who at times has taken great exception to the unemployment insurance rip-offs in the past, and I still keep a sharp eye on the unemployment figures and also UIC payouts. However, I firmly believe that the average Canadian would rather work than collect UIC benefits, and since it is the government which must find jobs for these people I suggest we start looking in the right direction, and the sooner the better.
We can start by easing the pressure on those who are already employing people. We are burdening small and medium size businesses with excessive paper work and regulations. The additional paper work inflicted on businesses by the Anti-Inflation Board has been the straw which broke the camel's back in many cases. That is not only poor economy; it is also stupidity. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, prior to six o'clock I was pleading the case for the small businessmen across Canada and pointing out how necessary it is that we give serious consideration to providing every kind of help, financial and in other ways, to this very important part of our economy.
In the United States assistance to small businessmen is much superior to what we offer in Canada. The essence of the Canadian economic system of private enterprise is free competition. Only through full and free competition can free markets, free entry into business, and opportunities for the expression of growth and personal initiative and individual judgment be assured. The preservation and expansion of such competition is basic not only to the economic well-being but to the security of this nation. Such security and well-being cannot be realized unless the actual and potential capacity of small business is encouraged and developed. It is the declared policy of this party that the government should aid, counsel, and protect in so far as is possible, the interests of small business concerns in order to preserve free and competitive enterprise.
We should have an act in many ways following the American small business act which is utilized to assist in the establishment, preservation, and strengthening of small business concerns. This would improve the managerial skills employed in such enterprises, with special attention given to small business concerns located in all rural areas where there are high numbers of unemployed or people on low incomes, or to concerns which are owned by low income individuals. Private as well as public managerial skills and resources should be mobilized in order to reach these objectives.
In Canada at the present time we have the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, the federal Business Development Bank, and the General Assistance Adjustment Board under the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. One plan which supplies working capital for small business is the general assistance plan which advances loans. This is restricted to manufacturers who have been threatened by foreign imports, however.
I feel we should aid small businessmen not only to get money for equipment so that they can expand but to obtain working capital. They should be allowed an opportunity to get off the ground, that is, they should not have to pay back the principle or interest for the first couple of years so that they may generate some cash flow.
The interest charged the businessman should be 1 per cent over prime for the bank and 1 per cent for the agency which guarantees the loan. At the present time the maximum loan is $25,000. This is a joke, Mr. Speaker. In the United States the maximum is $100,000. With the way costs are today it might be feasible to go higher than this, and in certain cases as high as $300,000. In the Small Businesses Loans Act, 1970 revised statutes, chapter 10 sets the limits on the total assets of a borrower at about $50,000, which is ridiculous.
The relevant act in the United States provides much needed and excellent services for the borrower such as managerial training and feasibility studies. Feasibility and market studies enable a businessman to know where he can sell his product

October 25, 1976
The Address-Mr. Darling
and also whether it is a viable enterprise. He is also given information which will probably enable him to avoid possible pitfalls and errors of which he may not be aware. The United States government has provided a fund of $6 billion for this project for the small businessman.
Our chartered banks should be induced to provide more risk capital for small businesses, say up to $500,000. Banks should be willing to accept security on a much lower basis, say one to three, rather than as in some cases at present, two to one in their favour. Expansion of our Canadian banking system will not improve until banks are influenced to make the types of loans which are available in the United States.
I have had many letters, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure have many of my colleagues, from frustrated businessmen who want to know how they can qualify for the so-called small business loan at a preferred rate of interest. I have a file here and I could read off the names of businessmen who want to expand and are unable to do so. I have figures provided by the Minister of Finance which show that his department has made loans under the Small Businesses Loans Act to the end of June this year of $5 million. That may seem like a great deal of money, Mr. Speaker, but it probably means no more than 200 or 250 loans. Spread across Canada, that is not very much.
In the past couple of weeks I have had requests from businessmen who want to expand their operations. They qualify for loans, having the proper assets and so on. They were not able to get these loans at the preferred rate. The reason they were given was that their credit rating was too good. The bank stated that these loans were for those whose credit was not as good. I am sure the bank would not even recommend a loan to a businessman or prospective businessman if there was not a possibility of it being repaid.
These people were finally able to negotiate with the banks in their home towns, but at a higher rate. I believe the so-called small business loan interest rate is lOVi per cent. One man was able to negotiate a loan at 11 'A per cent, and another at 12 per cent.
I wrote to the Minister of Finance last week as well as to the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) asking what the new plan will be and whether the government is going to do more than pay lip service with regard to providing money to small businessmen at the preferred rate.
The other night I saw a television report on the new minister responsible for small business visiting in Russia. I presume he will be contacting many small independent capital businessmen there to find out how they proceed. However, if he wants to talk to the most progressive of those, he will have to go to Siberia.

When I am finished, Mr. Speaker.
More than 50 per cent of the salary and wage earners in Canada are employed by small businesses. If all small businesses in Canada closed their doors at the same time, the economy would come to a standstill. Large corporations and their workers are protected from the vagaries of market conditions, bureaucratic harassment, cash supply, and other matters. The unionized workers are protected by their unions, and by our labour laws. The large corporations have batteries of lawyers to run interference for them, but not so the small businessman and his workers.
Big business has assets and productive capacity to use as collateral for loans. Small businesses very often have to borrow on faith, and there is never enough of this faith to go around. In the United States they have the small business administration to make loans to small businesses, and also to advise and train people in small business or who want to start up a small business. We need something like that in Canada. There is too much disparity between lending institutions, and between regions, with respect to the availability of small businesses to obtain loans for operating expenses, and to finance expansion.
Without a set government program of loan assistance or guarantee, lending institutions in Canada would rather lend large sums of capital to large corporations, against secure collateral, than to lend small sums to small businesses which often cannot offer blue ribbon collateral. In my view we must recognize that there is another kind of blue ribbon collateral; the initiative, resourcefulness, and determination of the small business entrepreneur in Canada. If we support the people who are presently providing the largest percentage of jobs in our country today, then they will be able to create still more jobs. This would be better than trying to solve the problem by paying out still more unemployment insurance, grants, welfare, and all the other government stop gap measures.
A large percentage of the chronically unemployed in Canada do not have the specialized skills and talents required by most of the large corporations. Small businesses do not require these specialized skills and rare technical talents for the most part. The only place where these unskilled unemployed can be absorbed is in small business, and that can only happen if the small business community is healthy and can grow.
Our leader spoke last Thursday in Winnipeg to a gathering of approximately 1,200 people, outlining some of the things this party will do after he is elected Prime Minister in 1978. He stated, and I quote:
-I place considerable emphasis on the role of small and medium-sized entrepreneurs. We all know the Liberal and socialist bias toward bigness and bureaucracy. I do not share that bias.
It is worth noting, too, that economies such as the United States, Japan and West Germany-all of which have achieved productivity performances as good or better than our own in recent years-all have a larger small business component within their economy than we have.
October 25, 1976

Each of these countries have governments with a genuine commitment to the small business sector and who support that commitment with concrete and positive policies... Tax policies that encourage-not discourage-the development of small family or employee-owned businesses and which permit such businesses to be passed along to new generations without prohibitive tax penalties.. .
On the available evidence at least, there is no indication that the Trudeau government has given even serious study to these successful policies of other countries. Its preference here-as in so many other areas-is for the quick and the cosmetic . .. name a Minister of State and hope that no one watches long enough to see whether he actually does anything.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed an honour to join those who have spoken before me in this debate to express my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I commend him for his attention to and thorough work on the policies relating to small business. I wish he would have done the same with regard to the whole question of national unity and bilingualism. If he had, he would not have made the remarks he did before the dinner recess.
As I understood the hon. member this afternoon, he expressed the hope that the constitution would not be patriated to Canada if the language rights of English speaking Canadians would not be protected, as indicated in a newspaper article published last week in Montreal. He insinuated that it would be the intention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to patriate a constitution that could endanger these language rights. That was a very unfortunate statement by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. He would not have made that remark if he had read the letter which the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) sent to the editor of the Gazette that same day in which he stated, in essence, that it was erroneous to suggest that under Article 137 of the BN A Act English language rights could be abolished by a single act of the National Assembly of Quebec once the proclamation had been effected, and that Article 30 of the draft proclamation was most explicit concerning language rights. The letter went on to say, and I quote:
Article 30 of the draft proclamation is most explicit concerning language rights currently existing in the BNA Act:
"English and French are the official languages of Canada, but no provision
in this Part shall derogate from any right, privilege or obligation existing
under any other provision of the Constitution".
I shall quote one further paragraph from the letter:
"The provisions of the draft proclamation respecting English and French language rights were designed to supplement existing constitutional rights at the federal level and not to replace, abrogate or lessen existing rights in the British North America Act at the time of patriation."

The Speech from the Throne is rich with exciting goals. It speaks of national unity, the subject which has been engaging much of our attention today. It deals with employment. It deals with labour management relations. It deals with collective bargaining information centres. It brings

The Address-Mr. Caccia
up the question of industrial safety and the establishment of health centres. It deals with the question of testing new methods of improving working conditions. It has to do with promoting competition in the market place, with placing emphasis on research and development in connection with renewable energy sources, and with means of improving the efficiency of energy use at home and at work. It speaks of a new social services act to help the aged, the children and the handicapped. It has thoughts on promoting partially subsidized day-care through a system of fees relating to income. It envisages improvements to the Canada Pension Plan, including the indexing of family allowances. It speaks of setting a goal of one million new homes over the next four years.
Other topics in the Speech include the amplification of Canada's role in the world in connection with shaping a new international economic order, for example, changes in the Law of the Sea, environmental protection, human settlements, food production, population growth, the control of nuclear armaments, and economic development. These are the issues of our time, Mr. Speaker, and these issues are dealt with in the rather fine document we are considering, perhaps one of the best ever produced by a Liberal government within our memory.

speechtext:
I wish the opposition would deal with some of these issues and put forward alternative approaches which might be taken with respect to them.
I shall devote the limited time remaining to me to only one or two of these topics. I shall deal, first, with the subject of renewable sources of energy because it seems to me that this is a matter of particular interest to Canadians today. At present, far too heavy an emphasis is being laid on research and development on the nuclear side, as well as on the development of non-renewable sources of energy as we have known them so far.
Far too little of the total budget-I believe less than 1.5 per cent-is devoted in the field of energy to renewable resources such as solar, wind and tidal power. The present approach of cutting up the research and development pie has to be changed. I was most impressed to learn last May that the U.S. Senate had appropriated an amount of well over S300 million to be expended on renewable resource research and development. This is not ten times-which is usually the ratio between performances south of the border and our own-what we allocate to this kind of research and development, but is well over 100 times what we spend, if the reports in the newspapers are correct.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that our present approach to research and development is too timid and too one-sided. We are endeavouring to discover how we can economically store energy in one medium alone-in water. Out of all the projects I have seen or heard about throughout the country, nine out of ten of our demonstration projects try to find out whether and at what costs we can store solar energy in water. Surely there are other alternatives which need to be tested and demonstrat-

ed. This is one of the suggestions I should like to put forward in relation to the trend of our present research.
There is another aspect in the field of renewable sources of energy which is very significant to our over-all energy conservation policy, that is, whenever it is planned to introduce systems of heating by means of power from the wind, the sun, or other such sources, we become very conscious of the need for conservation principles-anything which will reduce heat losses in the structure to be built. The two processes, solar heating and conservation, are closely related.
In regard to energy conservation and thrift in the consumption of today's energy resources, I find it rather unfortunate that there has been a lack of support on the part of hydro companies in Canada for the concept. Ottawa has been urging Canadians and other levels of government to reduce their consumption of energy. This has been done in a variety of ways and I hope that we have given a good example. Nevertheless it is rather discouraging to find hydro utilities today, from Yellowknife to Halifax and Vancouver, charging rates per kilowatt hour which, instead of rewarding thrift and saving of energy on the part of the consumer, result in the consumer paying a lower per kilowatt hour if he consumes larger quantities of energy rather than smaller quantities. In other words, there is no incentive toward lesser consumption on the part of the consumer. There is a flat rate up to a certain ceiling, which varies from area to area, and then above that ceiling, as consumption increases, the rate declines. If hon. members are interested in a detailed breakdown of rates in major centres I have this background information available.
I suggest that uniform electricity rates, something we do not have now in any given area, would reward the careful consumer and provide an incentive to save which is much greater and more significant in the eyes of the average consumer than the sort of rather costly advertisements that are sometimes published in newspapers by public utilities like Ontario Hydro. On October 18 they placed an advertisement in the Globe and Mail which attracted my attention and has prompted these remarks on my part.
Returning to solar energy, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make the following observation. We need to develop a technology in the field of solar energy that is suited to the Canadian climate. In this way we will create new jobs and a new industry, not only for Canada but eventually for developing countries that are suffering serious trade deficits because they have to import oil. This would benefit their technology and allow them to capture the energy stored in the sun, energy that is available free of charge, which is non-polluting and renewable. In this way they would be able to reduce their dependence on imported oil and thus achieve more readily a healthier economy than they have at the present time.
I am told that in the United States large companies like Corning, Phillips, Owen-Illinois, to mention just a few, are planning to open up markets worth millions of dollars, creating new jobs and developing a new industry in this field, in the
October 25, 1976

hope that they may capture one day not only their own market but foreign markets as well.
It is true that in the U.S. climatic conditions are more advantageous than ours, but there is really no excuse, particularly on our prairies where there is an extensive number of hours of radiation through the year, for us not to develop technology in this field. In this regard I was very impressed to observe on the roof of the legislature in Winnipeg last month a set-up made possible by the co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, whereby solar collectors manufactured by companies in different parts of the world will be tested during the next 12 months or so, and the results of these tests, which are designed to determine the quality of this equipment, be made available to the public.
I also suggest that we need tax credits. Canadians who change their heating systems in their homes, not only by improving insulation-on which we have already removed sales tax-but by making use of wind power and solar energy, should be rewarded. This would apply to those who renovate existing homes or build new homes. Use of these energy sources is, in the end, to the benefit of everyone.
We need a special program by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to encourage manufacturers in Canada to enter this field and compete in developing an industry, rather than our becoming importers of products developed by other countries such as Holland, which I understand is very much interested in this field, and by the United States.
Responsibility for solar energy is presently dispersed among three different departments, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Ministry of Science and Technology and the National Research Council. We need to bring these responsibilities under one minister. I am glad to see the Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Faulkner) turn round and look in my direction as if to indicate that this makes some sense, in theory at least, to him.
I should like to close this subject by referring to the Ark which was inaugurated a few weeks ago by the Prime Minister in Prince Edward Island. This is an experiment in the utilization of solar energy and it carries the following inscription:
The Ark-an early exploration in weaving together the sun, winds, biology and architecture on behalf of humanity.
I think it appropriate to put that quotation on record because it contains a statement of policy and also poetry. It seems to me that in solar energy we can bring together once again hope, policies, and poetry for the good of mankind. We have arrived at the point in our development where we do have the technology to harness solar power which is available to us daily, as we are all aware.
In the remaining time I should like to move on to another subject, namely, the statement on employment policies contained in the Speech from the Throne. I should like to refer to the very fine intervention made by the minister the other day. I should like to congratulate him on the speech he made because quite clearly it is a first step in the right direction. It shows the intention of the government to begin utilizing better our
The Address-Mr. Caccia
economic resources, namely, funds available through unemployment insurance, plus those available through general taxation, in an innovative manner. First, we would need to base our actions on the experience of preceding years and I hope his announcement will be regarded as the first step towards an employment strategy.
It will be a strategy when it contains certain elements of flexibility which the policy does not yet seem to contain. We can speak of a strategy when there is flexibility in our approach to institutional training. At present our hands are tied in relation to the provinces when it comes to the matter of spending money for the training of the unemployed. Our hands are tied by long-range agreements which do not permit us in periods of high unemployment to change the direction of our spending; we cannot decide that, instead of having institutional training programs, we could better serve Canadians with direct job creation. We do not have this flexibility now. Therefore I urge the minister to look at the nature of these long-range agreements with the provinces, and see how we can regain that flexibility which will enable us to have funds available when they are needed for direct job creation. I am speaking of times when the government concludes that direct job creation is a better answer for the reduction of unemployment. At present such flexibility is not available.
In order to have a strategy we must overcome our hang up, or the idea that we have to trade off inflation against unemployment. In the past decade we thought that we could have either high unemployment or high inflation, but not the two together. In the 1970's we have learned that both can exist together at the same. We can have high inflation, plus high unemployment; yet we still seem to think that if we reduce unemployment we may increase inflation. I do not subscribe to that economic theory, Mr. Speaker. I think we can reduce unemployment if we embark on proper policies and programs, particularly those related to direct job creation, without affecting the rate of inflation.
In order to have a strategy we need to know the effect of current programs such as the Community Employment Strategy. We must know the effect of other current training programs. What is the over-all picture? How do specific and specialized measures fit into the over-all scheme?
Our approach must be much bolder to unemployment insurance utilization and job creation. The minister mentioned this aspect the other night in his speech. I am glad. But it seems to me that we have reached the point at which the concept underlying the aims of the unemployment insurance fund needs to be changed.

Mr. Speaker, in the closing minutes of the throne speech debate I wish to draw the attention of the House to some of the problems facing Canada, problems which are the direct result of the government's lack of leadership and lack of sound policies.
The Speech from the Throne reminded me of the 1974 election campaign. In that campaign the Liberals made promises left and right; after they were elected with a majority government they did not fulfil those promises. We are seeing that process repeated. This evening I shall criticize the government and recite a litany of government errors and inaction. Then I shall try, through constructive criticism, to suggest alternative policies which I and my party think will put Canada back on the road to a healthy economy in which most are employed and enjoy a decent standard of living.
My first point concerns the infamous anti-inflation program which the Liberal government imposed on the people of Canada. We in the New Democratic Party have been persistent and consistent critics of this program, not because we are against controls, not because we do not want to see inflation limited in this country, but from the simple point of view that we think this program is unfair and unworkable. I fail to be convinced by the arguments of my Liberal colleagues opposite that the situation in 1975 was different from the situation in

1974,	and therefore was the reason why the government did an about-face and implemented controls to which it was so violently opposed less than a year ago.
We heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and from his cabinet colleagues that inflation was a world-wide phenomenon which could not be controlled merely by policies taken in Canada, and that no matter what policy this government followed it would not affect the prices of imported goods. In addition they said that if wage and price controls were imposed they would come down harder on the worker and that there would be inequities in the program, that it would create a bureaucratic nightmare, and that it would not only disenchant labour but would cause skepticism in the business community.
I fail to see that that situation has changed. In fact what the Liberals said against controls in 1974 is just as valid today in 1976. I think the Liberal members of parliament, many of whom were elected on the coat tails of the Prime Minister in 1968 and are currently down in the mouth because of his unpopularity, should look not just to their leader and point the finger of blame, but should look at themselves and at the kind of statements and promises they made to the Canadian electorate in 1974, and realize that now the chickens are coming home to roost. They should realize that they could not deceive the public in 1974 and expect to get away with that without repercussions.
There is a lack of trust in politicians by the people of Canada and much of that lies squarely on the shoulders of the Liberal party and the way they deceived the electorate by campaigning against controls in 1974 and imposing them in
1975.	At least the Conservatives are consistent. It is the Liberals who do an about-face and try to get away with it. I think the Canadian electorate in 1978 will pass judgment on that kind of political manipulation.
The anti-inflation program certainly has been effective in controlling wages. The unorganized find that their wages have been limited to an average of 7 per cent. We were told of course that this program was designed primarily to help the unorganized, those people not in unions, fight the ravages of inflation. Yet they have gained the least in terms of wage settlements. Organized labour has been able to obtain average wage settlements of about 11 per cent. The inequity is that they have not been based necessarily on the productivity or profitability of the particular industry in which workers find themselves. However, their wages are now arbitrarily set by the Anti-Inflation Board, or, more frequently, rolled back in an arbitrary manner by the administrator. I know my Liberal colleagues like to tell us that already they have controlled wages, or that they have kept prices rising at a slower rate than before the program was established. That of course is based on the assumption that wages are the primary cause of inflation.
In most industries today the wage component, especially in the manufacturing area, is somewhere around 10 per cent of

The other great problem facing Canadians, and where the government has again failed so miserably, is unemployment. I was speaking this afternoon to a group of West German trade unionists who are visiting this country. They asked me about the employment situation in Canada and were shocked to hear that we had an unemployment rate of 7 per cent, or over some
700,000	unemployed, whereas in most modern European countries an unemployment rate of 1 per cent to 4 per cent is considered horrendous. We lived with high unemployment in this country for too long, to the point where I believe governments and the general public are accepting it as the natural condition in Canada. In my party we reject that complacency. We argue that not only does unemployment degrade the man who cannot find work, not only does it bring hardship to his family and demoralizes both his family and himself, but in terms of crude economic costs to our economy it cannot be tolerated year after year.
When we tolerate that kind of unemployment at levels of 7 per cent, it means that the Canadian economy is losing each year some $7 billion in lost productivity. Add to that $1 billion in federal tax money to supplement the unemployment insurance program, and we can see the tremendous cost of unemployment to our economy. Rather than recognize this as the primary problem, the government continues its attack against inflation. Meanwhile the unemployment figures continue to mount and our economy continues to suffer in the way I have described.
We are growing rather tired in this party of the kind of band-aid approach the government takes toward unemployment. At the urging of many Conservatives and right-wing editorial commentators the government got on the bandwagon of cut-backs in government spending. Of course where did it begin cut-backs but in the meagre programs which exist to aid the unemployed? The Opportunities for Youth Program was scuttled, the Local Initiatives Program budget was cut in half, and people who were already in desperate straits took little solace from the fact that they could even get temporary employment through these programs.
Now with great fanfare the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) unveils a great new employment strategy. What it turns out to be is just renaming the band-aid programs we had in the past, such as OFY and LIP, and putting them together on a year round employment basis. But

On the issue of environmental health I know there is a jurisdictional problem between the federal government and the provinces. There are two concerns to which I would like to address myself this evening and over which the government has direct control. One concern has to do with native people, and the other is the issue of uranium and the problems of radiation pollution. First, on the issue of native people, there is a growing problem of mercury pollution among native people in northwestern Ontario and also in northern Quebec. This pollu-

tion has already destroyed the economic viability of two reserves in northern Ontario, Grassy Narrows and White Dog, which I had the privilege of visiting in September. Mercury pollution from the Reed Pulp and Paper Company polluted the English-Wabigoon river system to the point where all commercial fishing had to be banned.
Then of course fishing, which was the livelihood of the native people of that area, was no longer possible, and those people were reduced to receiving welfare and to receiving handouts of frozen fish from the provincial government. The provincial government did not take action against the polluter, Reed Paper Company. The provincial government dragged its feet in terms of meeting the request of the native people that sports fishing in the area also be banned. Many natives were still acting as guides to sports fishermen, eating polluted fish and showing symptoms of mercury poisoning. No action was taken.
Then, to the amazement of all Canadians, the province of Ontario last summer met with the federal government, and both governments came up with a proposal to solve the mercury pollution problem in the English-Wabigoon river system. The proposal was to create a national park. This was without consulting the Indians to see whether this was what they desired. This was without any attempt by the federal government to use the clean water legislation already on the books, to take action, to try to restore the environment of the area and compensate the people involved.

There is some concern that hyperactive children may have emotional disorders as adults. Hyperactive children may be at high risk for teenage alcohol and other drug abuse. The characteristics of these children, including, impulsivity, short attention span, attention seeking behaviour, low tolerance to frustration in the face of social and educational difficulties suggest that this group may become abusers of alcohol and other drugs in their teenage years. One study suggests that there may be a relationship between hyperactivity and subsequent alcoholism. A higher incidence of alcoholism and hyperactivity amongst the biological parents than the adopting parents of adopted hyperactive children was found in this study. In addition it was observed that hyperactives have a high incidence of hyperactivity and alcoholism amongst their relatives.
With respect to other types of anti-social behaviour, there are reports of cases of explosive personality characterized by aggressiveness with a "hair-trigger" temper. In these cases the explosive personality was preceded by hyperactivity in childhood.
While there are few follow-up studies of hyperactive children, most of the evidence indicates that there is a relatively poor outcome for these children. There is usually a high incidence of anti-social behaviour and contact with police, and many have become institutionalized as delinquents or become psychotic. Follow-up studies suffer from lack of comparison groups, small samples and inadequate analysis of behavioural pathology. The incidence of alcohol, and drug abuse in particular, has not yet been examined in detail. The study being supported by the Department of National Health and Welfare will address itself to some of these concerns.
Hypersensitivity reactions, commonly known as allergies, to foods have been described in the medical literature for centuries. In fact hypersensitivity reactions have been observed in humans following exposure to pollens, dust, certain chemicals and, in a few isolated cases, to some artificial food colours and additives.
Food allergies of various types affect 30 to 40 per cent of the human population while milk allergy in children alone range between 10 and 20 per cent. Individuals hypersensitive to foods will have symptoms ranging from rash to anaphylactic shock and even death. A person hypersensitive to milk, for example, may upon ingestion of milk or after eating milk-containing foods, develop nasal stuffiness, hives, eczema, migraine headache, nausea, diarrhoea, or even a serious attack of asthma.
The range of foods to which people can be allergic is almost limitless. The most common causes of food allergy are milk, grains-especially wheat-eggs, fish, shellfish, fruit-especially strawberries-chocolate, nuts. In addition to natural foods, food additives such as tartrazine, parabens, vegetable oils, protein additives, caffeine, cyclamates, flavors, etc., have been implicated in allergic reactions. The symptoms elicited vary from chronic and generalized urticaria, anaphylactic type of reactions, contact dermatitis, hives, itching and edema.
This belief in the relationship of food additives and hyperactivity has evolved primarily as a result of clinical studies

conducted by Dr. Benjamin Feingold, a San Francisco physician. He recorded a marked clinical improvement in 50 per cent of hyperactive children treated with his "salicylate free diet" (also called the K-P diet). This treatment permitted a discontinuation of all drug therapy and resulted in a substantial improvement in scholastic achievement in these children. The diet given to the children contained no food additives or foods such as tomatoes, potatoes, cucumbers, squash, jams, nuts and virtually all fresh fruits, that naturally contain salicylates.
These initial clinical studies, as Dr. Feingold agrees, were empirical in nature, and although beneficial effects were observed it is not possible to draw definitive conclusions from these data. Strict adherence to these diets necessitated a dramatic modification in family lifestyle to accommodate the child's needs. Therefore, it is unclear whether the improvement in the children was due to the diet or to the additional care given the children in these particular circumstances. In addition the severely restrictive diet has been criticized by many nutritionists as being nutritionally inadequate. It is worth pointing out that in Canada the addition of food colours to baby foods is specifically prohibited under the Food and Drugs Act.
Other investigators have designed projects with the purpose of determining whether a relationship exists between food additives and hyperactivity. In a pilot study, conducted by Dr. Esther Wender of the College of Medicine at Utah, six of eleven children demonstrated an initial behavioral improvement. However, the report states that of the responders, five out of six showed a return to pre-diet behaviour over the challenge period even though diet was continued. Conclusions from this particular study spring mostly from impressionistic observations and do not lend themselves to statistical analysis.
An important preliminary attempt to investigate the hypothesis is the study designed by Connor of the Pittsburg School of Medicine. This study involved 15 children diagnosed in accordance with the American Psychiatric Association's definition of hyperkinetic reaction of childhood.
In this study statistically significant difference was found between the K-P diet and baseline measures on both parent and teacher ratings, as well as between the special diet and the control diet based on teacher ratings, but no significant difference between the special diet and the control diet based on parent ratings.
Dr. Connor concludes that "the special diet may reduce hyperkinetic symptoms" but warns that:
-it would be hazardous at this point to draw too many conclusions from this experiment, given the small size of the sample and the lack of complete consistency in the results. Any thoughtful observer will understand that a major intervention into dietary habits of a family will produce behavioral effects, regardless of the specific diets, a phenomenon well understood in the management of such conditions as juvenile diabetes. The results would have been substantially clarified if it had been possible to have objective measures of function uncontaminated by the psychological factors which are bound to operate in the family-school-child system. At this point the results point to the need for considerable further investigation.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) made some reference to the government not taking any interest in the health of Canadians or Canadians not being healthy. Looking at the other side of the House that probably seems to be true but 1 can only wonder with whom he is comparing Canadians in terms of health and health standards. The whole world agrees we have one of the healthiest populations on the globe. I wonder whether he is comparing us with a country like India, for example, a country which certainly has a great many health problems but little problem with food additives.
At first glance I am tempted to agree with the motion of the hon. member for Athabasca. Upon closer examination, I am not. If he is suggesting that the Canadian government undertake research to examine the relationship between food additives and hyperactivity, then in fact this is already being done, as I will point out in my speech. If on the other hand, the hon. member is suggesting we should duplicate research already being undertaken in other countries merely in order that we, in nationalistic pride, can say that Canadians are involved in the area, then I completely disagree.
Science is international in scope and it would not be prudent for each country to duplicate the research of other countries. The costs for a complete understanding of the causes and treatment of hyperactivity are enormous and might be related to many factors which have not been identified. Surely we should not waste our resources in vain duplication of effort, but ought rather to engage these in areas which are not already covered but which show some promise.
Certainly with a new condition such as hyperactivity, the most urgent research needed is on the causes, but that involves a much wider list of possibilities than just food additives.
Today there is an increasing public belief that foods and food additives may be a major cause of hyperactivity in
Artificial Food Additives
children. However, there is some evidence that hyperactivity in children may be a manifestation of an allergic reaction. A child may be allergic to certain foods or components of foods. For exemple, it is known that some individuals are allergic to the food colour tartrazine, others are sensitive to certain analgesics, particularly aspirin. The Health Protection Branch is currently assessing the magnitude of this problem and possible courses of action to alleviate any potential problem in this regard.
Hyperkinesis or hyperactivity is the term used to describe a syndrome in children whose unusual behaviour becomes a major problem in the home and at school. These children may be described as being constantly active, flitting from one object or activity to another, restless and fidgety; exhibiting voluble, uninhibited speech, disorganized thinking and impulsivity. They are irritable and aggressive, have a short attention span and are easily distracted. This is how parents and educators describe children classified as hyperactive. Available evidence suggests that these behavourial characteristics may lead to other social problems such as mental illness, delinquency and alcoholism in later life.
Statistics on the incidence of hyperactivity in school children vary considerably among investigators. This variation stems primarily from the lack of agreement among scientists on either terminology or definition of the syndrome. For example, school authorities report the incidence of hyperactivity in children to be as high as fifteen to twenty per cent, while psychiatrists estimate the prevalence to range from four to ten per cent.
Little is known of the etiology of this syndrome. However, perinatal brain damage, genetically inherited metabolic disorders, accidental poisoning in infancy, environmentally associated psychologic disorders and hypersensitivity reactions to foods or food components all have been implicated as possible causes of hyperactivity in children.
Abnormal brain waves in some hyperactive children have been related to physical brain damage and/or damage due to hypoxia during birth; however, the relationship between brain damage and hyperactivity is unclear.
Hyperactivity occurs four to ten times more frequently in male than in female children. Consequently, genetically inherited metabolic disorders have been considered as a potential cause of hyperactivity. It should be pointed out that similar sex ratios have been recorded for many congenital syndromes in medicine but no firm evidence exists that the sex chromosomes are involved in the transmission of these abnormalities. Whether the hyperactivity syndrome is genetic or sex-linked is not known, because of a lack of knowledge of inheritance patterns involved in hyperactivity.
Some investigators have associated hyperactivity in children with accidental poisoning by chemicals such as lead but the clinical evidence to date is inconclusive. It is known, however, that hyperactive children have a greater tendency to accidental poisoning in the home, presumably due to their intense restlessness.

Based upon all available toxicological data, the food additive must have been found by properly qualified scientists to be without appreciable risk for human consumption. If the use of the additive is considered to constitute a hazard to the health of the consumer in the amounts which may be present in foods, its use will not be provided for under any circumstances.
The use of a food additive must be effective and its primary effect must not lead to deception. Provision for the use of an additive will not be granted if its use results in deception regarding the merit, composition or value of the food.
Although it has been shown that an additive is safe and its use will not result in deception, provision for such use will be granted only if one or more of several criteria are met. For example, the food additive must improve or maintain the nutritive value of a food. This may be accomplished by the addition of a food additive to preserve the natural vitamin content of a food.
Although added vitamins, minerals, and amino acids serve the same purpose, they are not presently classified as food additives. The additive must improve or maintain the quality or acceptability of a food. Preservatives, emulsifiers, stabilizers, antimicrobial agents, filtering agents, and thickening agents are examples of food additives which improve the quality or acceptability of the food. The additive must improve or maintain the quantity of food. This may be accomplished by the direct addition of substances to preserve the nutrient value of foods. For example, anti-oxidants preserve the natural vitamin content of food, while anti-microbial agents are used to prevent microbial growth, thus decreasing food wastage due to spoilage.
These principles of safety, lack of deception, and benefit to the consumer are consistent with those enunciated by the Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Health Organization, and the U.S. White House Conference on Food, Nutrition, and Health.

During the course of these studies daily observations of the general appearance and behaviour of the animals are noted. Weekly observations are made on bodyweight and food consumption, initial and subsequent observations are made on haematology, urinalysis, enzyme activity studies, and organ function tests. At the end of the study all appropriate organs are carefully examined.
Reproduction studies are also required. Observations in the parent animals should include fertility, length of gestation,
