In the offspring the following data are required: stillbirths, litter size, foetal malformation, newborn weight, sex ratio, rate of growth, and 24-hour, five-day and 21-day survival data. If there is any indication of embryotoxicity, then further teratogenic studies are required.
After all these data have been carefully reviewed, the highest level of the chemical in the diet of the animal which caused no harmful effect is determined. This level is divided by 100 and the resulting figure is the amount which is permitted for human use; that is, if 100 parts per million in the diet of the rat caused no ill effects, then one part per million would be permitted in man's diet.
Let me explain the term "the acceptable daily intake" as it applies to food additives and to pesticides. Expert committees of the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization have established over the years "acceptable daily intakes" for a large number of food additives and pesticides. This is defined as "the daily dosage of a chemical which, during an entire lifetime, appears to be without appreciable risk on the basis of all facts known at that time." It is expressed in milligrams per kilogram of bodyweight.
The two following examples relate the acceptable daily intake of food additives to the actual amount which is being consumed in Canada. Sorbic acid is an antimicrobial preservative which may be used in such foods as bread, cheese, pickles, jams and pie fillers. Assuming that it is used in all of these foods and assuming that one individual were to eat a reasonable amount of each of them in one day, then the intake of sorbic acid would be approximately 200 milligrams.'
The acceptable daily intake for sorbic acid suggested by the World Health Organization is 1750 milligrams for a 150 pound individual. Sodium nitrite may be used in preserved meat and preserved poultry. Again making the assumption that all preserved meats contain this chemical and that one ate these foods every day, a person would be ingesting approximately ten milligrams of sodium nitrite per day. WHO has suggested that a 150 pound individual could safely consume approximately 60 milligrams per day.
Once a chemical is on the list it does not mean that it is there forever or that it is forgotten. Health Protection Branch is constantly examining the world's scientific literature, as well as conducting its own research on the toxicity of these additives.
When one realizes that 85 per cent of all the scientists who have ever lived are living today, and when one knows that the techniques and instruments used by these scientists are becoming increasingly sensitive, it is not surprising that new facts regarding some of these additives are becoming available. These scientific facts are carefully evaluated and, when appropriate, action is taken to prohibit the use of a certain additive. Since September, 1964, when specific food additive regulations were introduced, some 26 food additives have been delisted. Included were several food colours, non-nutritive sweeteners, flavouring agents, antioxidants from stabilizers, bleaching agents in flour and so on.

Foods are being shipped greater distances and are being stored for longer periods of time. Consequently there is a need for food additives to prevent or retard spoilage. In

addition, there is a trend toward buying convenience foods, for which additives are necessary.
I should like to discuss the role which food additives are playing and will continue to play in the processing of foods. While the use of chemicals in our foods has greatly accelerated in recent years and has been given increasing publicity, their use is not new. Faced with the uncertainties of climate and rainfall, and of hunting and fishing, primitive man had to learn how to preserve his hard-won food. Thus it came about that methods of drying, salting, and smoking were discovered. Hence the use of chemical additives in foods probably began when man first learned that meat could be preserved by the addition of salt.
A committee on food additives was convened in Rome, in 1956, by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Health Organization. This committee was given the task of drawing up general principles governing the use of food additives, and it concluded that, provided a food additive is safe when consumed over a lifetime, its use could be justified when it served one or more of the following purposes: the maintenance of the nutritional quality of a food; the enhancement of keeping quality or stability with resultant reduction in food wastage; making foods attractive to the consumer in a manner which does not lead to deception; and providing essential aids in food processing.
It perhaps should be also mentioned that the committee pointed our certain situations in which the use of food additives would not be in the best interests of the consumer and should not be permitted. These were as follows: (a) to disguise the use of faulty processing and handling techniques; (b) to deceive the consumer; (c) when the result is a substantial reduction of the nutritive value of the food. These principles are being used in Canada when assessing the justification for the use of food additives.
Perhaps at this point I should say what a food additive is, as defined by our regulations. A food additive is any substance including any source of radiation, the use of which results, or may reasonably be expected to result in it or its byproducts becoming a part of or affecting the characteristics of a food but does not include: (1) any nutritive material that is used, recognized or commonly sold as an article or ingredient of food; (2) vitamins, mineral nutrients and amino acids; (3) spices, seasoning, flavouring preparations, essential oils, oleoresins and natural extractives; (4) agricultural chemicals; (5) food packaging materials and components thereof, and (6) drugs recommended for administration to animals that may be consumed as food.
This rather clumsy definition encompasses the chemicals which are added to foods as colours, stabilizers emulsifiers, preservatives, anti-caking agents, non-nutritive sweeteners, bleaching agents, pH adjusting agents, and for other purposes.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that it has already been mentioned that I am supposed to catch a plane. Perhaps I should not tell anyone at what time I am to catch it because I will not be allowed the 40 minutes to which I think I am entitled in which to answer all the questions that were put to me. 1 was asked to go to Toronto with the Prime Minister of Jamaica, and I have to be at the airport at 4.15 p.m.
I should like to put a couple of points on the record. First and foremost 1 should like to reply to the point made by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I realize that my job as Minister of Agriculture is not just to be responsible to the agricultural producers of this nation. My responsibility is to the total Canadian society. Also, as has already been mentioned by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone), 1 am responsible to a great many people outside Canada who benefit from our food aid programs, and I must ensure that our producers are able to fulfil our commitments which we as a government made to aid other people in the world.
On listening to the hon. member for Battle River one might think we were not doing anything with regard to distributing food in the world. Let me point out that in this regard we are doing more per capita than any other nation in the world, not only in actual food aid but in per capita dollars from Canadian taxpayers who are paying into those programs.
I have been making notes of some of the things that have been said this afternoon, and unfortunately I find it would take much longer than the time I have today to answer all the questions that have been put, but I intend to do it in committee. However, if we stick only to the bill in the committee, it will be very difficult to answer all the questions and to reply to the character assassinations by innuendo that have been placed

1 think groups generally have supported the principle of this bill, and all speakers on this side have said that we support what the bill is trying to do, However, as I have pointed out, there are a few things we want to know. There should be equity between western and eastern producers with regard to advance payments, but the department has not been able to detail how this is going to be achieved.
In general, my main objection and concern are with regard to the two crops that mean a whole lot to the economy of the farmers in the area I come from, and we are a little unclear as to how these farmers can benefit under this bill.

Mr. Speaker, 1 indicated to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) a few moments ago that I should like to say something about this bill. I do so because a large part of my constituency, certainly in terms of area and interest, is agricultural and the people in that area depend very much on the agricultural policies of the government.
One thing which concerns me, because of the policies of the government in part, and because of certain other circumstances perhaps in smaller part, is that fewer farms are being occupied by bona fide farmers. I see a change in the agricultural industry. I do not express concern for that merely in political terms but also in terms of the community.
What seems to have happened in respect of agriculture in my constituency, and in Canada to a great extent, was exemplified by the charade we saw this morning during the question period. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) asked whether or not the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) would mind at some stage going over and chatting with the Minister of Agriculture to underscore the truth of the division between those two responsibilities. For some reason unknown to me, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs got up in the full glare of the press gallery, marched over and sat down beside the Minister of Agriculture, and shook hands with him! It was a charade. I understand it was intended as a joke, although perhaps a joke in poor taste.
I do not blame the Minister of Agriculture who received the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, but perhaps it was symbolic as well because it seems to me, as an observer of the attitude of the government and the way it functions, that it functions on the basis that it assumes there will be some conflict and that there must necessarily be some conflict between the interests of the consumer and the interests of agriculture. If I am right in that assumption-and this is the information I receive from agriculturalists as well as consumer groups in my constituency-I think the assumption is wrong and that the government should act in terms that there can be some real basis for understanding between those two important communities in Canada.
I have never said and do not say that the agricultural industry in Canada is not in all its parts basic to the prosperity
Advance Payments for Crops
of the nation. I have said publicly, here and outside the House, that people in this country must understand that food and the food industry do not begin at the refrigerator door and that there is much blood, sweat, tears, and investment which go into that industry in its basic form, namely, at the farm inside the farm gate, before food finds its way to the consumer's table or cupboard.
I have followed parliament and the development of government and governmental responsibilities ever since I went to university in this city, and as I look back over the history of recent times there seems to have been an assumption that there must be a dichotomy or division. I say with some sadness that perhaps the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and the attitude exhibited this morning by the government House leader in the discussion we had on the rules of the House, indicate that the leaders of the government in the House of Commons do not believe in the principle of collective responsibility. It was perhaps since 1968 that this breakdown has occurred. Coincidentally that year was the year the Prime Minister became leader of his party.
The concept of collective responsibility is a very important practical element in the matter of understanding and shows itself in many ways, but particularly in the way in which an attitude of confrontation has developed.
The farmers face many risks, not the least of which is the weather. Some of my colleagues have said that in terms of weather perhaps 15 per cent may be added ultimately to the price of any commodity. In other words the Canadian farmers are faced with this atmosphere and climate which we have by the grace of God. If you believe, as I do, that the government's job is to create an atmosphere in which business, including farming, can operate properly, then that point alone places an additional degree of responsibility on the government. That is why, like my colleagues who represent much deeper agricultural interests than 1 do in terms of size and the nature of the business, I am concerned about the lack of interest in agriculture and the dearth of any initiative in respect of agriculture in the Speech from the Throne.
As I understand it this really is a bill to help agriculturalists finance their operations in respect of the crops covered by the provisions of the legislation. In that sense it is a good initiative. However, it raises some questions in my mind. The hon. member for Norfolk-Haldimand (Mr. Knowles) spoke of the corn producer in southwestern Ontario. There is a large corn industry in the sense he mentioned, in eastern Ontario. It is subject to the weather and to all the other vicissitudes and so on which other members have mentioned in respect of crops which interest them.
I would hope, either in committee or elsewhere, the minister could answer the question which was put and which interests me concerning whether the Corn Council would constitute an organization or whether it is necessary for a producer's group to be established. I am also concerned that the legislation does not seem to cover independent producers who may or may not belong to this organization. There may be a reason for this which I hope will be explained. Perhaps it is necessary for

October 29, 1976
Advance Payments for Crops
With respect to the tobacco grower, I personally do not see how at the present time he can benefit from the bill at all because tobacco grown on the farm, cured and packed for sale, is not in a condition to be stored on the farm. The only way to store it is to send it to a processing and packing plant, have it redried to proper humidity, packed in hogsheads and stored. This has been done by the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board, I believe since 1964, when they entered into an agreement with certain processing companies whereby it was processed, packed and stored at a flat rate. The committee that the board set up at the time really had the control of it, and whether the act would recognize that the farmer still retains control through his committee of the marketing board is something we will have to find out.
Even prior to this the tobacco growers set up a co-operative, the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Co-operative, and they have a plant right near Kingsville where the minister lives; I think he knows all about it. They operated there for a year or two. The co-operative bought the tobacco and paid money for it on the exchange. 1 am sure that tobacco that was stored in this manner would not qualify under the bill because the farmer no longer owns it and therefore does not control it. I ask the minister to explain in some detail, when he has the opportunity, precisely how the tobacco grower can benefit from this plan.
I suppose one immediate criticism of the bill is that of discrimination. For example, the corn growers-the other group I want to talk about in some detail-of southwestern Ontario were one of the major advocates of this type of legislation, an advance payments plan similar to that of the Wheat Board in the west. Now that Bill C-2 has arrived, these corn growers will find themselves ineligible because they have not set up a corn marketing agency.
This is a pretty important crop in southwestern Ontario. I do not have to remind the minister of that; he is right in the centre of a big corn growing area. Actually, the crop has been grown throughout southern Ontario since the advent of the new early-maturing hybrids, seeds that are now available in Ontario. Corn has become a crop all through the province. In 1975 the crop was 130 million bushels. In 1976 the estimate is about 125 million bushels, down a bit. The figures I have quoted come from the Ontario Corn Council. The value of the 1975 crop was estimated to be about $320 million. 1 suggest this is an indication of the size of the industry, and a significant number of farmers have a lot of money at stake and certainly would benefit from this legislation.
As I have said, however, they have no organization that would really qualify under the bill, as I read it. This council is an organization comprised of representatives of all facets of the industry, such as the growers, elevator operators, brokers and so on. I would doubt that they would qualify, so I repeat that we should find some way in which these individual farmers can receive some of the benefits of the legislation.
Another comment with respect to corn that I want to make is that the formation of a corn marketing board or agency in southern Ontario was discussed a good number of years ago,

but the plan was never put on paper in a concrete form that could be presented to the growers for a vote on it. Therefore I repeat that there is simply no organization for them.
1 do not know whether it would be fair to accuse the government of trying to force farmers to bring themselves under marketing agencies or marketing boards. Could these marketing agencies be the forerunners of compulsory supply management on a general scale? Or is this simply a means whereby the government is trying to appear helpful while really doing next to nothing? For example, producers will have to ask themselves whether advance payments are worth the bureaucratic cost of marketing agencies' administration, especially since these costs will have to be borne by the producers themselves. No wonder the government has limited its liability to $200 million.
By and large farmers-I do not need to tell the minister this because he is one himself-are rugged individuals and they like to have control of their product, especially when it comes to selling it. They like to be able to decide when is the time to sell or whether to hold their crop till next summer. So for a third time 1 return to the suggestion that we find some way whereby an individual, without belonging to an agency, can participate in this plan.
At the federal level the grains and special crops division of Agriculture Canada will administer the program. It is not expected that more manpower will be required, I suppose because the paper work and the detailed work of administration will be done at the local level, at the agency, as the bill provides.
The bill defines what are crops, and it is interesting to note that they are grains, oil seeds, root crops and so on. I should just like to make reference to two provisions of the bill which are a little confusing and unclear, to say the least. In the interpretation section "crop" is defined as "grains, oil seeds, root crops and such other field grown crops as are prescribed." However, when we come to the application of the bill, clause 3 provides that "This act applies in respect of crops grown in Canada" period. So evidently there is no limitation.
When I asked the departmental officials about this, the grains division could not give a definite answer as to whether potatoes would be eligible. I do not see why they would not, but that is the answer they gave. They said that apples were eligible, but not strawberries. As a result there should be a complete listing to clear the matter up. The minister, either in the bill or perhaps by way of regulation, should give a listing of what products are eligible.
The maximum advances set out in the bill, $15,000 for individual producers, $30,000 for partnerships, and $45,000 for three or more partners, are the same as on the prairies. In the Wheat Board area a producer can apply for an advance payment at his local grain company. The company is allowed to pay the producer one half of the total advance applied for on the spot, a good feature. The remaining half is forthcoming after the Wheat Board has checked the application for accuracy. This might also be incorporated in the bill or put in the regulations.

raise in committee, and we certainly want to voice at this time our objection to the government for failing to pay greater and needed recognition to the agricultural industry. Take the situation which has allowed the beef industry in this country to go into its fourth year operating at below the cost of production. We should stop and recognize that the meat industry is the third largest manufacturing industry in this country, a business involving nearly $3 billion. Yet the federal Department of Agriculture has failed to take the initiative it ought to have taken to find markets, to cut off imports from the oceanic countries that are literally making Canada a dumping ground for beef. The minister might respond that he has already done so, that he has put on some quotas-

Then he cannot go out to Western Canada and tell the farmers with a clean conscience that he has done anything to protect the meat industry when he recognizes that they are now in their fourth year of operation at below the cost of production. Otherwise it is not possible to gather together 300 ranchers at two day's notice in a protest meeting about what's happening to the meat industry. We know what has happened.
It is obvious to those on this side of the House what has happened to the Minister of Agriculture. He may well have a good conscience in terms of what he wanted to do in the agricultural industry, but he has lost his power in cabinet because at least twice, and probably three times, this summer there were policy pronouncements that something was to be done for the cow-calf operator. They never naturalized. Deadline dates came and went telegrams were sent by premiers to the minister, and there were never any responses to them. The truth of the matter is that the minister has failed to get his policies past his cabinet colleagues. In other words he has failed as a minister to demonstrate the importance of agriculture to the whole country, and that is obvious today when we look at the Speech from the Throne and notice the insignificant amount of attention given to the industry which built this country, the industry which is still the backbone of Canada, the industry which is still among the greatest of exporting commodities that we have in terms of helping to improve our balance of trade position.
Whatever feeling we may have on this side of the House that these is some acceptability attached to Bill C-2, that this is a bill the minister has not goofed up as much as some of the others, we have to chastise him most severely for his failure to recognize that the agricultural industry has been underplayed and underscored. Everyone in this House and everyone in Canada traditionally eats three times a day-I would suspect the minister may do so even more than that but we must recognize that if we are to have a productive land, if we are going to use slogans like "The Land is Strong" it is high time agriculture was given its proper place in our society.
I would hope that at the next opportunity the minister has he will be announcing policies that will deal with international sales of food products such as might be a stimulus to the
Advance Payments for Crops
agricultural producers of this country, encouraging them to produce to their maximum capacity with full assurance that the government will play its proper role in seeing that those foodstuffs are sold to the Third World nations and help alleviate what has been an obvious and most critical problem-four-fifths of the world suffering from malnutrition. The fact that there has been so little mention about agriculture in the Speech from the Throne underscores the government's failure to recognize Canada's most important resource, agriculture, and those engaged in it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make some comments about Bill C-2, particularly with regard to two specific products which are produced in large quantity in the area which I represent and about which I think I have some knowledge. What I have to say will be directed to the bill, supplemented by a few questions to the minister which I know he will take the opportunity to answer either here or in committee.
Bill C-2 authorizes the federal government to guarantee loans to producers in advance payments on their farm stored crops. Those advances would give producers some operating capital for the following crop year, that is, the producer would have some money for seed, equipment, etc. Once his crop has been sold, the producer would repay the loan with the interest on it being paid by the federal government. The bill before us extends to the other producers of Canada advantages which the Canadian Wheat Board producers have enjoyed since 1957. Bill C-2 has been modelled on the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act of 1957-58. However, there are certain differences, which will be pointed out later.
Under the terms of the bill before us, advance payments will be paid out by a producer organization. Bill C-2 defines an "organization" as an organization of producers. However, the intent of the government is that the producer organization be a marketing agency. Thus the bill is rather misleading. Would there not be some way to ensure that individual farmers might receive the benefits of this legislation? I suppose, on reflection, that the administrative difficulties of doing so might be too great; the department is obviously expecting that the organizations referred to would be responsible for the book work and the administration. One of my hon. friends suggested that the banks be involved in this type of program and the minister might well give that suggestion some thought. The problem as I see it is that certain farmers are going to be disqualified from the benefit of this legislation, as I shall point out later.
Presently there are only about 12 marketing agencies which would qualify immediately under the provisions of this bill. These are provincial agencies, such as the agencies for B.C. apples, Ontario wheat, Ontario white beans, and the Ontario Flue-Cured Tobacco Growers Marketing Board, of which I am a member. These agencies are generally centred in B.C. and Ontario. This leaves many producers and many areas of Canada out in the cold and ineligible for advance payments.

October 29, 1976
Advance Payments for Crops
1 challenge the minister to stand in his place and clearly demonstrate what kind of a program he has for the sale of crops in the international market place. It is my belief that if anything is weak in our society today it is the failure to sell aggressively agricultural products in the international market place.
We talked about the minister's inability to recognize the major problems of agriculture by introducing only this one bill. Bill C-2. The assumption that must go with that is that Canada has a lot of land and therefore agriculture is really an unimportant industry. In truth, only about 13 per cent of Canada's land area is agricultural, nearly one half of which is limited to permanent pasture. Only 7 per cent is suitable for cultivation, and subsequently, field crop production. The real restriction lies in the fact that only 2.4 per cent of Canada's land area is of excellent quality, namely class one and two soil. Most of the urban growth is taking place over these top two categories of soil. Now, the data shows a very different situation. The case is not .4 per cent out of 100 per cent, but rather .4 per cent out of 2.5 per cent, or approximately 20 per cent of our best land has been destroyed by urbanization.
During the past five years 200,000 acres of Ontario farmland were removed from agricultural production for other uses. At Ontario's present rate of farmland destruction, one half of the present foodland will be out of production by the year 2000, and 100 per cent destroyed by the year 2025.
Canadian cities now cover more than 9,000 square miles, most of which were once the very best of a food-producing resource. In the five years between 1966 and 1971, Canadians lost four and a half million acres of prime farmland to urban growth.
It is important to note that of the major cities on the prairies, Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Lethbridge, Red Deer, Edmonton and Grande Prairie are all built in the middle of old geological lakebeds. That means that every major prairie city except Calgary and Medicine Hat is built on silted out soil; a prime resource for food production. Nearly one half of all land used for urbanization is from the top one twentieth of our food resource land. The reason for this phenomenon is a natural one; towns and cities sprung up and flourished in those areas where the pioneers were able to maintain productive and profitable agriculture.
At the present rate of farmland destruction in Canada, our remaining 24 million acres of class one and two soil could be reduced to as low as nine million acres by the year 2000, at which point Canada could suffer a significant food shortage. To destroy such a vast amount of a non-renewable food-producing resource is morally wrong when four fifths of the world suffer from malnutrition.
Moreover, we need to bear in mind that the world's population increases by 70 million people per year. Therefore the farmer will have to increase his present production by more than 60 per cent before the year 2000 just to maintain our current miserable level of inadequate food supply. I would like to repeat that. Therefore the farmer will have to increase his present production by more than 60 per cent before the year

2000 just to maintain our current miserable level of inadequate food supply.
These are only two sources of food; they are fertile soil and water. In the temperate zone it takes 20,000 years to produce an inch of topsoil. Farmland should obviously be considered as a non-renewable resource. More than 80 per cent of Canadians live on land that is zoned or restricted. Cities have zoning departments to plan and organize growth. Note, however, that planning is practised only when land is treated as a commodity, but void of consideration on resource land. Why has food production become second rate to housing and industrial development? Why does the Minister of Agriculture permit continuence of the use of black soil for backfill for houses and factories, when at the same time the world's greatest need is for food to stave off conditions of malnutrition?
Some will choose to cling blindly to the false position that we have ample farmland. Those who previously took such views have left an unfortunate example but a valued lesson etched in history. The Coliseum in the Roman City of Thys-drus with its 65,000 seats is a conspicuous remnant of a mismananged land. So is much of North Africa, Tunisia, Ceylon, of the Indie region, the slopes of Peru and the City of Jericho, Southern Russia, etc.
It is too easy to conclude that agriculture is secondary to civilization, that industry and commerce are all-important to an advancing culture. The truth is that every human achievement to which the current technology world bears witness is based on successful agriculture, be it domestic or foreign. People who are hungry do not concentrate on cultural advancements as long as there is not enough food. I simply want to underscore, Mr. Speaker, that it is an absolute shame that in a land such as Canada with the food producing capacity we have, with farmers who have the managerial skill, the technical know-how and the willingness to produce in this country, we find only this one bill being placed before us in the second session of the Thirtieth Parliament.
I think it is an incredible mistake that we have been so late in our history coming forward with some piece of legislation showing a federal initiative in terms of the protection of agricultural land. It is one thing to talk about advance crop payments but how can we have any crops at all if we don't have any soil to grow them on? The federal government for example, confiscated 88,000 acres for Mirabel Airport, and talks about confiscating land by the thousands of acres for an airport north of Toronto, all on prime agricultural land. The truth of the matter is that we will not even need an agriculture minister if we are going to wipe out the one resource that produces almost all are food. The fact of the matter is that he only needs to stay around to the year 2,030 at the rate of our present destruction and there won't be any soil, and we won't need him at all. That might be the only advantage attached to the rate at which we are destroying our own farmland.
I just want to underscore that while we don't find fault with the principle of Bill C-2 we have some serious questions to
October 29, 1976

I hope this sort of thing will not happen under Bill C-2. I hope changes will not be made unless they are announced well in advance. We all recognize that change must come from time to time, but I hope they will not occur in the sort of circumstances I have mentioned in which people face awkward and then uncomfortable situations. Indeed, Department of Agriculture officials at levels below the minister make rulings such as the one which denied purebred status to registered animals. I am not convinced that the minister is aware that that change took place. Yet that decision cost one farmer in my home province nearly $500,000 when his purebred herd was destroyed because it had brucellosis.
To turn to other aspects of Bill C-2, let me say that the advance payments program will not really encourage the production of crops in this country. As I said before, if we are to take our agricultural industry seriously and make it produce even more, we must sell our produce aggressively on the world market. If we do so, our farmers will produce as never before and make a good living. Our present system is less than satisfactory. The ups and downs of the market are often governed by the size of crops. When there is a scarcity, prices go up; but when there is an abundance of produce, as there is at present, it tends to depress the world market. This, in turn, tends to have a depressing effect on the farmer.
Advance payments will not provide the farmer with more money than he would earn from the sale of crops. They are simply an advance of the money he would earn, paid to him at an earlier date. The truth of the matter is that a man cannot operate in that kind of climate.
We on this side of the House are prepared to approve in principle Bill C-2, but we will want to have many details cleared up in committee, because some matters have yet to be specifically dealt with, one of them being consultation with other farm organizations. We shall want to know more about the mechanism through which advance payments will be paid. In other words, is there to be another bureaucracy established, or will the government allow the private sector, which already possesses the necessary organization and structure, to conduct this business?
I forewarn the minister that approval in principle by members on my side of Bill C-2, an act to facilitate the making of advance payments for crops, is by no means to be construed as an indication that we on this side of the House, or farmers across this country, will allow the government to become more involved in agriculture; and 1 am particularly referring to any supply-management system in respect of beef. In that regard 1 would like to respond to one of the answers the minister gave in this House in reply to a question by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga). I quote from page 147 of Hansard for October 18, 1976 where the Minister of Agriculture is reported as stating:
-it is obvious that the beef industry needs a supply-management program. It is obvious these producers cannot deal in the world free market under the present conditions and exist.
Advance Payments for Crops
If there has ever been an example of something in which lack of consultation has taken place, that has to be one of the clearest examples that could be placed before this House.
About two weeks ago, on two days' notice, 300 ranchers gathered in the city of Lethbridge to protest any intentions the minister might have in relation to a supply-management system. On October 22 of this year in the town of Stettler 800 ranchers gathered. They were attempting to disseminate across the four western provinces, on very short notice, a petition which we intend to table in this House. One of the main points of that petition is that we do not want a supply-management system in the beef industry.
1 hope the minister will soon recognize that any approval of Bill C-2 and the government's involvement with advance payments on grain is by no way a licence to consider that the Department of Agriculture can go forward and manage all parts of the agricultural sector.
The petition that will be circulated for a very brief period of time has caught on like wild-fire in my province. People from other provinces have started to telephone to see where they can get this petition. What they are saying is that they do not want a supply-management system for the beef industry. That underscores one of the real cautions that we must have with regard to government involvement in industry of any kind.
In the beef industry, there were 29 ad hoc short-term policy pronouncements in a two-year period. That surely is good reason to recognize why the industry is presently in trouble. If supply management is not working well in the poultry business, and not working well in the dairy business, and the minister should be well aware of that, surely it cannot be a program that will work well in the beef industry which operates on a three and one half to five year cycle.
Advance payment on crops is not nearly as important as increasing the amount of foodstuffs. That ought to have been within the programs and obligations of the Minister of Agriculture. His thrust in this legislation ought to have been to recognize the world need for food. In light of that recognition there should have been more than 48 words in the Speech from the Throne related to agriculture. There should be more than Bill C-2 coming before us to give us something that talks about a guarantee to farmers that, if they produce at their maximum, they will be justly rewarded for their production.
There is nothing more urgently needed in world society today than an increase in the amount of foodstuffs. It is abundantly clear that in a year like this, when there has been a surplus of grain and cereal grain production in Canada, one thing that is required is an assurance to farm people that this will not depress their prices. However, no sooner did they raise a bumper crop than the price began to plummet. That came at a time when the Anti-Inflation Board was holding all other people in this country to essentially a 10 per cent increase. However, this group of people, the most important people in our society, have to run the risks in the market place, not because the market is weak but because the Department of Agriculture is failing to sell their product abroad.

and, at best, to 17 million acres. The minister should realize it is not enough to bring in ad hoc or short-term policies, or policies that affect only one sector. We should have an over-all agricultural policy that would help meet the worldwide demand for food.
This bill falls far short of what is needed. It will give an advance payment to farmers, and I have no argument with that; but it does not take into consideration the increased crop production of this country. When we stop to consider that four-fifths of the world's population is suffering from malnutrition, and that every year there are 70 million more mouths to be fed, surely the minister should encourage farmers to produce to maximum capacity. I know he will make the response that our farmers are efficient and have increased their production faster than the non-farming sector of the country. Of course, I do not disagree with that. The minister makes good speeches in this regard. But the fact is this country is falling far short of its capacity.
This year we have abundant crops from the Atlantic to the Pacific. But the Soviet Union, Australia, America, and other major wheat producing countries also have abundant crops. It simply does not make sense, in a year of abundance, to depress prices or be discouraged about finding an outlet for our crops on the world market. The truth of the matter is that Canada's major failing is that it does not sell agricultural products abroad aggressively and forcefully. This country puts agricultural products on the shelf and hopes a buyer will come.
1 feel that the Department of Agriculture is under the important obligation of encouraging farmers to produce to the absolute maximum. The department should adopt the attitude that we can sell aggressively on the international market, that we cannot tolerate any longer people living in dire poverty. I challengt the minister, who I know will speak shortly because he wants to catch a flight away from here, to tell the House how he intends to sell food products abroad and how the performance of the agricultural industry, one of this country's major industries, compares with that, say, of the automotive industry.
Let us consider what is happening in the field of meat. We know that the meat industry is one of the three largest in Canada. It is a $3.5 billion industry in Canada, ranks second in the cost of materials used-it spends about $3 billion on materials-spends about $6 million a day on livestock, and employs nearly 33,000 people. Yet when you compare that industry with General Motors or any other industry of the same size, you note that its product is not being sold as aggressively on the markets of the world, markets which obviously have a tremendous need of food.
There is not even full consultation with our producer groups, with farm groups in this country. My colleague for Wetaski-win has justifiably said that there is no reason at all to seek the establishment, through Bill C-2, of a new organization or structure through which advance payments could be paid to farmers. There is no reason at all for any new bureaucracy.
[Mr. Malone.)
The necessary mechanisms already exist in the private sector in the form of banks which have the personnel for administering the program and for keeping records of transactions which take place. But the government must take the responsibility for the payments.
1 should like to underscore three things which ought not to happen as a result of the passage of Bill C-2. First, we feel that farmers do not need, as so often happens when the government passes a law, any extra burden of paperwork. When the government passed its anti-inflation program, one of the biggest complaints of small businessmen was that they were overburdened with paperwork. I hope that will not prove to be the case following passage of Bill C-2.
Second, and more importantly-I hope the minister will lend a careful ear-I hope the payments will not be late, as is traditional when payments of this kind are made through the Canadian Wheat Board.
One of the things that frustrates farmers is that they expect money to come in, but then realize that they can place no dependency on the federal government as to when the payments will be made. If we are to operate a really efficient agricultural industry in this country and maintain it as one of our largest industries, we must make such payments predictable. We must let the farm producer and manager have some clearly defined idea as to when these sorts of finances are to be made available. We must give our farm producers a sense of assurance; they must know that there is a guaranteed period within which advance payments will be made.
Third, if I may raise another point relating to what may happen after the passage of Bill C-2, I hope that this government or this minister will not, as has been traditional, permit a change of the rules in mid-stream. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) should make particularly sure that once the rules have been established they are not changed without due announcement.
1 will underscore my concern by relating an example which will show how the Department of Agriculture inflicted a tremendous injustice on certain people in this country by changing certain rules without notice. I am alluding to what happened within the health of animals branch in relation to cattle suffering from brucellosis and Bang's disease. At one time it was held that any animal termed as "registered" was considered a purebred. Then suddenly a case involving diseased cattle ended up in courts because the Department of Agriculture lawyers said that "registered" no longer meant "purebred" animals.
One farmer in my province who owned a purebred herd, a herd registered as sixteen-seventeenths Charolais, was not able to collect. He lost a $500,000 herd because a change had taken place without announcement. The final statement of the judge presiding in the trial was, "1 have done my duty; I have ruled in accordance with the law, but I do not believe 1 have done justice." That is how the judge felt about rules being changed without notice.

There are some questions about this bill, however, even though it has not done the damage we have witnessed in other legislation put before this parliament. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin noted that one of the very serious concerns we have about the bill is that it speaks about an "organization" being established to administer the funds in the advance payments for crops program, extending beyond the traditional Wheat Board system that has been the practice. No response has been forthcoming from the minister, but when we get into committee of the whole I hope he will recommend that we use the existing mechanisms of the banks and treasury branches, etc., to finance the program rather than establish a new bureaucracy.

We do not disagree with the bill in principle. One objection that we make most strongly, however, is that it is the only piece of legislation to flow from the Speech from the Throne. I think it is an insult not just to the Canadian people and not just to the Canadian farmer but to the whole world that there were only 48 words on the subject of agriculture in the Speech from the Throne. No greater problem faces humanity today than the need for food. We know that there are only two sources of food: one is soil and the other is water. Four-fifths of the world's population suffers from malnutrition. We know that 12,000 children each day die of starvation. This means that 12,000 died yesterday, today another 12,000 children died, and 12,000 will die tomorrow. That is the average death rate due to lack of food. That the Speech from the Throne devoted only 48 words to agriculture, and this is the only bill to be brought in as a result, is a shame, Mr. Speaker.
Previous speakers have mentioned the lack of consultation between the government and producers, and this fact cannot be underscored enough. The minister claims there has been consultation with various producer organizations, but he has not established which organizations were involved and investigations on this side of the House have not revealed any consultations. The organizations deny any consultation with the minister in regard to Bill C-2. Obviously, any consultation should come before the enactment of this bill into law, and not as an afterthought.
Clearly, this is the only bill affecting agriculture that will flow from the Speech from the Throne and, clearly, the minister has failed to recognize the serious problems affecting agriculture today. Where is the legislation in respect of soil conservation? The minister well knows that a promise was made to the provinces a decade ago that the federal government would undertake a soil mapping program. This was to establish and unify a soil classification program from coast to coast, indicating areas of rich and poor quality soil-but it has never been completed. The only classification that exists was done more than 30 years ago, so the promised program is long overdue. If we are to have a productive agricultural industry, one of the most important aspects is preservation of present agricultural land, but the minister has taken no steps to establish the promised soil classification and mapping program.
In 1978, Mr. Speaker, the International Soil Science Conference will bring some 3,000 soil scientists to Edmonton from all over the world. The last conference was held in Moscow. As these scientists look at what is happening to agriculture in Canada, they will realize that as a country we aregiot paying enough attention to this valuable resource. You cannot grow crops unless you have soil, Mr. Speaker. It is all very well for the minister to speak about advance payments for crops in Bill C-2, but he is missing the major point about what is happening in agriculture-that you cannot grow crops if the soil disappears.

The final difference is that whereas grain producers market their produce through the Canadian Wheat Board, there is no requirement in Bill C-2 that producers must market their crops through the organization. Presumably they are free, as they are today, to choose their own marketing channel. One wonders what is the purpose of setting up a number of producer groups if, first, they are not necessary to the act as a marketing channel and, second, the banks could perform the lending function more efficiently and more directly. When we look at the experience with cow-calf grants, we see that farmers in western Canada today go to their district agriculturalists to pick up a form which provides a government guarantee; then they go directly to the bank for the loan. This seems to be a very efficient manner of getting a grant or a loan, but under this proposal the farmer will have to belong to an organization. He gets word from the organization that he is eligible, and the organization then borrows the funds from the bank and turns them over to the producer.
Why involve the organization at all? It seems to me that an amendment could be proposed here to clarify the position and to make it much simpler by allowing the farmer to go to a bank, declare his interest, declare the amount of crop he has, provide the necessary security and get an advance with a government guarantee that if he fails to produce the crop there is some security beyond the collateral he has put up for his loan. So I question the whole procedure advocated in this bill. If in committee we are not satisfied with the answers to these questions, I think it would be logical to propose an amendment to make this a much simpler procedure.
In clause 5(A)(b)(i) of Bill C-2 there is mention of a named buyer. Does this mean that the individual producer must provide the details of the future sale of his crops in order to obtain an advance payment? If so, what would be the implications of this requirement? I have visions of a producer being forced to give the details of his sale well in advance of actually making that sale.
When we look at the case of rapeseed producers in western Canada, we see that many of them sign contracts in advance of seeding to supply to a crusher so many thousand bushels of rapeseed, and the price is set then. But we are talking here about many other commodities the future marketability and price of which we do not know. The price may fluctuate, and if producers tie themselves into a contract they could then get a very much lower price than if they allow the market to work as it will and take the best price possible for their commodities. This is where the advance payment comes in: it allows the farmer to hold on to his commodity until such a time as he can get the best price. But why put this clause in the bill whereby

producers must provide the details of their future sales by naming a so-called named buyer?
I must also express my disappointment about the fact that we have this mysterious term "organization" in the bill. Has the minister contacted these organizations and asked whether they are prepared to take this bill under their wing and set up the required mechanisms to put in place the advance payments to the farmers? I have been reading the farm journals and 1 have been talking to a number of organizations, and none of them has mentioned that they have been asked whether they are prepared to set up this type of arrangement.
As a westerner, 1 am very familiar with the problems of the prairie farm economy. By and large, these problems are the same as those which plague farmers right across Canada. While it is true that realized net income for Canadian farmers is up 8 per cent over last year, there is a continuous spiral in the cost of farm input-the costs of fertilizer, petroleum, electricity, operation and depreciation are up 15 per cent over last year-and this gives farmers little reason to be happy with their position.
We just heard from the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) that the situation in the export market does not look very bright this year. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) recently returned from the Soviet Union. He said there has been a tremendous crop in that country and that the Soviet Union may not be prepared to provide a market this year. This causes farmers some concern, because they have been getting reasonable prices for their grain for the last couple of years. This year there was a tremendous crop of high quality grain, but things do not look good with regard to a market. They are still faced with these high costs.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak on this bill today I welcome the proposed legislation because I think it provides greater equity between the Wheat Board area and the growers of crops who do not come under the Wheat Board. This legislation should help the rapeseed grower in particular because in the past he has been unable to get an advance on his crop since it did not come under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board.
One of the principal questions that has been asked by various members who have spoken on this legislation is about the mysterious wording in which it is couched, specifically the definition of the word "organization". The bill defines "organization" as an organization of producers, and that is as clear as it gets. I suspect that the organization to which the minister refers means such organizations as the Agricultural Federation of Canada, the Rapeseed Growers of Canada, and the potato associations in the various provinces. However, this is unclear.

1 suppose we will only get a clear definition of this word in the committee, unless the minister, in concluding the debate, clears up this matter.
It is probable that the producer groups which could gain the greatest benefit from these advance payments at present do not qualify because they do not belong to any organization. Let me refer, again, to the rapeseed growers in western Canada, many of whom do not belong to any organization. They grow rapeseed as a cash crop, a crop that has had a good quota in the past. As a result, if markets for this commodity decline, the only way in which they could qualify for an advance is by joining an organization.
Before this legislation becomes acceptable, a number of questions must be answered to satisfy the legitimate concerns of many of the farmers who will be affected. The first question is: If there is no existing organization and producers are forced to set one up in order to qualify for advance payments, who will cover the costs of the expenses incurred in setting it up? The second question is: Who will cover the administration expenses of such organizations? The third question is: What happens to the independent farmer, of whom we have many and who want no truck or trade with producer groups? Will he lose out because of his independent status? The fourth question that comes to mind is: What crops are really covered by this legislation? The bill states that root crops and other field crops will be covered, but I think it should be stated more specifically.
While there are similarities between Bill C-2 and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act of 1957, three major differences separate the two. The first is that the administration of advance payments for grain is carried out by only one organization, namely, the Canadian Wheat Board. Because a number of organizations will be entrusted with the implementation of Bill C-2, there is greater latitude for inequities and inefficiencies, in my view. The disparity in the size of the various organizations and the financial resources available to them are only two of the problems which they will be facing.
The second difference is that while the Canadian Wheat Board is not liable for advance payments made by it, the organizations expending advance payments under Bill C-2 will be liable. Although this liability amounts to only 10 per cent of the actual advance, it is a significant risk because many of these organizations are small. This risk may be particularly onerous for new organizations which will have to be set up to reap the benefits of this act. Yesterday's Globe and Mail reported the observation of the Anti-Inflation Board that food prices are going down. I think it can fairly be said that most of the decline resulted from prices at the farm gate and not, as has been suggested by the AIB, in the retailing and processing or distribution end of the business. For instance, the outlook for sales by the Wheat Board does not appear to be good. Certainly on the Chicago exchange the world traders indicate they feel that what they think should be the price of wheat has shown a drastic fall in the last year. Perhaps media sources and worldwide communications tend to exaggerate the effects of drought and natural disasters and the expectation that food sales and food exports will always continue to rise.
Indeed, with the anticipated rise in world oil prices in the immediate future we can anticipate that world trade in food products may drop. Certainly it can be said that the world can only consume the most that it has in its worst year. There are bound to be periods of surplus far into the future. Indeed, if there were not, it is obvious that many people would starve when the inevitable natural disasters reduce the world supply.
Exports of agricultural products are an important source of foreign exchange and have a great effect on the standard of living of Canadians. Generally speaking, we have exported more agricultural products than we have imported. This has not always been the case. Should world trade drop, we would find severe competition from American grain growers who seem to have increased their efficiency substantially more than the western Canadian farmers. The structure of the western grain industry, which provides nearly all the exportable surplus of food from this country, has changed substantially in the past eight years. Many people have left the farms, which means that productivity is dependent on greater use of machines. However, with the expected and, indeed, inevitable rise in farm costs both in respect of machinery and fuel there may well be a relatively greater rise in the cost of production in Canada than in some of the other exporting countries. Indeed, we hear a great deal about how much higher prices are in Canada than in the United States in respect of comparable commodities, both in relation to production and transportation. Agriculture is no exception. Certainly, our cost of produc-

tion and transportation will be higher than is the case in respect of our neighbour to the south.
Canadian agricultural policies in many instances appear to help denude the farms of manpower. It is true that farms are not as attractive for most people as are alternative jobs in towns, villages and cities. Many agricultural policies projected by the federal and provincial governments seem to have hurried the change-over from labour-intensive agriculture to capital-intensive agriculture. This has promoted the holding of larger farms and perhaps more immediate efficiency, but it also raises the question of whether or not this is important in relation to strong agricultural industry. Much of the efficiency of agriculture during the past 25 years can be attributed to relatively cheap oil and gas and the attendant input of fertilizer and herbicides made from oil and gas. With the projected rise in prices of these inputs, agriculture could face some rather severe adjustments and in the long run there could be relatively higher prices for food for the consumer.
I should like to turn to a few comments about our present agricultural policy which I think deserve attention. There is an editorial in the Western Producer of October 7 under the headline, "It's time to make changes in two-price wheat policy". This article points out that since 1973 Canadian millers have been buying wheat from the Wheat Board at S3.25 per bushel for Canadian consumption, with the difference being made up by the federal treasury when prices were between $4.75 and $5., and the farmers contributed to the program when world prices were above $5.
Now, wheat prices have dropped drastically. In September the selling price of No. 1 CW red spring wheat at Thunder Bay was $3.43, almost $2 less than a year ago. It seems likely that it will go even lower, given the amount of wheat on hand throughout the world. It is pointed out than an immediate review of this two-price system should be instituted. The Wheat Board has said it has sold large volumes of grain on international markets for future delivery, but it is not altogether clear whether this grain is in the hands of the importers or whether it has merely been sold to brokers and will have to be resold on world markets some time in the future.
Certainly, the farmers of western Canada face greatly reduced prices. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board has announced that he asked the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to ascertain what is the proper floor for wheat sold to Canadian millers, and that they stated they need cost-plus, and so on. I think it is important that this be done immediately.
1 would also like to point out what I think has prevented the sale of a considerable volume of Canadian barley abroad and has reduced the sale value of Canadian barley to the producers by perhaps $100 million, and which has perhaps prevented the increase of foreign currency by that amount. I refer to the policy in respect of barley sales into the eastern market. Order, please. 1 have the matter under very careful consideration. Regrettably, one of the most interesting aspects of the question so far as the Chair is concerned is this: it is a well recognized principle of the operations of the House that although members of the House have the right to put questions during the question period, there is no corresponding obligation to answer. The failure to answer, or the quality of an answer has been ruled as not being a ground for a question of privilege. The quality of an answer, the failure to answer, the quality of performance-or content, if that is the right description-which may lead to any continued failure to make an answer are matters of long-time political responsibility, not technical responsibility, under the procedures of the House.

If, therefore, there is no obligation to answer questions put, it is difficult to say that a mere attempt to answer on the part of a parliamentary secretary, acting minister or another acting in his stead is not an adequate response when no response is required by the rules. That, to me, is an interesting procedural aspect of the matter which was not raised in today's discussion. In any case, to get back to the procedural point raised by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), obviously it is a matter of great concern. The Chair must always recognize that there are occasions when the niceties of procedure simply do not enable the rules exactly to fit the kinds of tensions and difficulties that can arise from the practices of this House.
While the technical requirements of a question of privilege may not apply to this particular situation, it is like others that arise from time to time when the intense interest in the debate at least signals to us that we have an area of deep concern which touches all members of the House and raises great concern on both sides in respect of the rights of members to seek information through the question period, which all defend as not only a vigorous exercise but one that sets us apart in terms of quality from some other parliaments of the world, and one about which we can be justifiably proud. Certainly, all of us want to do everything possible to ensure that the question period in this House of Commons continues to have the vitality for which it is famous. Therefore, the points that have been raised and discussed so vigorously are not lost.
Whether there is a procedural answer to the problem is very difficult for me to say. However, I do say to the House that I have no obligation to carry on in this matter because there is no motion associated with it. I do want to assure the House that I will continue my interest in these remarks today to see whether some solution can be found in the near future to clarify the status of parliamentary secretaries in this regard.

Privilege-Mr. Diefenbaker
That is what the Standing Orders say. The reason the parliamentary secretary is singled out particularly with respect to the adjournment debate is that that was the place where the Procedure and Organization Committee, in advancing these rules in the context of the law as it existed-as explained by the right hon. member for Prince Albert-determined parliamentary secretaries could take part in that capacity. The committee, having singled that out, it is my respectful submission that the omission with respect to other responsibilities is very clear: they have no responsibilities in those other areas. Why ought they not to? The right hon. member for Prince Albert referred to that, and other members who will speak will refer to it. But there is a very good reason, Mr. Speaker. One of the more distinguished members of the House of Commons who told us why parliamentary secretaries have no responsibility is the present Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), at that time the hon. member for St. Paul's. On November 5, 1974, a question was raised in this House and the Secretary of State, who unfortunately is not here and perhaps could contribute to the further understanding of the point put forward by the government House Leader, said as reported at page 1062 of Hansard:
There is a difference between the position of a parliamentary secretary and that of a minister. Ministers are collectively responsible-
Not individually, as the government House Leader said, but collectively responsible.
-for the presentation of government policy and programs; they speak with many voices.
Of course, that is the problem with this government, Mr. Speaker; it speaks with many voices. He went on to say: Parliamentary secretaries are not part of the government; they are not part of the collective responsibility of the government; they are not bound by the obligation to speak with a common voice, as are members of the cabinet. Governmental responsibility, in so far as it exists, exists within the confines of the responsibilities of the minister whose parliamentary secretary one is. Outside the bounds of that responsibility the parliamentary secretary does not participate, nor does he have special access to the decision-making process of government.

I watched him all during the debate on capital punishment when he did not have too much concern for the minority on that committee. As recorded at page 25 of the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee proceedings on June 22 last, the Solicitor General said this:

The part that scares us as an opposition party, Mr. Speaker, is that the Solicitor General felt this way just a few months ago about closing off the debate on capital punishment. Because of the shortness of time that he has allowed for this committee, we are hoping that the members on his side will not sit on that committee with the attitude that they have the majority and they will do what they want. The government has not solved the penitentiaries problem. 1 have only been in this House four years, Mr. Speaker, but the problems have been getting worse. None of the programs the government has set up have helped at all.
The British Columbia Penitentiary is in total chaos right now. The Solicitor General says that it is going to close down in 1979, yet he is willing to approve $1.5 million to repair the damage the inmates have done. I have not heard the Solicitor General say that perhaps the inmates who did that damage inside the institution should form the labour force that puts it back together, or that they can stay in the gymnasium until the government is ready to replace that penitentiary. I do not know why we have to feel sorry for people who bust their penal institution down to the ground and then complain that the living conditions in the gymnasium are not so good.
1 think it is time that the government took a tough line with inmates inside our maximum security institutions. We do take a fairly tough line inside our medium and minimum security institutions. We have very tough rules there and, if they are broken, prisoners are sent back to a maximum security institution. In most of the medium and minimum institutions I have visited in this country everything runs fairly smoothly because there is some sense of law and order inside the institutions. It is in our maximum security institutions that the administration and the classification sections have taken a very soft attitude toward the very vicious people who are inside them. In the B.C. penitentiary the authorities went out of their way to make the institution a better place to live. Then, after a couple of million dollars worth of improvements, the inmates tear the place down. This is the sort of problem that this committee will have to face, Mr. Speaker, and hopefully come up with some recommendations that will be acceptable to the government.
I want to stress that the Conservative party did have its committee set up ready to investigate penitentiaries. If we are not satisfied at the end of this committee hearing, or if the government tries to close off the hearing before the reports are

ready to be made, or if we feel we are not getting to see the people we went to see, or that we are not able to spend the amount of time with them that we want to spend, we will continue our own task force. It is our right as members of parliament to visit penitentiaries in this country.
Hear, hear!

I have before me a copy of a report that was sent to the former Solicitor General by the late hon. member for Louis-Hebert, Mrs. Morin, who served on the last committee, and I must say that her presence in this House is sorely missed. She was very concerned about this problem and I have the reports which she completed after the last investigation.
Most of the reports of the hon. lady are very condemnatory of the government, and sometimes I wonder whether that is not one of the reasons why the reports were never made public. There was a list of proposed recommendations contained in the report of the penitentiaries sub-committee made at this time, which would have been 1974. These recommendations called for tight perimeter security coupled with optimal internal conditions, and very little has been done in this regard in the penitentiaires about which I have been talking.
Another recommendation is decentralization of the penitentiary service structure, and that has not taken place yet, Mr. Speaker. Another is an eight hour day and salaries for inmates, something which perhaps we will have to examine in our maximum security institutions to keep the inmates busy for some time of the day, instead of locking them up in their cells for 24 hours a day. The recommendations also called for the upgrading in quality of prison staff, and obviously called as well for an urgrading of their salaries. I know this is one of the problems in British Columbia where the sheriffs department working at Oakalla are making more money than federal penitentiary guards. That has to change.

He is new at his job and maybe it took him a few days to get through the bureaucracy before taking the action necessary to set up the committee.
Members who were here in 1972-73 may recall that I proposed a motion in the House that a committee be set up to investigate the question of the security of our penitentiaries. I brought the subject up under Standing Order 26, and a motion was put forward by agreement later that day which resulted in a committee being established to investigate penitentiaries. Members from all parties were represented on that committee. They investigated penitentiaries for more than a year-I do not know with what result, because it does not appear we are getting anywhere with the operation of the penitentiary system right now. But they spent a year going back and forth across the country visiting penitentiaries, coming up with ideas and making recommendations. Unfortunately I do not have the time tonight to discuss the reports in detail, those I managed to get my hands on. I might add that those reports were never formally presented in the House of Commons; the results of their findings were never published.
Anyway, they took a year to do this work, yet the Solicitor General is now asking us to come up with a report by February 28. I really think he must be looking for some kind of report which will cover up what is really going on if he expects us to produce a report so quickly. Nevertheless, I hope we shall receive co-operation from members on the government side of the House and an understanding that if we do not finish our investigation by the date which has been proposed we shall be allowed to continue until the work has been done. It is time we looked closely into the situation and produced positive solutions on a non-partisan basis. I say this because there are problems in the system which we simply must solve and we cannot do so if we sit on a committee on a partisan basis, trying maybe to cover up mistakes in the ministry or in the bureaucracy.
It is our duty to get the facts and come up with solutions, and we in the opposition parties must make sure that those solutions are presented before the government loses power in the next election, and make it known that we support the action which has to be taken and that we approve the expendi-

I want to show that things really have not changed since that committee was set up in 1973. The members of that committee said the entire system was in disarray. I quote:
Guards did not seem to understand Ottawa's aims where detention and possible rehabilitation of inmates were concerned.
A recommendation was made along this line at the time to initiate regular meetings between administration and guards to increase their awareness of the objectives of the system. Has this been done? Are guards and administration communicating, and is the administration more aware of the action of the guards than it was in 1973? One member of the committee noted that within our women's prisons there was no program of work or rehabilitation. A further observation urged the Department of the Solicitor General to implement a training program which would encourage inmates to rehabilitate themselves. Has this recommendation been carried out?
It is unfortunate that the recommendations of the committee back in 1973 were not listened to by the government. This makes one wonder whether the committee now proposed will really work. Despite the many committees and commissions which have been set up to investigate in this field,-I have in mind the B.C. Penitentiary riots and the Steinhauser affair- nothing seems to have been done. I myself, as a member of the House, have spent a lot of time visiting penitentiaries, talking to all sides. One of the frustrations which visitors to these institutions encounter is this; the people who work there say they have read all these reports and are aware that nothing has been done about them.
Further in the report by the committee which investigated the situation in 1973, we read that it was no secret then, as it is no secret now, that access to drugs in prison is too easy. One observation was: "In prison there seems to be no problem about obtaining drugs." Apparently the administration accepted this situation because of the pacifying effect on inmates. If you encourage drugs in institutions you are encouraging people who are lowly paid on the scale to smuggle drugs into the institutions. You are encouraging friends of the underworld who are visiting inmates to bring them into the institution.

Communication as we all know is a binding force-whether it is in the home between members of a family; whether it is in trade unions at the bargaining table; whether it is in a nation of two or more cultures, actually a source of our intellectual and sociological richness.
But conversely, lack of communication can be suicide; destructive of family, of unions and their health, and of Canada. I pray and hope for your prayers with me that we will communicate, that we will stop hating, stop committing national suicide.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank hon. members for allowing me the courtesy of speaking for the next 15 minutes and winding up this debate. One was the Anti-Inflation Board. She had a lot of ideas, and she knocked the NDP, but what I was wondering, when I was thinking of that protest day coming up, was whether we would not have done better as an opposition- and this applies too to members on the government side-if we had advised the workers that they might have been better off staying on the job that day and protesting by donating a day's salary to the opposition parties in the federal parliament to help defeat the Liberal government which is causing the whole problem.
They would donate it to the NDP.
