They already donate to the NDP.

Well, I get elected by a big majority in my riding where a lot of the electors are working people who did not want to take a day off on that day. I know they liked the idea of donating a day's pay to the political system, and the irony of this situation is that if they did devote a day's pay toward defeating the government which is causing the problems in this country, the government would have been obliged to return 75 per cent of their donations in tax credit.
The members of the opposition ought to give one day's pay and show an example.

I believe a number of people did donate a day's pay. The Premier of British Columbia made it very plain he had donated a day's salary, and I think it was a very good example to the working people of our province. I remember when the teachers of British Columbia wanted to replace a provincial government which they did not like. They donated a day's pay to help defeat the government, and they certainly did defeat it. I do not know what the end result was; I think most of them were back voting for the former government eventual-

for an ouster of the executive but could not get a seconder for the motion because of fear or threats.
The night of October 13 a call came to my Ottawa office from a busdriver who told me that the British Columbia Federation of Labour intended to mount pickets to stop the drivers, and if the drivers tried to move the buses there would be bloodshed. The caller said, "I intended to go to work Thursday, it is my right to work. We voted and I will be there." There was a pause, and then he said, "Mrs. Holt, who will look after my family after this is all over?"
The Liberal government.
If you people did something positive once instead of tearing the whole of our society apart, we could all live in peace.
Hear, hear!
I lived in your kind of society-an NDP society-for three years. It was bankrupt, it was sick, and it was evil.
Oh, oh!

I will put that aside for a moment to discuss what might be done to correct the incessant industrial paralysis. I would like a little more time to tell hon. members about a process called "Med-Ar" and a man named Sam Kagel, a leading western American lawyer who specializes in labour relations. Sam Kagel is a legend in the west. I called him the other day to ask him to share his wisdom in dealing with labor strife in Canada. I would like to say what he told me, but I will have to save it for another time since there is another subject that is very important that I think should be discussed. I refer to my concern for Canadian unity.
I feel compelled tonight to deal with the unity of Canada and the suicide course we are on as a nation because we will not understand. Perhaps we are not listening and will not communicate. Many Canadians are uneasy. They are angry because we are making judgments about fellow Canadians without knowing them, and without full knowledge of what it is all about.
Racism is rampant in Canada and it is alive and thriving in this very House of Commons. I hate to say that. This place where we know each other, were we want to understand the great differences that we share in our representation of 264 constituencies, where we are the microcosm of the disparities and the richness of cultural and regional variations, we should be engaged in mending and melding this country.
And I plead with the Fourth Estate up there to use their important communications service to play a positive role-not the game of provocation a few are engaged in-to save the unity of Canada.

sanctions, pickets, accusations of scab for all who worked that day, and all the devices of the most heinous strike were used, it is strike. It was a deliberate attempt to debilitate, if not tear down the economy of Canada.
The claim was that it was to fight inflation, but the leader of the Canadian Labour Congress, in an address to the trade union congress in Britain told them that really was not the reason; that he wanted the power of the tripartite, that new huge bureaucracy in which he would play a major role in running the economy and the social structures of Canada. It was a great lie, and the workers of Canada were forced to lose a day's pay by intimidation, threat and fear, for this man's power trip.
It was a mischievous and immature act. Perhaps the NDP might know the real reasons since they shared in the conspiracy. Many could perceive it as a conspiracy of subversion to manipulate and force 2.5 million good and responsible citizens, who belong to the Canadian trade union movement, to participate in a project with one goal-a despicable goal-to damage Canada's delicate economy.
October 14 may have had a positive backlash that the CLC, the NDP, and those other few in the plan did not anticipate. The rank and file trade unionists are angry-angry at their loss of freedom-angry at their lost wages, without having a right to vote on the matter. It was a strike with all the goon and bully-boy techniques.
It was rather interesting that the vice president of the CLC called October 14 "Labour's finest hour". God help the mass of people in the trade union movement if things ever get bad and this is the best their leaders can do. I would have thought a more accurate description would be "the nation's greatest industrial abortion".
To enlarge this point: thousands of trade unionists, well aware of the threat to their job opportunities in the future and threats to their very lives and the lives of their families, treated it as an enforced holiday; tens of thousands were deprived of their salaries; not only was there no secret ballot for many but in some cases-and, Mr. Speaker, I can prove this and I am ready to go to court if I am required to-they actually had their ballots torn up by International Woodworkers of America leaders. Is this what they call their finest hour?
There are about 30,000 International Woodworkers of America in British Columbia. They did not get a vote. They were told they must stay off work because their leaders had made the decision. Even with that and with British Columbia being the most militant trade union province in Canada, and Vancouver its front line of militancy, the turnout for this demonstration was 7,000, by a generous estimate.
This might interest those who participated so excitedly in this demonstration: that 7,000 represented half the numbers of buttons I gave out to trade unionists who wanted to go to work. The button said: "I'm going to work for Canada today".
Even more interesting is the composition of the demonstrators-the CLC in the lead, then the communists, Trotskyites, the Maoists, and then the Gay Liberation Alliance! The first

groups were together with one cause-disruption of the economy-on the pretext of fighting anti-inflation controls. Hon. members who served on the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and heard witnesses for the Gay Liberation Alliance, learned then what controls they wanted removed- controls over their sexual freedom, and the age limit for their sexual partners lowered to 16, as I recall. Thus, to build statistics the CLC and the NDP who were part of it-certainly in the west and here-embraced the Gay Liberation pickets, backed by the NDP-allegedly to fight controls. What controls were they fighting, Mr. Speaker?
In that "finest hour" the CLC had to rent pickets on the prairies. When asked if he would have done it without pay, one of these hired mercenaries in the CLC war on Canada, smiled wryly and said, "I don't think so".
On Parliament Hill newspaper reporters could have counted the demonstrators as easily as we and the police did. The count was 700. The Globe and Mail, that great newspaper of record, reported 1,800 on Parliament Hill, and headlined that 1,035,445 participated in the protest. If they were 200 per cent wrong on the Parliament Hill statistics, then we can gauge their accuracy on the other figures, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

I want to tell one story as an example of the determination of the CLC to stop the workers in Vancouver and possibly throughout Canada. It was an attempt to disrupt transportation in order to keep people from their jobs. The details of the story poured out in my constituency office. It began with one bus driver who came in to get some of the buttons I was giving out, for a group of drivers who were revolting against the executive decision to stop the buses. The stoppage was based on a vote of 69 out of 3,000 members; the membership had not been advised in advance of this June vote.
The drivers posted a petition on the bulletin board near the end of September demanding a full membership right to vote to reverse the decision of the executive. A union official ripped it off the bulletin board. The drivers then circulated it by hand and called a meeting for October 4 because of the massive response. At that meeting all attempts to persuade them to support the executive strike plan failed. Those opposed to the executive were ordered to stand on one side of the room and those who supported the strike on the other. It was deliberate intimidation. But, Mr. Speaker, those wearing my buttons stood together. Suddenly others donned their buttons in protest against this technique, and joined them.
The executive then demanded a referendum for 4 days later-Friday, October 8, because they were not satisfied. Even though they got their troops out, there again an overwhelming majority opposed the executive strike order. The executive would not tell the public or the press the result but I will tell the public and the press, Mr. Speaker. It was a vote of 1,485 to 460 in favour of working that day. The executive is refusing to reveal the results because it was a vote of non-confidence in the leadership. The members tried to get a seconder

I would also like to congratulate the seconder, the hon. member for Lafontaine-Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), our youngest member, who gives all of us who are older such pride and joy in his intellectual insight and diplomatic skills, a promise of great service to Canada, beyond measure at this time.

The Address-Mrs. Holt
government succeeded in doing what the NDP failed to do. Even with labour's excessive demands, and the NDP support of these demands, they failed. The controls increased the actual purchasing power of the dollar 3 per cent, and thus increased the real worth of salaries. So perhaps it is time members of the NDP started worrying about the real truth and about the rank and file of the trade union movement, about whom they seem not to care one whit.
Hon. members of the NDP talk and hide behind the skirts of the old, the poor and the worker, but they would not go and pick one of them-a hungry person fallen on the street or save the threatened worker from the Joe Morrises and his ilk.
Hear, hear!

However, to come to the essence of my response to the throne speech, the mood and forces within our huge and disparate land are such that they could even now solidify confederation or tear it apart. Two major factors which affect Canada's future, whether we commit national suicide or whether we pull together, are the essence of what I want to speak about tonight.
We have only one choice, and that is to use our differences as a blend for the greatness, beauty, enrichment, and to continue the building of a strong and unified Canada-this wonderful, wonderful land that so many of us have shared in building, as did our parents and forefathers of many cultures, including the two founding cultures.
One of the two forces that could disrupt confederation is the unreasoning anger and intransigence, born of misunderstanding on both sides of the official languages debate; the other is the senseless strikes in which a few leaders have recklessly, and perhaps deliberately, deprived tens of thousands of workers of their democratic right, the choice to work. You people over there can answer for that. The other day I tried to bring in a motion in this House to protect the rank and file from the threats, intimidation, to give them a free vote in making decisions governing their economic well-being-to give them the same freedom we expect for all our citizens in our democratic society. The only voice opposed was the so-called "people's friend" over there, the NDP. Everyone else in this House agreed that protection of the freedom and the very safety of the rank and file trade unionists was vital.
Today the strike is a needless tool. When the founders of the great institution of collective bargaining risked their jobs and careers, it was important; but today, if both sides negotiate in good faith, they know they can get a contract. They know they do not have to go out on strike and that even if they do strike they must eventually return to the bargaining table. That is where it is settled.
1 think the most shocking example of the abuse of the strike tool and also the exploitation of rank and file trade unionists, was the October 14 attempt by the Canadian Labour Congress to mount a national general strike. Another study conducted in California involved placing nineteen hyperactive children on the special diet for a period of two to three months. This particular study revealed a significant difference between pre-test and post-test population means. No significant changes were noted by teachers' evaluation.
The validity of these findings is questionable, and has been criticized for the lack of adequate control for dietary intervention and the introduction of numerous biases. These biases occurred by exposing the parents and children to the anticipated outcome of the study at the beginning, by rewarding children for staying on the diet, and by sending an informative letter to teachers reflecting what beneficial effects may be expected.
Perhaps the most significant of all studies is that conducted by a team at the University of Wisconsin. This research, funded by the Food Research Institute of the University of Wisconsin, Madison, represents the first systematic investigation of the hyperactivity-food additive hypothesis. It includes objective psychologic, psychophysiologic and classroom observational data in addition to parent and teacher ratings of behavioural change associated with dietary manipulations. The study was designed in such a way that teachers, parents, clinical investigators and classroom and laboratory observers of the children's activity level were unaware throughout the course of the investigation whether the child was on the special diet or on a diet containing artificial colours and flavours. Both the experimental and control menus were prepared from commercially available food stocks.
Available results indicate that of the 36 mothers with boys in the 6-12 year group, 13 rated their son's behaviour as improved on the special diet, while six rated their child's behaviour as worsened. Of the 30 fathers rating the behaviour of this same age group, 14 rated their son as improved, three as worsened and 13 essentially unchanged. In comparison to the parent ratings, classroom teacher ratings showed a marked decline in the frequency of judgement of behavioural improvement during the experimental diet period. Only six of the teachers rated the child as less hyperactive, 10 rated the child as showing more active behaviour while on the experimental diet, which is supposed to improve the child, and 30 of the teacher ratings showed little change between the two diet conditions. Agreement between parent and teacher ratings of improved behaviour while on the experimental diet occurred in only four of the 36 children.
The observational data collected on a number of behaviours in the classroom and in a standardized laboratory task yielded very few ratings of improvement in association with the experimental diet. Preliminary statistical analysis of these data has been completed and no-I repeat, Mr. Speaker, no-statistically significant diet effect was apparent.
The younger children aged 3 to 6, however, showed a greater positive response on the experimental diet as indicated by parent rating. All 10 mothers in this group rated their child's behaviour as improved, as did four of the seven fathers in this sample.
Artificial Food Additives
Thus with the possible exception of the youngest age sample, the preliminary analysis completed to date in the Wisconsin study does not appear to offer strong support for the efficacy of the experimental diet, at least with respect to group effects. The University of Wisconsin research team, however, has repeatedly emphasized the still incomplete status of their project, saying that a number of the objective measures obtained on the subject have not yet been tabulated.
A research proposal was submitted to the food and drug administration of the U.S.A. by Dr. Leon S. Otis, of Stanford University, requesting funds to study development of behavioural aspects of food additives on mice and rats. This proposal has not been funded to date. Members of the National Institute of Mental Health in the U.S.A. and Dr. Frank Cordle of the U.S.A. food and drug administration are not aware of any related studies being conducted at Stanford University. Dr. Cordle is familiar with all interagency funding in the U.S.A.
A study was recently conducted in Canada at the University of Western Ontario to determine the relative effectiveness of dietary and drug management of hyperkinesis. Preliminary findings suggest that the effect of diet was ambiguous. Parents and teachers were of the opinion that dietary infractions involving artificial food colours and flavourings had minimal and insignificant effects.
The aforementioned studies conducted to date clearly indicate the potential difficulties in any attempt to test the food additive-hyperactivity hypothesis. The small sample size used reduces the significance of all findings and makes the use of statistical analysis extremely difficult. Furthermore, the use of outpatients in all these projects makes difficult the control of compliance. Also, specificity of responsiveness must be studied by challenging subjects with individual groups of substances such as artificial colour or flavours or salicylates. Finally, results are meaningless if strict adherence to guidelines is not preserved throughout the entire duration of an experiment.
Several other studies currently under way have been funded by the U.S. food and drug administration. These include a study on the hyperkinetic syndrome in children, being conducted at the Kaiser Permanent Foundation Research Institute in California. The study should be complete in about one year. A second study at the University of Wisconsin is designed to identify children who respond to the K-P diet.

Arrowroot biscuits, perhaps 1 might say a word, One thing which is quite clear is that there are not any additives in Arrowroot biscuits which produce hyperactivity or anti-social behaviour. Certainly there cannot be any red dye in Arrowroot biscuits.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take only a moment or two to congratulate the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) for introducing this motion.
I would point out that in the city of Vernon, B.C., in my constituency, on October 1 an international conference on hyperactivity was held. The conference started off in a small way. A maximum of 500 people were expected. Before the
opening evening it was found that the demand was much greater and space had to be added for an extra 100 people. I am sorry the hon. member was not able to develop his thesis on the relationship between food additives and hyperactivity to the extent I would have liked him to do. I particularly would have liked to have heard him develop the thesis of Dr. Feingold, although the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) dealt with that.
